Star Trek actor Walter Koenig, who played Pavel Chekov, dies aged 90

BBC News Mon, 26 Oct 2026 18:34:15 GMT

Walter Koenig, who played the spirited Russian crewman Pavel Chekov in the original Star Trek TV series, has died aged 90.

The US actor was a mainstay on the show as the eager and earnest navigator of the Starship Enterprise from season two in 1967 until it ended in 1969, later reprising his role in the six original cast movies from 1979 through to 1991.

In the mid-late 1990s, Koenig portrayed a very different character, the ruthless Psi Corps telepath Alfred Bester, in another sci-fi space series, Babylon 5.

His Star Trek co-star George Takei led the tributes on social media on Monday, writing: "Walter was more than Chekov. He was a writer, a teacher, a thoughtful man, and a loyal friend."

Koenig's Chekov added heart and humour to the adventures of the crew, led by William Shatner as Captain James T. Kirk.

Takei, who played Hikaru Sulu, added: "Rest well, my dear friend. Keep navigating a steady course."

Representatives for Koenig said in a statement given to the BBC: "Today we mourn the passing of Walter Koenig, whose talent, warmth, and unforgettable performances left a lasting mark on generations of fans around the world."

They confirmed he had died "of old age at home in North Hollywood" on Sunday night, "surrounded by his daughter and niece".

Born in Chicago and raised in Manhattan, Koenig was the son of Soviet Jewish immigrants whose family had lived in Lithuania.

He studied at the famous Neighborhood Playhouse School of the Theatre in New York, alongside the likes of James Caan, Christopher Lloyd and Dabney Coleman.

His big break came as the capable young Chekov, who would often joke that everything was invented in Russia.

The character was introduced to appeal to younger audiences, with his Monkees-style mop-top haircut.

But Star Trek creator Gene Roddenberry's studio also publicised the role as a response to reported criticism in Pravda, the main newspaper of the Soviet Communist Party, about the lack of a Russian character. This was a claim Koenig later denied.

The American show, which aired during the Cold War and Space Race between the US and Soviet Union, imagined a future in which nations worked together to explore the galaxy, and Chekov's Russian heritage fitted that ideal.

Koenig once said that the character's purpose on the NBC show was to "set out the bones of the plot and let McCoy, Spock and [William Shatner's Captain] Kirk fill it in", according to the Hollywood Reporter.

He was arguably more integral to the plot of the movies, being nominated by the Academy of Science Fiction, Fantasy & Horror for his work on The Wrath of Khan (1982) and The Voyage Home (1986).

His seventh Star Trek film appearance was a brief one in Generations (1994) - mainly a next generation film - and he later voiced President Anton Chekov in Star Trek: Picard in 2023.

He also wrote an episode for the original show's animated spin-off.

A published author, Koenig's other on-screen credits included Columbo and Futurama.

Earlier this year, his performance in the short film Mr Fleischmann saw him collect the Platinum Award for best actor at the 2026 Independent Shorts Awards, in recognition of his craft and career.

He married Judy Levitt, who appeared with him in three Star Trek movies and Michael Straczynski's futuristic space opera Babylon 5, in 1965. And they were together until her death in 2022.

The family suffered a personal tragedy in 2010, when their son Andrew, who played Richard "Boner" Stabone on the ABC sitcom Growing Pains, died by suicide aged 41.

Koenig is survived by their daughter, the actress and screenwriter Danielle Koenig, who worked on the animated series Star vs. the Forces of Evil.

Keir Starmer's government discussed moving out of 10 Downing Street

BBC News Mon, 26 Oct 2026 18:33:31 GMT

Sir Keir Starmer's government discussed moving out of Downing Street because of concerns about its suitability as a workplace, senior figures from his administration have said.

Ministers and officials from successive governments have privately complained that Number 10's rabbit warren-like layout can lead to a lack of collaboration among those working there.

James Lyons, who served as Sir Keir's director of communications, said over the weekend that "moving out was something that was discussed" during his time in post.

Two other senior figures confirmed that discussions were had about moving staff into an open plan space in another government department.

One source said a space inside the Foreign Office building, a short distance from Downing Street, had been identified.

Both stressed that discussions did not go beyond an early phase and it's not known whether Sir Keir himself was consulted.

There's no suggestion that the prime minister would have stopped living in Downing Street if the plan had gone forward.

10 Downing Street is more than 300 years old and is an amalgamation of three houses, which comprises more than 100 rooms.

The building was given to Robert Walpole, widely regarded as the UK's first prime minister, by King George III in 1732.

Lord Walker, the boss of supermarket Iceland and a former adviser to Sir Keir, told the Financial Times on Friday that Number 10 was no longer "fit for purpose".

He said: "I think we should turn it into residences, or a museum. It's a national treasure. It's amazing. But it's ridiculous.

"It's just a Stuart-era building, not fit for purpose. It has tiny, tiny meeting rooms, all on different levels. There are hazards."

Lyons, who led Sir Keir's communications operation from October 2024 to September 2025, posted on LinkedIn that "Lord Walker is 100% right".

He added that staff were "deeply envious" of other departments and described Number 10 as a "gloomy, mice-infested, bomb-curtained rabbit warren".

Lyons added: "Moving out was something that was discussed when I was in 10 Downing Street."

One source said "there were chats at senior staff level about moving to an open plan office in FCDO" (Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office).

They said they didn't believe the idea went far, but said "the reason for discussion was serious" and added that the alternative plan was "about staff being open plan and able to collaborate".

Sir Keir became increasingly frustrated at Whitehall's ability to deliver change during his time as prime minister.

He was accused of picking a fight with civil servants when he said "too many people in Whitehall are comfortable in the tepid bath of managed decline".

Darren Jones, who served as Sir Keir's chief secretary, told MPs last week that he "tried to abolish the Cabinet Office three times but failed".

He proposed replacing it with a new department that would "abolish those barriers and walls and make them just one integrated team, focusing on the same things and really supporting each other to move it forward".

In his first days after succeeding Sir Keir, Andy Burnham created the Office for the Prime Minister and Cabinet.

The move was seen as an attempt to ensure that things happen when metaphorical levers of power are pulled.

It comprises Number 10, Number 10 North and other key parts of the Cabinet Office and is led by the UK's most senior civil servant, Dame Antonia Romeo.

The government says the new office will "ensure the centre of government is focused on our top strategic priorities".

Those around Burnham say he is yet to form a view about the adequacy of Number 10 as a workplace.

England-Republic of Ireland U15 World Cup game ends over alleged racism

BBC News Mon, 26 Oct 2026 18:17:25 GMT

England players gathered at the side of the pitch after the alleged incident

England walked off the pitch during a match at the Under-15 World Cup after an allegation of racism by a Republic of Ireland player, which resulted in the game being abandoned.

Following an altercation between players from both sides, shortly before the end of the match in Azerbaijan on Monday, an England player approached his bench and made a complaint to coaching staff.

Match footage then showed England staff members relaying the complaint to the referee, alleging a racist slur had been said, and calling their players off.

The Republic of Ireland were leading 4-1 at the time of the incident.

World governing body Fifa told BBC Sport it is investigating and gathering reports.

"Fifa is aware of an incident at the U-15 World Cup and Festival match between England and the Republic of Ireland," a spokesperson said.

"The match was abandoned by the referee following England's refusal to continue.

"The official reports are being gathered, and the matter will be referred to the independent disciplinary committee, who will decide in due course."

The Football Association (FA) told BBC Sport it is awaiting more information and was in touch with Fifa, adding the wellbeing of players is a priority.

The Football Association of Ireland (FAI) has also been contacted for comment.

The alleged incident happened in the final minute of the Group C match in Baku.

Immediately following the allegation, England head coach Matt Thorpe was seen on the match coverage on DAZN asking for the referee to come over, before calling his players off the pitch.

After an initial report from Thorpe, the referee told England's coaching staff, "I cannot hear".

One of Thorpe's assistant coaches can then be heard telling the referee "we are reporting racism", before adding "we do not want to play".

When another official came over, talking about what would happen after the match, the assistant told him: "No, our players do not want to play".

He was later heard saying that a player was "upset".

Heated words were then exchanged between each set of coaching staff, with both saying they were trying to protect their players.

This is the first time the U15 World Cup and Festival has been played, and involves 189 countries and territories.

Matches are played in an eight-a-side format, on smaller pitches, with 20-minute halves.

England are scheduled to play their next match against Zimbabwe at 20:45 local time (16:45 GMT) on Monday, with Republic of Ireland facing Cambodia at the same time.

Kane prematurely announced as Ballon d'Or winner - but he wasn't only one

BBC News Mon, 26 Oct 2026 18:10:26 GMT

Harry Kane could become the first Englishman since 2001 to win the Ballon d'Or

For a moment, it seemed as though Harry Kane's dreams of winning the Ballon d'Or had come true.

It was shortly after 17:15 GMT on Monday when an article from the award's official website titled "Harry Kane wins the 2026 Ballon d'Or" began to circulate online.

It was more than four and a half hours before the winner of the game's most prestigious individual award was due to be announced at a star-studded event at London's Palladium Theatre.

The widespread sharing of the article caused confusion online, with some wondering whether France Football - the organisers of the award - had fallen short at the final hurdle of keeping the winner, who was voted for by journalists at the end of September, under wraps.

That was until further digging on the Ballon d'Or website revealed that some of the other favourites to win the award - including Barcelona's Lamine Yamal, Real Madrid's Kylian Mbappe - had also had similar pieces penned and published about them.

When asked about the articles by BBC Sport, a Ballon d'Or spokesperson said: "Some profiles of nominees prepared by BallonDor. com were inadvertently published online.

"These articles had been prepared for all nominees and should in no way be considered as an indication of the final results or rankings"

Just before 17:40 BST, the articles about Kane and Mbappe had been removed from the website.

Similar articles were also written about London City Lionesses star Alexia Putellas and Barcelona's Ewa Pajor, who are two of the favourites for the corresponding women's award, also taking place on Monday night.

If Kane is to realise his dream and become the first Englishman to win the award since 2001, he will have to wait a little longer to find out.

Tributes paid to man killed by falling tree in Storm Boelo

BBC News Mon, 26 Oct 2026 18:03:53 GMT

Tributes have been paid to a man who died after being hit by a falling tree in Dumfries and Galloway.

Richard Baines, 60, the long-serving curator of Logan Botanic Garden near Stranraer, died during Storm Boelo on Sunday morning.

It is understood that he was walking near his home in Mid Kelton, just outside Castle Douglas, when the accident happened.

David Knott, director of horticulture at the Royal Botanic Garden in Edinburgh, said they were "desperately sad, devastated" by the news.

"He had a warmth, a genuine sense of humour, he always made time for individuals and that's one of the tributes that has been said many times this morning," Knott told BBC Scotland News.

"He always found time for his colleagues. And he was always very supportive in providing opportunities for the next generation of horticulturalists. He was a very genuine and warm human being."

Logan Botanic Garden is home to a range of exotic plants as it benefits from the warming influence of the Gulf Stream. It is one of four Scottish gardens run by the Royal Botanic Garden in Edinburgh.

Knott said Baines came up with the description of Logan as "Scotland's most exotic garden" and worked hard to promote both the garden and the south-west of Scotland.

Knott said his colleague would be remembered for his "passion and enthusiasm for plants" and for significantly expanding the plant collection at Logan.

During his tenure, he was primarily responsible for significant developments including the first public conservatory to be powered by green energy in the UK.

Baines also participated and led fieldwork in China, the Canary Islands and Vietnam, from where seven plant species new to science were catalogued.

"Richard's contribution as an enthusiastic plantsman and curator at Logan and to the Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh's wider work and culture has been immeasurable, and he will be deeply missed by many," Knott said.

Dumfries and Galloway MSP Finlay Carson also paid tribute to Baines, a former school friend.

"Richard was a remarkable gentleman and a good friend to many, always ready with a warm smile, a kind word and an infectious enthusiasm for life," he said.

The Scottish Conservative MSP said that Baines' work at Logan Botanic Garden had earned him national recognition.

"His expertise, commitment and achievements brought credit not only to his profession but to Galloway as well," he added.

Baines died as Storm Boelo swept across Scotland, causing flooding, travel disruption and power cuts over the weekend and into Monday.

The wind picked up on Saturday and an amber warning was in place from Saturday night.

Galloway Mountain Rescue Team (GMRT) said they had responded to "one of the most gruelling callouts our team had faced in recent history" on Saturday.

They were called to Curleywee in the Minigaff Hills to help a runner who was injured while taking part in the OMM mountain challenge.

In a post on Facebook, they said 10 members of their team pushed through "torrential rain, severe wind and unforgiving boggy ground" to reach the casualty.

A coastguard helicopter had to turn back due to the deteriorating weather.

The team said they had to carry the casualty off the hill, with the help of members of the OMM safety team, before handing the runner to the Scottish Ambulance Service.

OMM has faced some criticism on social media for allowing the run to go ahead in the poor weather.

A spokesperson said the course was closed and all competitors accounted for before the amber wind warning took effect at 21:00 on Saturday.

"The event team continually assessed the mountain weather forecast in the build-up to and throughout the event, with competitor safety guiding every decision," they added.

The spokesperson said they were grateful for the "understanding and support" shown as the event was adapted to the forecast conditions.

They said they would be making as a donation to GMRT, as is usual practice at OMM events whether or not a callout takes place.

No 10 appears to backtrack on PM's freedom of movement referendum suggestion

BBC News Mon, 26 Oct 2026 17:50:00 GMT

Downing Street has appeared to backtrack on the prime minister's suggestion that he could call another referendum on whether to join the EU's freedom of movement.

Asked earlier by broadcasters if he could introduce freedom of movement without a referendum, Andy Burnham said "no".

But sources told the BBC no decision on that has been made and the prime minister's deputy spokesperson later said the government was not going to "get ahead" of how to consult the public.

Burnham has ruled out major changes to the UK's relationship with the EU before the next general election but says he wants start a conversation about potential options.

He told broadcasters that he would "never move ahead of the British public when it comes to Brexit".

Migration dominated debate during the 2016 Brexit campaign, with the Leave campaign raising issues about freedom of movement allowing any EU citizen to move to the UK.

Burnham has said he is committed to Labour's 2024 election manifesto, which ruled out a return of free movement, single market membership or a customs union.

And he has previously stressed any changes would require a mandate at a general election, which is due by 2029.

After lengthy questioning about the issue, Number 10 sought to clarify the prime minister's remarks, saying: "The prime minister isn't proposing a return to freedom of movement or any option."

"He is crucially not leaning either way and that will be for the British public to decide," the prime minister's deputy spokeswoman said.

"What he wants to do first is have a conversation with the public. The process will follow."

She added: "The PM thinks the Brexit deal is not good enough."

Freedom of movement, which allows EU citizens to travel, live, study and work in any member country, is a precondition of membership of the EU's single market.

The single market enables goods, services and people to move freely between member states, with countries also applying many common rules and standards.

In an interview with the Sunday Times, Burnham said he would welcome an "honest discussion" about the prospect of returning to free movement between the UK and the EU.

The PM argued that the type of migration had changed since Brexit, with more foreigners moving permanently.

In contrast, he suggested that when the UK was a member of the EU, migration was "generally younger people", who would spend a few years in the country before returning home.

However, Burnham added: "I can't see myself ever recommending anything that would involve joining the euro or Schengen."

The Schengen Agreement, which the UK was not part of when it was in the EU, allows passport-free travel across member countries.

The UK was able to keep the pound when it was an EU member, but the bloc has pushed new members to adopt the Euro.

Burnham has argued that since Brexit, the UK has lost immigration control the country previously had.

"For instance, the small boats crisis has arisen in the last 10 years because we lost that returns agreement when people came here that we could work with other countries to return them," he told broadcasters.

The Conservatives and Reform UK both oppose a return to free movement with the EU.

However, the Liberal Democrats have argued that allowing freedom of movement would help economic growth.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch argued most people who voted for Brexit did so because they did not want free movement, while Reform leader Nigel Farage has said such a move would be "a total betrayal of Brexit Britain".

Farage told broadcasters he was "up for the fight again" on the EU and an "election is coming" to decide that.

"Crucially, [Burnham] goes to Brussels on 20 November for a key summit - he must not sign up to anything there without at least putting those minor changes to a general election," he said.

Storm Boelo leaves 22,000 without power as Met Office issues new wind warning

BBC News Mon, 26 Oct 2026 17:22:51 GMT

A clean-up operation is under way in parts of the UK after Storm Boelo caused flooding and property damage, leaving thousands without power.

The Energy Networks Association (ENA) said around 22,600 properties are still without power as of Monday afternoon.

Two men were killed by falling trees during the storm on Sunday - a man in his 20s whose car was hit in north London and a 60-year-old man in Dumfries and Galloway identified as Richard Baines, the long-serving curator of Logan Botanic Garden.

The Met Office has issued a yellow warning for strong winds from 18:00 on Monday to 03:00 on Tuesday across the west coast of England, Wales and Scotland and eastern parts of Northern Ireland.

The Met Office has warned that further power cuts in areas covered by the warning are likely and people should make sure they have essentials prepared, including torches and batteries.

Coastal communities could also be affected by spray or large waves, while travel delays are expected.

Boelo is the second storm to have hit parts of the UK in recent days, following Storm Austen.

Leo Slade, CEO of the ENA said it had been "a tough weekend" and that efforts to reconnect some properties were being hampered by the weather, with sustained winds of 50-85mph across parts of Scotland and northern England.

"Until that weather system passes, we can't safely get engineers out to replace poles, to get wires back up, so today is going to be a hive of activity in getting engineers out into the field," Slade told BBC Radio 4's Today programme.

He stressed that the UK's power network was very resilient and money was spent to prepare for these sorts of scenarios, but said a debate was needed over how much more investment was required to mitigate for further storms brought by climate change.

Marcus Reed, the operations director at a home fragrance manufacturer, said his factory and shop in Lyndal, Cumbria would be without power until Tuesday evening.

He told the Today programme that he has had to turn away employees and customers.

"To lose two days manufacturing and distribution is going to be really disruptive," he said, adding that it was bad timing as it was "the busiest time of the year" for his business in the lead-up to Christmas.

"This is probably the worst situation I've experienced in my time here; we've had ad hoc issues over weekends where we've lost power, but it's been contained within a 12-hour period. It's the first time anything like this has happened, it's very serious."

Wendy McKinney, whose bathroom shop in the seaside town of Largs in North Ayrshire was flooded on Sunday, told the Today programme the storm had been "devastating to local businesses".

She said the local council only handed out sandbags after flooding had already started:"[They] were just left in the middle of the street yesterday afternoon on pallets just for everybody just to try and help themselves, but it was too little too late."

North Ayrshire Council told the BBC that it had distributed almost 300 sandbags in Largs and Saltcoats and would continue to "respond where it has been safe and appropriate to do so".

A spokesperson said council teams "followed established resilience procedures" but would review flooding reports and "consider any lessons that can be learned".

Disruption to travel has continued on Monday, and some schools in Scotland have been shut either due to lack of power, heating, water or damage.

Another yellow warning of wind has been issued by the Met Office, covering much of Scotland, as well as parts of northern England and Northern Ireland from 03:00 to 23:59 on Tuesday.

Monday morning has seen rain in many parts of south-west England, Wales and Northern Ireland, and this is moving north-eastwards reaching central, eastern and northern England, as well as most of Scotland, by around lunchtime.

Winds will also strengthen throughout Monday, and it will turn even windier overnight as the area of low pressure passes close to Northern Ireland and north-west Scotland with gusts peaking on Tuesday.

Additional reporting by Ben Rich, lead weather presenter.

Former US Open winner McDowell confirms LIV exit

BBC News Mon, 26 Oct 2026 17:17:31 GMT

McDowell joined LIV when the breakaway tour launched in 2022

Northern Ireland's Graeme McDowell has become the latest major champion to confirm his departure from LIV Golf.

The 2010 US Open winner, 47, announced on Monday he has "decided not to pursue" LIV 2.0, the new version of the breakaway tour which is due to start in 2027.

Major winners Jon Rahm and Louis Oosthuizen have also confirmed their departures, while McDowell's fellow countryman Tom McKibbin said he was exiting LIV to return to the DP World Tour last week.

England's Tyrrell Hatton and Ian Poulter have also left the competition.

Saudi's Public Investment Fund withdrew its backing from LIV in April - having pumped in more than $5bn (£3.8bn) - leading to the league filing for bankruptcy protection in the United States last month.

It has secured a possible $300m (£224m) in financing from BC Partners Credit to try to move forward with 'LIV 2.0', but only a handful of players have so far committed.

Former world number four McDowell joined LIV when it launched as a lucrative Saudi Arabia-backed project in 2022.

The 11-time DP World Tour winner's best finish on LIV was a tie for second in Virginia in June 2025.

"I've decided not to pursue LIV 2.0," said four-time Ryder Cup player McDowell.

"I'm grateful for the opportunity I've had over the last four years and want to thank everyone who has been part of that journey.

"I look forward to the next chapter in my career."

Earlier this year, McDowell told BBC Sport NI he had held "really positive" talks about returning to the DP World Tour next season, adding he was "lucky to have that option".

Poulter & Hatton leave LIV as exodus continues

Rahm sacrifices £75m to secure exit from LIV Golf

Former Open champion Oosthuizen quits LIV Golf

Meanwhile, LIV has announced the appointment of former Taylor Made and Adidas executive Mark King as senior adviser.

King said: "Having spent much of my career in golf, I believe there is a tremendous opportunity for LIV Golf to establish itself as a competitive and enduring force in the game."

In the same announcement, the league said it "remains laser focused on advancing its conversations with players regarding their participation" in LIV 2.0.

A deadline for player sign-ups had been set for Sunday, although BBC Sport understands there is a degree of flexibility to enable ongoing discussions with players.

The lawyer representing LIV told a bankruptcy court hearing earlier this month it needed to sign a "sufficient number of players to have a bona fide golf league", and would know by the end of October whether it could proceed with LIV 2.0 or move to winding down the breakaway league.

League sources told BBC Sport that LIV 2.0 is generating "inbound interest from established, elite professionals and emerging talent across global professional golf".

Israel and the US are both going to the polls - the consequences will be global

BBC News Mon, 26 Oct 2026 16:30:34 GMT

In the next week, two sets of elections will be held on two continents, the outcomes of which could have profound consequences for the world.

By a fluke of electoral timetabling, millions of voters around 6,000 miles apart will unite in exercising their democratic rights within days of each other.

Voters in Israel go to the polls on Tuesday to elect a new parliament; a week later, voters in the United States will elect a new Congress.

A former speaker of that Congress, Tip O'Neill, may have once said that "all politics is local". But the consequences of these elections will undoubtedly be global.

For these elections are not just proximate, they are intertwined.

The future governance of Israel will have a lasting impact on the Middle East and wars raging across the region.

And any change in the electoral map of America could shape not just those wars but also the future of the global economy.

Between the two there is a physical connection: the lobby group Republicans Overseas Israel estimates about half a million Israelis with American passports can vote in both polls.

Marc Zell, the group's chairman, said these electors could influence tight races in the US, such as the Michigan senatorial contest, in which he estimated 10,000 absentee ballots would be cast from Israel. "They can really make a difference," he told the BBC.

But the policy connection is perhaps deeper - and most acute regarding the US-Israeli war on Iran. The massive aerial attack, which began in February, destroyed many military targets and killed much of Iran's leadership. But it failed to overthrow the regime which hit back hard across the Gulf and seized control of the Strait of Hormuz and the energy that flowed through it.

The sheer fact of the elections has already shaped decision-making.

Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has used the campaign to talk up the possibility of launching a fresh attack on Iran.

He has made new claims – without providing evidence – about Iran's nuclear threat, insisting again the Islamic regime must be overthrown.

His aim: to shore up his reputation as a security leader, which took such a battering after the deadly 7 October Hamas-led attacks on Israel.

US President Donald Trump has added to the speculation of renewed attacks on Iran by endorsing Netanyahu's re-election campaign, saying both men should "soon finish the job" in Iran.

Yet for all the sabre-rattling, there have also been contradictory reports that Trump intervened to restrain Netanyahu from attacking Iran before polling day, fearing a fresh spike in energy prices would remind US voters of his unpopular war.

So might an attack on Iran, then, be delayed until after the elections? Israel's media is full of speculation Netanyahu could try to engineer his survival by attacking Iran as caretaker prime minister after the election.

He would argue, so the theory goes, for a government of national unity – involving him – rather than a coalition between opposition parties. Netanyahu has long been seen as a great survivor of Israeli politics. If he were to lose power, he would face an official inquiry into his actions before the October 7 attacks and renewed legal proceedings involving allegations of corruption.

So real is this speculation that Netanyahu's rival, the former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, has already ruled out joining any unity government. Like all mainstream Israeli politicians, Eisenkot sees Iran as an existential threat to Israel and supports military action against the Islamic regime. But he has explicitly warned against escalating the war for political purposes.

Certainly, Trump may be more willing to attack Iran after the midterms if he is unconstrained electorally and hoping to extract himself from the war with one more push. Some analysts believe Iran is so economically weak from the war and economic sanctions that a fresh round of military strikes might encourage Iranians to overthrow the regime. Others see this as yet more wishful thinking. It is a strategy that has repeatedly failed, but still has currency in Washington.

"After the midterms, he will be in legacy mode," one well-placed Western diplomat told me. "He will want to show agency on anything that is not the quagmire at home."

In Israel there is a broad consensus across most parties about the threat from and the need to constrain Iran. But if voters elect a new government, they might have a prime minister with less political and personal investment in fresh attacks.

In those circumstances, Trump has suggested his thinking may change, too. "If Israel has the wrong Leader, which would be anyone other than Bibi [a nickname for Netanyahu], America will have to do this work ourselves, and I am not inclined to do so," he wrote on social media.

Little wonder policymakers in Tehran have been following US opinion polls as closely as any analyst inside the Washington beltway. The risk, of course, is that any post-electoral strikes would plunge the Middle East into fresh chaos if Iran were to retaliate hard.

Publicly and privately, Iranian officials have threatened to hit airports, pipelines, undersea cables, energy facilities, desalination plants as well as US bases and warships.

Iran's foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, wrote in the Financial Times that new attacks would put "civilian lives and the wellbeing of all regional states and the global economy at great risk".

The two elections again intertwine around the global economy. Affordability and cost of living have dominated campaigning for the midterms, issues made worse by Trump's war that raised prices as Iran choked the flow of energy through the Strait of Hormuz.

The economy is also an election issue in Israel, where voters face high costs and low wages. But here, too, the war plays its part with soaring defence spending putting even more pressure on the public finances.

Trump has sought to appease voters ahead of the midterms. He has lifted sanctions on Russia, hoping in vain that by importing diesel from Moscow, prices might fall significantly. He has been taking a tough line with Ukraine, calling on its leadership to make concessions in the hope – also so far in vain – of claiming a foreign policy victory.

But Republican ire at his controversial strategy is growing. Senator Thom Tillis of North Carolina, a frequent critic of Trump, told CBS News: "If the President wants to actually bring down energy prices, he can do it by solving the Iran problem, not by doing a solid [favour] for Vladimir Putin."

One consequence of the Iran war – along with Israel's military operations in Gaza and the occupied West Bank – is that traditional bipartisan support in the US has fractured. Abdul El-Sayed, the left-wing Democratic candidate for the Senate in Michigan, campaigns on cutting military aid to Israel. "An ally that takes your money, to push you into wars you shouldn't be fighting, is not an ally," he told ABC News.

The US and Israel initially attacked Iran to destroy its ballistic missiles, degrade its nuclear capability, weaken its support for proxy militias and even oust the entire regime. Since then its war aims have changed to reopening the Strait of Hormuz.

Brad Lander, a Democratic congressional candidate in New York who also sits on the left of his party, chose even to travel to the West Bank only days before polling. He helped Palestinians harvest olives and was briefly detained by Israeli forces, all grist to his social media electoral mill. In the history of US politics, this is not normal. Even Netanyahu is warning that Israel may in future have to survive without a US security blanket.

Of course, if Israel's prime minister were to lose, his departure would end a scratchy bromance that has seen Trump blow hot and cold. Last week the president called his Israeli counterpart a "great warrior prime minister". During the summer, he said Netanyahu was "effing crazy". A new Israeli leader would have to forge a new relationship with an outgoing US president, a very different dynamic.

If the Democrats were to win greater control in Congress, that might place some check on blanket US support for Israel. Congress has traditional powers that it can use to restrain military spending. It could also cut military aid to Israel. But as president, Trump would retain significant executive power – and a veto – to continue prosecuting the conflict as he saw fit.

The decision by Israel and the US to go to war with Iran earlier this year transformed the global economy and international geopolitics. The choices voters in both nations make in coming days may shape where the world goes next.

Anthropic warns of 'catastrophic risk' to humankind ahead of blockbuster share listing

BBC News Mon, 26 Oct 2026 16:27:17 GMT

Anthropic has warned artificial intelligence (AI) could pose "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity" as it unveiled details of its planned blockbuster stock market listing in the US.

The firm's valuation is expected to exceed that of SpaceX, which was the biggest-ever listing at an initial valuation of about $1.8 trillion in the summer.

Anthropic has not yet disclosed the number of shares to be released, their price range, or a date for the listing.

The Claude chatbot developer reported $16.3bn (£12.2bn) of revenue in the first half of the year, with losses of more than $80.7bn.

Anthropic, which said it will list on the Nasdaq under the symbol ANT, will be the first fully AI-focused company to go public, making it a test case for the future of the technology.

In a filing ahead of its listing, Anthropic said concerns had been raised by policymakers, regulators and researchers as well as by people within its organisation that AI systems posed a significant risk to humanity.

It said advanced AI systems "could, if not developed, deployed, and operated with appropriate safeguards, oversight, and security measures, pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity, particularly if such systems were misused, replicated, weaponised, or allowed to operate with a high degree of autonomy".

Anthropic was founded five years ago by chief executive Dario Amodei, his sister Daniela Amodei and five others, and announced its intention to go public in June.

Its main rival, OpenAI, quickly followed suit. That listing is now expected to occur early next year, according to a person familiar with OpenAI's plans.

Those announcements were followed by a wave of cyber-security and other technological breaches involving their AI agents - bots designed to operate somewhat autonomously.

Current and former staff of both companies also warned AI technology was being developed without the ability to protect humanity from possible future harms enacted by AI tools.

As Anthropic revealed its stock debut plans on Monday, the owners of the rights to Elvis Presley's music sued the AI firm accusing it of using hundreds of the rock-and-roll star's songs to train its chatbot Claude.

In Anthropic's new documents, it reiterated promises it has made in the past to develop AI in a way that is beneficial to people, while at the same time warning investors of its dangers.

Anthropic detailed losses in its financial filings that exceeded its revenue for the first half of the year, but said it would often make forward investments "that may seem irresponsibly large at first glance".

"In general, we will aim to be bold but sane, and to win trust with a track record of successful bets," the tech giant said.

Its success depends largely on its ability to develop the most advanced AI models, Anthropic said, adding, "any failure to do so could adversely affect our business".

Across about 90 pages detailing possible risk factors, Anthropic set out the potential threats to its ability to safely and competitively develop AI.

Anthropic warned it relies on a cluster of cloud computing providers, Taiwanese chipmakers already facing huge demand and data centres concentrated in the US.

It also warned of "regulatory action arising from harms associated with our AI models" - citing concerns over AI being used by children or individuals at risk of suicide - and uncertainty about where and how it might be held liable for actions taken by its systems.

However, Anthropic also used the filing to laud the potential benefits of the tech itself, envisioning it unlocking "millions of virtual agents with the ability to revolutionise every area of human endeavour" across a range of fields.

"We believe that AI is one of the most consequential technologies in human history," the firm said.

Anthropic said AI would also "profoundly accelerate the rate of progress in biology and medicine", potentially finding cures to diseases including cancer and Alzheimer's.

The firm added it could also establish "sustained acceleration in economic growth" by boosting productivity.

Matt Orton, chief market strategist at investment management firm Raymond James Investment, said investors expected to see rapid growth as well as rapid financial losses in Anthropic's finances, so Monday's filing would not come as a surprise.

"Getting the details from this filing, I think will help provide the market with more visibility, because we need to know where its revenue growth is coming from," he told the BBC.

Peter Andersen, founder of Andersen Capital Management, told Reuters that Anthropic's plans to list was "a significant milestone in the development of artificial intelligence".

He added that the outcome of its stock market debut would be "fairly indicative of the sentiment" among investors to continue ploughing cash into AI development.

Independent review announced into murder of student Henry Nowak

BBC News Mon, 26 Oct 2026 16:15:16 GMT

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood has announced an independent review into the murder of Henry Nowak.

The 18-year-old student was fatally stabbed in Southampton in December by Vickrum Digwa, who falsely claimed he had been racially abused and had acted in self-defence. Digwa was jailed for life on 1 June, with a minimum term of 21 years.

Following the teenager's murder, police bodycam footage of him being handcuffed as he lay dying led to intense scrutiny of the Hampshire and Isle of Wight Constabulary and sparked wider debates around knife laws, race, policing and public trust.

The review, which was welcomed by Nowak's family, will be led by former Justice Secretary Alex Chalk KC.

"We must get to truth of what happened before, during and after that awful night and we must do everything in our power to ensure that no family suffers the same fate," Mahmood told the House of Commons on Monday.

Mahmood said the review will investigate what was known about Nowak's killer and if there were missed opportunities to intervene as well as the treatment of his family in the justice system and whether they received enough support.

In a statement published on Monday, the Home Office said the review will be carried out in two parts.

Phase one will cover the police, health services, local authorities educational institutions and faith organisations, including if any concerns were raised relating to weapon possession and violent behavior, the statement said.

It will also look to determine if there were missed opportunities to prevent Nowak's murder.

Phase two will follow after the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) has concluded its investigation into the actions of police officers who attended the scene.

It will consider the actions of the IOPC and "if necessary" the police, the Home Office added.

The IOPC launched its own investigation into the response on the night of Nowak's death after bodycam footage showed the 18-year-old was handcuffed and left dying on the floor despite informing officers of his injuries.

The investigation was launched despite a sentencing judge ruling Nowak would not have survived his injuries, however quickly he received treatment.

The Nowak family described the announcement as a "significant moment in our fight for justice."

"We hope this review, alongside the ongoing investigations and inquest, will finally uncover the full truth and deliver the accountability and meaningful change we have fought so hard for," they added in a statement.

"Our experience of the criminal justice system has been deeply disappointing, and we are determined that no other family should have to endure what we have."

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch welcomed the decision to launch the review.

"There must be proper accountability for those who failed Henry and his family," she said.

The review is due to report in five months.

Nowak, from Chafford Hundred in Essex, was a first-year accountancy and finance student at the University of Southampton when he was murdered.

On the night of Nowak's muder, it was Digwa's brother who called 999, claiming Vickrum had been attacked "racially".

Bodycam footage released by Hampshire and Isle of Wight Constabulary, with the permission of Nowak's family, showed officers speaking to Digwa and others while Nowak lay on the ground.

Nowak could be heard repeatedly saying that he had been stabbed and could not breathe.

Violent disorder broke out in Southampton in the days following the release of the footage.

After Digwa's sentencing, Nowak's father Mark called for a "full, fearless and transparent" investigation into the police response.

But he also urged people not to use his son's death to "create further division, hatred or tension".

Angry players urge ATP rethink over doubles cuts

BBC News Mon, 26 Oct 2026 16:07:20 GMT

Finland's Harri Heliovaara (left) and Britain's Henry Patten - the world number ones and reigning Wimbledon champions - have signed the open letter

More than 150 men's doubles players - including British world number one Henry Patten and the legendary Bryan brothers - have urged the ATP Tour to rethink "drastic" changes which they believe could kill the format.

In a show of collective action, the players have written an open letter to the men's governing body as they fight proposals which would cut draw sizes and reduce prize money from 2028.

"We're at risk of losing a discipline of tennis which is historic - but has a big future," Dutch player Sem Verbeek, one of the architects of the letter, told BBC Sport.

"These proposals would destroy careers, livelihoods and dreams."

The ATP proposed halving the doubles draws at its flagship Masters 1000 events to 16 teams, with smaller tournaments reduced to eight teams.

The percentage of prize money devoted to doubles could fall from 20% to 10% - with the difference redistributed to singles players.

'You're taking our jobs' - doubles players angry at proposed cuts

On Monday, a group of 137 current players, 28 legends and 20 national federations signed a letter which they hope will pressure the ATP into rethinking the proposals.

The tour's board - comprised of chairman Andrea Gaudenzi, four tournament representatives and four player representatives - will vote on the plans at next month's ATP Finals in Turin.

The doubles reform is part of a wider review by the ATP, which it says is designed to "strengthen" the tour from 2028.

The ATP aims to create "a more sustainable long-term model", insisting it wants to "maintain the important role" of doubles.

"Commercial success matters. Fairness, player welfare and the long-term health of tennis matter just as much," the players' letter says.

"Let us grow tennis together, without leaving doubles players behind."

The proposals provoked an angry response from the men's doubles cohort when they were revealed in July.

British pair Lloyd Glasspool and Julian Cash, who won Wimbledon in 2025 and became world number ones, accused the ATP of trying to "kill part of the sport".

Others within tennis believe reform is needed. They suggest a 20% share of the prize money for doubles is disproportionate to the interest shown by fans.

The doubles players argue the ATP should do more to promote their discipline and attract greater audiences, pointing out it is the format played by most club members and therefore more relatable.

The ATP says the proposals are based on data-led analysis centred on costs, revenue and viewership.

With fewer singles players now competing in doubles, it believes the current size of the standalone doubles events puts severe strain on tournaments.

"We support progress. We also understand the need to grow the sport, strengthen tournaments and increase commercial value," the players' letter says.

"Still, the proposed reforms go much too far."

Reigning Wimbledon champion Patten recently told BBC Sport the players were facing "an uphill battle", but remained "optimistic" the tour would consider counter-proposals. Since Wimbledon there have been several meetings between both sides, including recently at the Shanghai Masters.

The players still believe there is little appetite for negotiation from the ATP. But ATP sources insist a compromise is likely to be found.

Mike and Bob Bryan - the identical twins considered the greatest doubles pair of all-time - said they would support the group considering legal action to protect their discipline.

In 2005, the American brothers led players in a lawsuit against the ATP, when it planned radical changes to doubles.

"The tour's in the healthiest financial state it's ever been - in our opinion it should be creating more opportunities," Bob Bryan told BBC Sport in an interview at Wimbledon in July.

Mike Bryan added: "These proposed changes are anti-competitive. That's the stance we had to take in 2005. We still believe in doubles and we believe in the players fighting for this."

Drivers who killed mum and girl while racing jailed

BBC News Mon, 26 Oct 2026 15:39:39 GMT

Two men who killed a mother and her four-year-old daughter as they raced their high-performance cars along a Leeds city centre road have been jailed.

Justyna Hulboj, 27, and her daughter Lena Czepczor were killed when they were hit by an Audi TT RS as they walked to the girl's nursery on the A61 Scott Hall Road on 16 January 2023.

At Leeds Crown Court on Monday, Hardeep Bhachu, 29, was jailed for 12 years and Jasskamal Riyat, 37, for 16 years.

Sentencing the men, Judge Singh said the road was "not a race track" and told them the deaths had consequences that were "immeasurable", with an "immense" impact on those left behind.

Bhachu, of Grant Row in Adel, had earlier admitted two counts of causing death by dangerous driving, while Riyat, of Buckstone Avenue in Moortown, was convicted by a jury after denying he had been racing him.

The court heard the pair, who did not previously know each other, accelerated away from traffic lights on Scott Hall Road shortly before the crash.

Prosecutors said Riyat's BMW reached speeds of up to 89mph in the 40mph zone before Bhachu lost control of his Audi, mounted the pavement and struck Hulboj and her daughter.

Judge Singh said the victims had "done nothing wrong" and were "simply walking to school".

Addressing the defendants, he said: "A road is not a race track. A powerful car is not an invitation to test its limits on a public road.

"The consequences of competitive driving at extreme speed can be, and in this case were, irreversible."

He added: "Justyna and Lena should have gone to school that morning. They should have returned home. They should have continued with their lives.

"Instead, their lives ended on a pavement because two drivers chose to drive in a manner which placed speed and competition above the safety of everyone around them."

Susannah Proctor, for Bhachu, told the court that her client was a "normal person who's made a massive mistake".

She said he "must live with himself in the knowledge of the devastation he has caused".

And she said: "He did not intend to cause this devastation but cause it he has."

Hulboj's fiancé Dominik Czepczor watched the sentencing hearing in court.

A statement from him was read, which said: "My whole world collapsed in one second.

"Every day I feel a huge void after their departure.

"We had so many hopes and dreams and in one moment it all ended.

"My dream was to have a wonderful family, and I must say that it came true for a short while, but that was taken away from me on January 16.

"Unfortunately, all that remains are wonderful memories and a constant fight for the next day, which is not easy."

Det Insp Paul Conroy, of West Yorkshire Police's Major Collision Enquiry Team, said: "A woman and her young daughter have died because of the actions of these men, and I know no sentence will ever feel enough to compensate for the lives that have been lost.

"This sentencing hearing though does mark the end of a long criminal justice process for Justyna and Lena's family.

"It is over two years since Bhachu admitted his part in this tragic incident and I know that the wait for justice has taken its toll.

"My thoughts are firmly with them today."

How 'Lula's Army' WhatsApp channel helped turn Brazil election around

BBC News Mon, 26 Oct 2026 15:37:33 GMT

A WhatsApp channel created to support Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva's re-election campaign is being credited by allies with helping deliver one of the most unlikely comebacks in recent Brazilian politics.

Brazil's left-wing president had been trailing right-wing challenger Flávio Bolsonaro, but managed to turn the race around in just three weeks.

At a moment when many doubted Lula could reverse the result, a WhatsApp channel called Lula's Army emerged, and rapidly grew to 10.8 million followers.

Led by Congressman André Janones, the operation encouraged supporters to share videos, promote hashtags and recruit new voters.

Its dramatic growth between the two rounds was particularly notable because it appeared to reverse a long-standing imbalance in Brazilian politics.

For years, conservatives aligned with former President Jair Bolsonaro had been widely seen as dominating online political mobilisation, especially on platforms such as WhatsApp and Telegram.

The emergence of Lula's Army convinced many supporters that Brazil's left had finally found a way to compete in a digital arena. The shift was particularly significant because social media has played a central role in Brazilian politics since Jair Bolsonaro's 2018 election victory, when WhatsApp networks became a defining feature of political campaigning.

Lula's Army messages often included ready-made templates for followers to share with friends and family. Each one assigned supporters a specific task aimed at boosting Lula's visibility on social media.

Janones frequently instructed his "troops" to "blow up" the latest campaign video or help a new hashtag "take off".

"Guys, urgent!", "Don't go to sleep yet", "No food before the mission!", and "I have one more task before you're dismissed", were some of the instructions.

On the eve of the election, the congressman also hosted a 24-hour live event - dubbed the "turnaround livestream" - even as polls continued to suggest a victory for Bolsonaro.

The tactic worked, despite worries by some members of the Workers' Party that Janones's often-confrontational style on social media could undermine the more moderate image they hoped to project for Lula.

In his victory speech, Lula referred to Janones as "our General" and thanked him for "raising the morale of our troops every day".

Measuring the electoral impact of online mobilisation, however, is notoriously difficult.

While Lula's allies credit Lula's Army with helping fuel the comeback, political scientists caution that it is impossible to determine how many votes, if any, were directly influenced by the WhatsApp operation.

Political scientist Denilde Holzhacker argues that a shift in Lula's campaign strategy was key to his comeback.

Rather than relying solely on online engagement, she says the Workers' Party candidate succeeded in connecting digital campaigning with grassroots mobilisation on the ground.

According to Holzhacker, the campaign intensified local efforts and adapted its messaging - linking a Bolsonaro victory with concerns about potential changes to social programmes and the loss of rights.

"It was to Lula's credit that he recognised his own weakness and completely changed his style," she says. "And Janones managed to do something that had seemed unthinkable for Brazil's left - dominate social media."

By contrast, Holzhacker argues that Flávio Bolsonaro entered the run-off overly confident of victory and failed to communicate his message to his supporters as effectively.

Sociologist and political scientist Mayra Goulart, a professor at the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro, also cautions against attributing Lula's comeback solely to social media.

"It was a combination of social media and street-level mobilisation," she says. "The physical world enabled a form of mobilisation capable of reducing abstention and persuading undecided voters."

In her view, Lula's supporters succeeded in turning online enthusiasm into real-world political engagement.

"Those committed to Lula's victory worked to bring people together and persuade them to vote," Goulart says.

She argues that the effort not only helped increase turnout but could also prove valuable for Lula's next administration.

"I believe this collective effort was an important learning experience and will prove valuable for a government that still faces many battles ahead. It not only helped reduce abstention, but also converted a significant number of undecided voters."

Lula himself suggested that the mobilisation behind his comeback could shape the way he governs in the years ahead.

In his victory speech, he said the election had taught him many lessons and pledged to change the way Brazil is governed.

"We are going to give people a greater say in decision-making, and digital communication will play a much bigger role in my government."

Berger added that she never "witnessed anything against the law" but that "everyone normalised and dismissed his behaviour" so it "made me think it was accepted."

She told the court Brand used MySpace to find women for sex, and said: "At his house, women often came over and it was clear they were there for sex."

Russell Brand's defence team says any sexual activity was consensual and accounts have been twisted in the light of a defamatory TV documentary in 2023 which made allegations of sexual abuse against the entertainer.

How a movement of students brought down Serbia's Vučić

BBC News Mon, 26 Oct 2026 14:29:31 GMT

Theirs is a movement born from tragedy that began with students blockading streets and turned into almost daily protests and a national movement against corruption and government negligence.

In just under two years the students have succeeded in tearing up 14 years of political dominance under Aleksandar Vučić, who has seen support for his Serbian Progressive party (SNS) ebb away and ultimately fail in what became a referendum on the future of Serbia.

From Belgrade to Novi Sad and Niš, the mood was euphoric as supporters gathered in town centres or in front of Student List headquarters. In a post on social media, the students declared "Serbia is free".

Most symbolic of all was the demise of so-called Ćaciland, a pro-Vučić tent camp set up 18 months ago at Pioneers Park in central Belgrade in front of the Serbian parliament. Metal fences were torn down amid shouts of "Vučić is leaving".

They have no obvious leaders and have no grounding in politics, and yet the "Student List-Students Win" movement attracted anti-government voters across Serbian society.

They fielded candidates for all 250 parliamentary seats, and yet no students were among them.

As he joined the students marching towards Belgrade last week, lead candidate and cardiologist Ilija Srdanović said history was being rewritten: "The energy is unstoppable."

"We offer our citizens the core values of civilised society, which this previous regime has taken away from our citizens for the last time," he told the BBC.

It all began on 1 November 2024, when the concrete canopy collapsed outside Novi Sad train station, in Serbia's second biggest city, killing 16 people.

The tragedy was seen as emblematic of widespread corruption. Critics linked the station's fatally flawed renovation to a president who had closely associated himself with the project.

"When the canopy collapsed that served as the last straw," says Helena Ivanov of the think tank the Henry Jackson Society.

It was an emotional moment that triggered a spark and a national campaign of marches and events, she said, that captured the hearts and minds of Serbians in a way no opposition party had been able to do.

What started as weekly student protests demanding justice on university campuses and city streets soon became a national movement, often at a local level, that encompassed far more sections of Serbian society, including farmers, actors and judges.

Vučić's SNS was clearly shaken and by January 2025 his prime minister had resigned "to defuse tensions". In March 2025 Belgrade saw Serbia's biggest ever anti-government protest and as the leaderless student movement increased in strength, they organised themselves through student assemblies or plenums.

By the time Vučić had announced snap elections last month, they were ready. "They have been able to take that emotional momentum into a proper organisation and have people learn how to protect fairness at polling stations," Helena Ivanov explained.

"The message was clear: the rule of law and not ruled by the law," said Gordana Delić, head of the Balkans programme at the German Marshall Fund of the US, who said Sunday's vote was in effect a referendum.

Initially Vučić sought to praise the protesters as "well-intentioned", but ahead of the elections he accused them of trying to "bring down" Serbia. Even after conceding victory on Sunday night he made the unfounded allegation that they had the support of unnamed "European countries and the American deep state".

One thing is clear, it will not be the students, as they were not standing for election. That was a calculated decision as the electorate would probably not have voted for a list of candidates with little life experience.

Although their top candidate was Ilija Srdanović, a cardiology professor in Novi Sad, he is not really seen as a likely prime minister.

Few candidates stand out as potential leaders.

According to a final projection by independent polling groups CeSID and Ipsos, 141 people on the list have won seats in parliament. They include ex-basketball star Dejan Bodiroga (24th on the list), renowned actor Tihomir Stanić (8th), opera singer Nikola Mikić (46th), former National Bank of Serbia governor Dejan Šoškić (27th), and a rather large number of professors.

Šoškić's name has been mentioned in connection with the top post. He has spoken out about reforms he would make to the economy, and he has been widely criticised in pro-government media.

The elected MPs will have the task of fulfilling what is in effect a manifesto.

In the words of the students themselves, they were looking for people who could enter institutions "do their jobs responsibly and not forget why they are there".

Under an 11-point programme, the student movement wants to:

Vučić and the SNS party deny corruption and seeking to influence the media.

Although they have not been elected, it is the students who have made the promises to the Serbian people and they will come under pressure to follow through on their manifesto.

The ordinary Serbian citizens they chose to represent their movement have "been entrusted with transferring part of the struggle we have been waging on the streets for the past year into the institutions", the students say.

In his speech on Sunday evening, Vučić told party supporters that the students had destroyed two years of life in Serbia and they would be defeated "faster than they think".

Five ways Trump has changed immigration in the US

BBC News Mon, 26 Oct 2026 11:29:02 GMT

Immigration has always been central to Donald Trump's message.

When he famously stepped onto the golden escalator at Trump Tower to announce his candidacy for his first presidential term in 2015, he accused Mexico of sending drugs and crime north of the border - and it's been a constant rallying cry ever since.

Some of his first-term ambitions to stem the flow of would-be immigrants were constrained by the courts.

But restraints have been weaker in his second term, with a more accommodating Supreme Court and tens of billions of additional enforcement money from Congress.

Who should be allowed to live in the US remains a big issue on the minds of voters in the upcoming midterm elections, which are largely seen as a referendum on the Trump presidency.

He promised a closed border and mass deportations in his successful 2024 campaign - and few can deny that he's delivered on both.

But even among those who voted for a tougher stance, there is a concern that the crackdown has gone too far.

His signature policy has played out in five key ways.

Crossings exploded during Joe Biden's presidency, with over 4.5 million migrant "encounters" recorded at the southern border in 2023 and 2024 alone, reflecting the massive numbers of people headed north to the US border.

His administration eventually brought the monthly figures down significantly by restricting asylum claims and removing migrants entering the US illegally without processing.

When Trump returned to office, that stream of migrants became a trickle. Border encounters plummeted.

By the end of Trump's first year in office, the chaotic scenes that had generated headlines around the globe during the Biden administration had largely gone.

On a trip to the border city of El Paso, Texas, in November 2025, for example, the BBC found quiet streets where there had previously been makeshift camps housing thousands of migrants granted parole in the US to await immigration proceedings.

To achieve what he often describes as the "most secure" border in US history, the Trump administration has taken an aggressive, multi-pronged approach.

That has included effectively freezing asylum applications at the border, ending "catch and release" of detainees into the US, deploying troops to the border and pressuring Mexico to clamp down on the flow of migrants headed north.

"President Trump promised the American people a secure border, and the data proves he delivered," Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in a statement on 16 October.

"The results could not be clearer: strong enforcement works."

A vow to build a "big, beautiful wall" at the nearly 2,000-mile (3,218km) US-Mexico border was a signature promise of Trump's 2016 campaign.

Progress on it has speeded up in his second term, boosted by $46.5bn (£34.7bn) in new funding from Trump's "One Big Beautiful" spending bill.

According to government figures, about 644 miles of "primary wall" - closest to the border - existed before Trump returned to the White House, in addition to 75 miles of "secondary" wall set slightly further inside the US.

Since then, 250 more miles of new wall have been completed, including primary, secondary and waterborne barriers, along with the technology that helps detect illegal crossings. An additional 1,443 miles of barriers are currently under construction.

Experts, however, paint a more complex picture of what has been actually built rather than just improved or updated.

Additionally, the impact the wall is itself having on the broader immigration figures is up for debate.

"Since new wall construction has really begun in earnest, there has been no significant change in the number of people crossing the border," said Aaron Reichlin-Melnick, an immigration enforcement expert at the American Immigration Council.

There is no indication the border wall has reduced migrant crossings, he added. The reduction has been more down to Trump's policies and messaging.

Trump, for his part, continues to point to the wall as a successful policy - and continues to claim that Mexico paid for it.

"I'm the King of the Wall," Trump said at a rally in Kentucky on 17 October. "By the way, Mexico did pay for that wall. I charged them tariffs and I charged them costs like they've never paid in history."

Most of the headlines generated by Trump's immigration policies have come from the US interior, where operations by Immigrations and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents to round up people they say are in the US illegally have rocked cities across the country.

During his campaign, Trump promised an immediate start to what he described as the "largest deportation operation in American history", which officials said would begin with people who have committed crimes first.

Arrests - and subsequent detentions in immigration facilities - have shot up significantly since Trump returned to office, including a record of nearly 50,000 in July this year alone, according to data obtained by the Deportation Data Project, a repository of US immigration data run out of University of California, Berkeley, and UCLA.

But the same data shows that a large chunk of the arrests involve people without criminal convictions. In July 2026, detentions of immigrants with criminal histories reached an all-time low of 27%.

Deportations have also ramped up significantly. By mid-July this year, ICE was removing an average of 1,255 people from the country per day, compared to about 770 in Biden's final months in office - although Biden's own removals had sharply risen in his final year in office.

But the tactics used by ICE in US cities have made many Americans grow uncomfortable, including many of those who supported stricter restrictions broadly. This became increasingly evident following Operation Metro Surge, a two-month large scale enforcement action in Minneapolis in early 2026 that left two US citizens dead.

A New York Times and Siena poll released on 21 October found that 50% of voters trust Democrats to handle the issue, compared with 46% for Republicans - despite the issue being a traditional Republican strength.

A separate poll, from Politico and Public First in late September, found deep splits between Republicans on the issue, with 31% of non-MAGA Republicans, meaning those not aligned with Trump's movement, believing that campaign has become too aggressive.

After returning to the White House last year, Trump almost immediately suspended refugee admissions, saying at the time these could only restart if they were shown to be in US interests.

In February, however, an executive order signed by Trump narrowly re-opened that process for Afrikaners from South Africa, who the White House has repeatedly said are being killed and "persecuted" - a claim that the government in Pretoria has denied.

The cap for refugee admissions for the 2026 fiscal year was initially set at 7,500, which was raised to 17,500 in May this year because of what the administration described as an "unforeseen emergency refugee situation".

Overall refugee admissions have slowed to a relative trickle. State Department data shows that 16,292 refugees were admitted into the US in the 2026 fiscal year - of whom 16,287 were South African.

By comparison, in the final two fiscal years of the Biden administration - 2023 and 2024 - 60,000 and 100,000 entered the country, respectively. In the 2024 fiscal year, the highest numbers came from Democratic Republic of Congo, Afghanistan, Syria and Venezuela.

Hundreds of thousands of people protected from deportation lost that protection when a humanitarian protection called Temporary Protected Status (TPS) was also ended in Trump's second term. It gave vetted individuals the right to live and work in the US if their home countries were deemed to be unsafe to return to.

One of those countries was Haiti. In June, the Supreme Court upheld the Trump administration's decision to end TPS for some 350,000 Haitians in the US.

Other legal pathways to come to live and work in the US have also been tightened up, through various policy changes.

Dozens of countries the Trump administration has deemed a security risk have been subject to a full or partial freeze on visas and travel.

Enhanced vetting and new rules that send people residing in the US back to their home countries to apply for green cards has slowed that process down.

And in September 2025, a $100,000 fee on new H1-B visas for skilled workers, mostly held by Indians, stunned the US tech industry. In May this year, the US Citizenship and Immigration Services said on X that registrations for 2027 were down 40%.

"The data is a clear sign that the days of abusing the program with mass, low-wage registrations are over, and that the program is better serving its intended purpose of attracting highly skilled foreign workers and protecting the wages, working conditions and job opportunities of American workers," the statement added.

While a court has blocked the $100,000 fee - for now - the threat of it appears to have deterred employers. But some experts have cautioned the administration's aim of protecting American jobs, raising wages and stopping firms from outsourcing may prove elusive.

One study, from the Wharton School of Business, found that the H1-B changes would have "no significant impact" on the wages of US-born workers, with any reduction in competition offset by reduced productivity growth.

Other pathways to the US have been opened, however - if you have a spare million.

The "Trump Gold Card" launched in 2025 sought to entice wealthy foreigners to come live in the US in exchange for a $1m "gift" to the US government, plus a non-refundable $15,000 application fee.

At the time, Trump said that the programme would boost the US economy. Its uptake, however, appears to be minimal so far. By April, only one applicant had been accepted.

Healey to shield low-income pensioners from income tax in the Budget

BBC News Mon, 26 Oct 2026 10:28:12 GMT

Pensioners on low incomes will be shielded from income tax by Chancellor John Healey in his first Budget on Wednesday.

The full, flat-rate state pension is expected to increase by 3.9% to £13,036.40 a year from April. This would take the payment above the £12,570 personal tax allowance and therefore be liable for income tax if no changes are made.

The government had already committed to not taxing people who only get an income from the state pension. Healey will explain this pledge will be met by plans for a new tax allowance for low-income pensioners.

Healey's plans come as the Conservatives and Reform UK unveil their alternative Budget proposals, including deep cuts to the welfare bill.

The chancellor's allies argue his plans for pensioners will mean they do not need to face an administrative burden just to pay a small amount of tax.

More specific details, including how many pensioners this will affect, have yet to be confirmed by the Treasury.

The Budget is due to be printed this evening, with Healey's speech likely to be fine-tuned right up until it is delivered on Wednesday lunchtime.

Treasury sources concede it will not involve the scale of tax and spending announcements seen from Labour and Conservative governments in recent years.

The Tories are calling on the chancellor to cut green taxes, red tape and benefits to bring down energy bills.

Reform is recommending the chancellor adopts 60 policies which they claim will create jobs - including approving the controversial Rosebank oil field - a project Healey is understood to back.

Liberal Democrat Treasury spokeswoman Daisy Cooper has called on the government to agree a new growth and defence partnership with the EU, including joining the single market. She argued this would help "ease the huge tax burden weighing people down".

The Green Party has urged Healey to use his first Budget to "make the UK affordable", including by funding energy bill support by ending a tax relief for data centres.

Senior Green politicians, including leader Zack Polanski, MPs and peers, made clear their suggestions in a letter to Healey.
