Daughter wins £127k claim for caring for mum at home

BBC News Mon, 26 Oct 2026 06:23:01 GMT

A woman has described her "phenomenal" relief after she won a legal case that means she is entitled to be paid £127k from her mother's estate for caring for her in her final years.

Bern Rogers, from Bristol, told the BBC of the "harrowing and deeply sad" family dispute since her elderly mother Sheila died in 2020, which led to her facing criminal charges.

Legal experts said the "hugely significant" High Court ruling would lead to other claims.

The executor of Sheila's estate, Bern's brother Andrew, said it had "always been willing to pay" her "genuine expenses" and an extra amount for her efforts. But the estate intends to appeal against the judgment that awarded Bern £127,500 for care provided.

Bern looked after Sheila, who had dementia, for two-and-a-half years.

After Sheila moved into Bern's house in Bristol in September 2017, she wanted to be cared for by her daughter rather than get costly home care or go into a residential care home.

Crucially, Bern said she agreed with her mother she would be paid for the round-the-clock care.

After Sheila died in April 2020, Bern took £100,000 from her estate. It led to her being reported to the police for fraud and theft.

The money was seized and Bern was charged. But, at a trial at Bristol Crown Court in 2022, she was found not guilty by a jury.

After being cleared, Bern turned to the civil courts.

In 2025, a High Court judge ruled she had entered into an informal contract with Sheila for payment of a reasonable sum for her care.

The estate was also ordered by a judge to pay Bern's legal costs.

In August this year, another High Court judge worked out the amount Bern was due and ruled she was owed £127,500 for the 850 days of care she provided.

"Mum came to live with me, she became very confused and was seen wandering in the garden and obviously needed care," Bern said. "We didn't know what was wrong with her."

She said caring for her mother had been like a full-time job, adding: "I couldn't leave her really. She became unpredictable."

Sheila became more frail, was diagnosed with dementia and also had a series of physical health problems, including a "chronic" and "disabling" prolapse.

Bern's husband Jon said: "It was relentless after she moved in with us. We couldn't go out even to the shops. It was a 24-hour job.

"It was a privilege, but we had to put our lives on hold for more than two years and revolve our lives around looking after her."

He remembered that in Sheila's final weeks, his wife was sleeping on the floor of her mother's bedroom to make sure she was alright.

Bern said "of course" she would have looked after her mother if she had not been able to pay her.

But she said her mother had wanted to be looked after by her daughter rather than getting professional carers or going into a home, which would have cost thousands of pounds a month.

"She was very insistent and would tell anyone that would listen that she wanted to make sure that I sorted out money for her care, I was to make sure I got paid properly," she said.

Multiple messages from Bern's five siblings were shown in court saying that she should be paid something for the care, although no amount was agreed.

That is why, she explained, shortly after her mother had died, she transferred £100,000 from her mother's account.

Bern was reported to the police for theft and fraud, which she describes as a "terrible and devastating betrayal".

"It has been harrowing and deeply sad for it to go from a normal family relationship to being treated like a scapegoat, five against one," she said.

After the two separate High Court judgements in her favour, Bern said: "The weight off my shoulders was phenomenal.

"It has been absolutely wonderful to be vindicated. It means I can get on with my life now, the rest of my retirement."

Jon said: "I'm very proud of her, actually, because she has stuck up for her mother, for carers and for herself.

"It's been a very long and tough journey of nine years, and we've finally got justice."

Legal experts have told the BBC that while this case does not automatically set a legal precedent, it is likely to lead to similar claims in future.

Emma Holland, partner in trust and litigation at Stewarts, said: "What this case demonstrates is that the courts are willing to apply ordinary contractual principles to family relationships, which wasn't clear before."

This means family members are more likely to be entitled to payment if there is an informal agreement, she said, even without an amount being agreed.

"These are considered, well-reasoned judgements by highly esteemed judges, so I would think it's very likely that future courts will follow them," Holland said.

Beth Middleton, senior associate in private wealth and disputes at JMW, said this was a "hugely significant" case that would "open a floodgate of claims".

Samara Dutton, partner at Collyer Bristow, who specialises in trusts, inheritance and wills, said the judgements were likely to be "influential".

"It demonstrates a willingness to look beyond individual care tasks and acknowledges the broader reality of providing care to an elderly relative, including the continuous supervision, responsibility and restrictions on personal freedom," she said.

Bern said she was "terribly proud" that her case could influence others in future, which she said was her mum's "legacy".

"It's a huge win for carers everywhere," Jon added, but stressed families still needed to have open discussions about what was fair.

The ruling that states that Bern is entitled to payment cannot be appealed against, however, the estate intends to lodge an appeal against the second ruling that decided the amount owed.

The executor of Sheila's estate is Bern's brother, Andrew Wills. In a statement on behalf of the estate, he said: "The only agreements that we (her siblings) were aware of was for my mother to give Bernadette £50 per week 'keep' and to ensure that Bernadette was not to be out of pocket.

"We were not made aware of any other contract between our mother and Bernadette."

The statement added: "At all times I have attempted to be independent and to act in the best interests of the estate.

"The estate has always been willing to pay Bernadette her genuine expenses as well as an additional gratuity in recognition of her efforts for our mother.

"We have always tried to be fair. Unfortunately, our offers were not accepted by Bernadette who instead issued legal proceedings against the estate."

Healey's Budget needs to sustain the stronger economy through gathering clouds

BBC News Mon, 26 Oct 2026 00:26:49 GMT

There have been almost no Budget leaks.

The chancellor's aides are using intelligence-style security measures to guard its secrets: the Budget has been split into "compartments" with very few given access to all of them. There are codenames. The IT has been locked down and ministers viewing the plans have to sign a digital promise not to brief media.

Such security is a response to the feeling that speculation around the last Budget, sometimes informed by insiders, was economically destabilising.

As a recent former defence secretary, Chancellor John Healey has embraced such strict procedures, and has approached most of his public engagements and interviews with a sturdy refusal to break the Budget omertà, akin to his fellow Yorkshireman Geoffrey Boycott's at times ultra-defensive stance on a cricket pitch.

The economic news has been good - growth has been better than expected and the International Monetary Fund has endorsed the UK for "standing out" among the G7 countries for at least planning to cut borrowing.

The bond market's reverse beauty contest, in which investors single out the countries they distrust most, has moved on from Britain. Traders I occasionally hear from who were once focused on UK borrowing costs are now more preoccupied with "le spread" - the widening gap between French and German borrowing costs (the former being higher than the latter) - and with America's long-term debt outlook.

And yet there are clouds on the horizon. The inflation rate rose more than forecast to 3.5% in September, and borrowing numbers were also higher than forecast. This means an imminent Bank of England rate rise is very much on the cards, with the resultant rise in mortgage repayments for some.

Credibility with investors requires not just that Budget maths add up on Wednesday, but also belief that growth plans are realistic, and the perception that Downing Street can actually convince MPs to pass its Budget.

The question for John Healey is whether he can deliver a Budget that can sustain the revival in growth and offer the help with the cost of living that his backbenchers demand. At the same time he needs to reassure the markets that his budget will keep a check on borrowing.

"Is it resilient, or is it actually strong?" has been the tone of the debate among economists about the curious case of the UK economy ahead of what is a vital Budget.

The UK is the fastest growing G7 country so far this year, at 0.6% in Q1 and 0.5% in Q2. The widespread assumption of stagnation in the second half is being defied with Q3 heading for 0.6 to 0.8%.

Each quarter has seen growth twice as fast as predicted by the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) in March and independent forecasters. This is the fastest growth in the first eight months of a year since 2017, ignoring the post-lockdown re-opening.

It's more resilient than it was in 2022. Back then, the Ukraine war, massive energy bailouts, and Liz Truss' mini budget all culminated in the UK facing the highest borrowing costs in the G7, in what was derided in financial markets as a "moron premium".

Then last year, with constant policy u-turns, UK borrowing costs rose the most of the G7.

This year the gap has narrowed, as uncertainty about the US and France takes centre stage, but all advanced economies are feeling the heat from the Iran war energy shock.

Inflation has risen, but not just in Britain. The link between gas and electricity prices has weakened, meaning spikes in gas prices have less impact on electricity bills than they used to and helping to keep inflation lower than it otherwise might have been.

The fact that up until now the Iran war has been more of an oil shock than a gas shock (where the UK is more exposed) has been another saving grace. Meanwhile, the significant amount of AI and tech investment in the UK is another boost to the economic numbers.

The net result is that doom-mongering predictions of recession, of being hit worst by the Iran war, and, in some quarters, of imminent national bankruptcy, have been defied.

That economic defiance of the early part of 2026 has persisted in the first three months of the Burnham-Healey tenure in Downing Street, buoyed by a lull in the Iran war and the energy price shock.

Burnham was advised upon entry to Downing Street that if consumers could at least feel more confident, they might save less and spend more and therefore help boost growth.

So far Burnham and Healey appear to be relying on a series of relatively inexpensive "feel-better" policies - such as capped bus fares and a temporary VAT cut on household energy bills - that have improved confidence without significantly increasing spending.

But there isn't a lot of spare money, which limits just how much can be offered for "temporary and targeted" measures. And come January, the clouds on the horizon could be overhead, with typical energy bills predicted to rise by 16%, interest rates potentially up and an enduring fear that the AI bubble could burst.

At a gleaming hi-tech robotics research facility in Coventry last month, John Healey sought to set out the broad contours of his approach to the economy. On a walkabout at the Manufacturing Technology Centre, I asked him if there had been too much doom-mongery.

"I know the global conditions mean that it is hard… we have huge latent potential in this country. Great talent, and deep capital markets.

"The challenge now is to make sure that we balance the books, we manage and control public spending, and the prime minister and I are in lockstep in our determination to meet the fiscal rules with a buffer," he said.

The giant orange robot arms whizzing around were being trained by AI to use lasers to carve the most intricate metal shapes for prototype parts for the jet engines of the future. The Budget manoeuvres required by Healey may require even more precision.

The essential question is whether he has chosen to impress the markets and explain himself to his MPs, or impress his MPs and explain himself to the markets. Judging by my three interviews with him in recent weeks, it is more the former than the latter.

The answer may not be found in his speech at all, but in the borrowing tables that will reveal how much money the government expects to borrow over the coming years, published in the OBR's forecast released - assuming no repeat of last year's disaster - when Healey sits down in the House of Commons around 13.00.

Just after that, as Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch is delivering the Opposition's response, the real reaction the chancellor's team will be looking for is whether the markets move, particularly when the Debt Management Office publishes the "gilt remit" - the detail of any changes to its plan to sell UK government bonds to investors.

My sense is that every effort is being made to minimise this number, and help guide down medium and long-term borrowing rates for the government and for mortgages. (It was at this moment in 2022 that markets vomited at the prospect of how much extra they thought the government would need to borrow after Liz Truss' mini budget.)

From Healey's first day in office, the prudence message was practically tattooed to his head. He has spent more time working in the Treasury than any recent chancellor. He spent five years from 2002 to 2007 as a junior minister when Gordon Brown was chancellor - five finance bills, five Budgets, pre-Budget reports and two Spending Reviews.

For his Labour Party conference speech, Healey sported Brown's old conference tie. But the Treasury he returned to this year is a changed place in important ways. When his predecessor wore the tie, the Treasury was running an annual surplus, not a £120bn deficit adding to a £3 trillion total national debt.

I asked him just afterwards, and just before he was whisked off to a meeting of the government's emergency COBR committee on RAF Fairford, if he was going to have another go at some of the things that proved so difficult for his predecessor, former Chancellor Rachel Reeves.

He replied: "100%. I was very clear to the conference today and the public beyond. There isn't the money that there was in the 1990s. People understand that. The public aren't daft.

"Running through the Budget I deliver must be fiscal discipline and the maintenance of control on the public finances, because otherwise we won't get on top of the debt costs."

One intriguing element of what we may see on Wednesday is that this theoretically more left-leaning Labour government appears to believe they have the political capital to save money on welfare payments.

The aim is to get some of the 1.35 million people currently off work with mental health issues back into jobs.

Some reporting suggests some affected younger people may see benefits payments cut, with the government instead investing more in getting them into jobs and keeping them in them through the offer, for example, of in-work therapy.

Back in Healey's time under Gordon Brown, there was no OBR. Back then it was not unknown for late budget maths problems to be settled with an optimistic tweak of a forecast, a date change to the economic cycle, or choosing a stronger rate of long term growth.

The OBR's verdict is crucial now - to what extent it agrees with projected welfare savings or even the importance it places on stronger GDP figures matters now.

The bigger point here is that the chancellor must be shocked by the contrast between the sheer power of the Brown Treasury to do what it wanted, and the reality of what he currently faces: the constraints of the OBR, manifesto red lines, bond markets, significant debts and an energy shock.

There are reasons to postpone some of the toughest decisions beyond this Budget, such as how to fund desired increases in spending on defence and social care. The economic outlook could improve were the Iran war to settle at some point in the next few months, and after revised statistics the OBR may also have cause to rethink last year's downgrade to long term economic growth.

There is an imaginable pathway to a forecast next year with higher growth, lower inflation and lower debt interest costs, plausibly improving the public finance projections by tens of billions.

This would be a much more agreeable basis upon which to decide the pace of those big ticket spending rises. It also may be a tempting option for anyone thinking about an election. Former Treasury officials lament: "There is always a reason for procrastination."

Expect the Chancellor to laud the resilience and strength of the UK economy and seek to sustain it, and spread growth geographically. His key judgement, however, will be a balance between extra financial and economic support and the peril of still elevated borrowing costs.

He will try to offer breathing space. It may be needed not just for households and families, but for the Exchequer itself.

Wind turbines have killed 19 million bats in 40 years in the US

New Scientist October 26, 2026

Wind turbines have killed nearly 19 million bats in the US over the past four decades, according to the most comprehensive analysis of its kind to date. The problem seems to have worsened in recent years, with more than 1.5 million deaths now occurring annually.

But there may be ways of making this green energy source safer for wildlife without overly affecting energy production. This data can help “advance research to really support effective conservation measures and science-driven decision-making in the future”, says Charles Labuzzetta at Fort Collins Science Center in Colorado.

Endearing photos of bats show clever adaptations like long tongues

Bats play a vital role in ecosystems, particularly by controlling insects like mosquitoes and moths that produce crop-killing caterpillars. But many species face growing threats from habitat loss, disease and human activities, with some now classified as threatened or endangered.

Advertisement

Wind turbines are one of these human-activity threats. Researchers have previously found large numbers of dead bats at wind farms during monitoring that is required to comply with wildlife protection regulations. But not all wind farms share their results, and monitoring methods vary from site to site, says team member Bethany Straw, also at Fort Collins Science Center.

“We know bats are being impacted, but could we change the engineering or sites of a turbine to minimise those impacts?” she asks. “There’s been an increasing interest in this, but we just haven’t had the appropriate data yet.”

Free newsletter

Now, Straw, Labuzzetta and their colleagues have analysed 499 reports from wind farms across the 48 adjoining US states to estimate how many bats were killed by turbines from 1981 to 2024, focusing on 10 species. They used a statistical model that considered differences in how wind farms searched for dead bats, the size and design of their turbines, and the surrounding environment.

Their results suggest that wind turbines killed an estimated 18.7 million bats between 1981 and 2024. Annual deaths seem to have exceeded 1.5 million from 2021 onwards, which may be the result of more wind turbines being installed.

Hoary bats (Lasiurus cinereus) had the greatest losses, with an estimated 6.7 million deaths, followed by 5.8 million deaths among eastern red bats (Lasiurus borealis), 3.4 million among silver-haired bats (Lasionycteris noctivagans) and 1.5 million among big brown bats (Eptesicus fuscus).

Wind farms near rivers and turbines with longer blades were linked to more deaths among certain species, while having more space between the blades and the ground may reduce the risk.

As newer homes are built or older homes are renovated, empty attic spaces are disappearing – this eliminates a vital refuge for birds and bats during a biodiversity crisis

The researchers aren’t sure why bats fly so close to wind turbines. Previous work suggests that migratory bats mistake the structures for trees, and approach them in search of food, shelter or mates. A recent European study also found that male bats sometimes sing courtship songs around turbines, potentially attracting females into the path of spinning blades. Differences in species prevalence and behaviours may partly explain why some seem to be more at risk than others.

The researchers hope their findings will help wind farm developers protect bats by choosing safer locations and adjusting turbine designs. Research suggests that stripy wind turbines could prevent seabird collisions, for instance.

Changing when turbines operate might also help. Research shows that temporarily shutting them down during periods of high bat activity, particularly in low winds, can substantially reduce fatalities with limited loss of electricity production.

Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences DOI: 10.1073/pnas.2612674123

‘Oddball’ test lets us glimpse how monkeys see the world

New Scientist October 26, 2026

We can never know what it is like to be a bat, philosopher Thomas Nagel famously agued. But what about monkeys? Do they see the world in the same way we do?

To find out, neuroscientists in India used an “oddball” test to compare visual performances between people and macaques. They found that, although the different species scored similarly on many aspects of perception, there were two intriguing differences: the monkeys were less phased by images being flipped upside down and they seemed far more focused on fine details.

Chimps, bonobos and orangutans grasp how others view the world

There have been previous attempts to compare human and monkey vision, but the tests often require extensive training, says S. P. Arun at the Indian Institute of Science in Bengaluru. “The worry becomes: did their perception change because of all that training?” Different aspects of vision have also been studied using different tests, so it is hard to compare the results.

Advertisement

Now, Arun and his colleagues have chosen just one test, the oddball search task, which can be adapted to different visual features. Subjects are shown a set of pictures on a screen, identical apart from one, and must identify the odd one out by touching it.

When the oddball appears more similar to the other images, “it takes us longer to find the odd one out”, says Arun, providing an objective measure of perception. The researchers taught the test to three monkeys, using juice as a reward, and 24 people.

Free newsletter

In several tasks, the people and monkeys performed similarly. For instance, they both categorised inanimate objects (such as a mushroom or leaf) as more similar to each other than to animate items (such as a bird or cat).

They also both obeyed Weber’s law, which states that the smallest noticeable change in a stimulus depends on its baseline magnitude. In this case, the researchers showed that the brighter a spot was, the bigger any change in brightness had to be before either monkeys or humans could perceive it.

But there were also intriguing differences. The researchers tested a phenomenon in which people find it harder to differentiate mirror images flipped across a vertical axis compared with a horizontal one. An example of this is when young children confuse the letters “b” and “d”. This “mirror confusion” is thought to arise because we often see the things around us, such as trees or chairs, from different angles around a vertical axis, so we perceive these images as more interchangeable. We more rarely come across them upside down, so images flipped across a horizontal axis seem more different and therefore easier to tell apart.

It is impossible for us to know exactly how another person’s experience of the world compares to our own, but a new experiment is helping to reveal that colour is indeed a shared phenomenon

This is exactly what happened among the human participants in the oddball test: they took longer to identify outlier images if they were flipped around a vertical axis compared with a horizontal one. But the monkeys didn’t experience mirror confusion, and consistently showed similar performances whether images were flipped vertically or horizontally. Arun suggests this might be because these agile creatures are more used to seeing familiar objects from a range of angles. “They are swinging across stuff, and sometimes they’ll hang upside down.”

The monkeys were also highly attuned to small features, yet seemed oblivious to larger shapes. The researchers tested this using large shapes – a diamond, circle or X – made up of smaller shapes. People find it easier to tell when the overall shape changes, compared with the smaller units. “You can see the forest before you see the trees,” says Arun. But the monkeys only seemed interested in the details, and were no faster on the task when the overall shape changed as well. It isn’t clear why this is, says Arun.

This question was posed as part of New Scientist’s Last Word series, in which readers give scientific answers to each other’s questions. Here’s what our readers had to say

Rufin Vogels at KU Leuven in Belgium says the differences identified in the study are “striking”, although he cautions the results could be affected by differences in attention as well as perception.

As well as providing a glimpse into the monkey visual world, the study could have broader implications for research, says Arun, as these animals are often used as models for human vision. Although they are similar in many respects, he says, “it may not be OK to assume they see everything the way we do”.

Arun hopes the oddball approach could be used to chart vision in other systems, too. The test is so simple, even birds and bees could be trained to do it, he says. His team is now using it to investigate vision in children of different ages, including those with ADHD and autism, to understand how they might perceive the world differently than adults.

bioRxiv DOI: 10.1101/2025.01.30.635614

Predatory amphibians swam the seas 237 million years ago

New Scientist October 26, 2026

The Late Triassic seas contained a multitude of marine reptiles, but lurking on the sea floor was something different: a marine amphibian. A fossil of the large, bottom-dwelling ambush predator discovered in China is the first evidence that amphibians once found a way to adapt to life in the ocean.

Named Gerrothorax maritimus, the near-perfect and exquisitely preserved 74-centimetre-long fossil was found by farmers in what is now a national geopark in Guanling county, China.

The researchers who studied the fossil think that its secret to survival in salt water, which is normally fatal to amphibians because of their permeable skin, probably lay in its strong body armour.

Advertisement

Stunning early mammal fossil sheds light on the evolution of suckling

“It was a flat animal that lived on the sea floor,” says Ryosuke Motani at the University of California, Davis, who was part of the team that analysed the fossil. It was probably an ambush feeder, he says, as its wide mouth and the strong hyoid bone in its neck suggest it used suction feeding, as is seen in some modern bottom-dwelling predators of a similar size that use an ambush strategy, such as wobbegong sharks.

As soon as the researchers began to study the fossil, they knew it was neither fish nor reptile. It had to be an early amphibian because of its tell-tale anatomy, which included its four legs and gills.

There is, however, no evidence that the creature underwent metamorphosis, as many modern amphibians do, such as when tadpoles become frogs, says Motani.

Subscriber-only newsletter

To prove that the animal was indeed marine and not just a land-based creature washed into the sea after death, the researchers studied the strontium isotope ratios of the fossil bones.

They found that the remains of the new species had a clear signature of sea water, meaning G. maritimus grew to adulthood while in the ocean. Palaeogeographic reconstructions also suggest that, 237 million years ago in the Late Triassic Period, the location in which the fossil was discovered was at least 30 kilometres away from land.

The fossil was also recovered alongside that of a large marine reptile: an ichthyosaur called Guizhouichthyosaurus, which reached lengths of 7 metres.

Fossil mammal with reptile-like teeth changes picture of our evolution

Interestingly, the closest relative to G. maritimus lived in freshwater environments. A fossil of this amphibian, Gerrothorax pulcherrimus, was first described nearly a century ago.

This has led the researchers to suggest the marine lifestyle of G. maritimus was an accident of evolution. “There was a freshwater amphibian that happened to have the equipment needed to colonise the sea – the body armour,” says Motani.

The armour originally protected the Gerrothorax genus from predators in fresh water. But because it formed an impermeable barrier, it could also help the amphibians survive in seawater, he says.

Although it is commonly believed that “amphibious” means the ability to be on land or in the water, this is a misconception, says Motani. There are many modern newts that never leave the water, yet they are amphibians, he says.

A stunningly intact marine reptile named Austronaga minuta that lived around 245 million years ago may have looked like a miniature version of more famous later ocean predators, like plesiosaurs

“My take is that it is similar to calling a snake a tetrapod, when it does not have limbs,” says Motani.

John Long at Flinders University, Australia, says the fossil is a first, given that none of the 8000 or so living species of amphibians today is fully adapted for life in the sea.

“If not for the marine invasion by many groups of reptiles at the same time, they might have even had a chance at diversifying in this niche, but that clearly didn’t occur,” he says. “It shows us that amphibians closely related to modern forms were able to adapt to different environments, like seawater, in ways we never thought possible.”

Nature Ecology & Evolution DOI: 10.1038/s41559-026-03209-9

Your brain’s unexpected ability to regenerate and how to harness it

New Scientist October 26, 2026

For seven years, molecular biologist Ionut Dumitru and his colleagues played what felt like the world’s most exhausting game of hide-and-seek.

Yet instead of peeking around doors or under beds, they were examining brain tissue in a lab at the Karolinska Institute in Sweden, looking for something that had long evaded neuroscientists: concrete proof that the adult brain can form new neurons via a process called neurogenesis. Scientists have spent decades debating whether this is possible. As soon as one paper turned up positive clues, another would yield nothing at all.

Can we harness the brain’s deep-cleaning system to prevent Alzheimer’s?

But it seems the search may finally be over. A slew of new findings, including those from Dumitru and his team, have revealed near-certain evidence that adult neurogenesis occurs in the human hippocampus, part of the brain central to learning and memory. The discovery is forcing us to rethink long-held assumptions about our most indispensable organ, from how it functions to how it changes with age.

Advertisement

Even more exciting is the potential neurogenesis holds for brain regeneration. Some of our most devastating medical conditions, including Alzheimer’s, stroke and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), involve neurons dying at massive scale. If the brain is capable of replacing some of those lost neurons, we may be able to harness and enhance that ability, stimulating neurogenesis to help treat neurological conditions that are currently incurable.

“To many of us, we think the question is no longer whether it exists or not,” says neuroscientist Hongjun Song at the University of Pennsylvania. “It’s, how can we take advantage of that?”

Neurons are the brain’s key messengers, transmitting the signals that underpin our most basic functions, from moving and talking to thinking and dreaming. They form when a stem cell – which can morph into other cell types – transforms into a “parent” progenitor cell, which then births an immature neuron that eventually matures.

Scientists long believed this process played out only during development in the womb and, to a lesser degree, during childhood and adolescence. In other words, humans were born with essentially all the neurons they would ever have. The brain would change in many ways over one’s lifetime – forming new connections between neurons and pruning away those that were no longer necessary – but it wasn’t going to get a windfall of new neurons. Or at least, so we thought.

In the early 1960s, Joseph Altman, a biologist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, went against the grain by looking for signs of neurogenesis in adult rats. He injected the animals with a radioactive tracer used to track cell division, then identified cells bearing it in the rodents’ brains, revealing what appeared to be freshly generated neurons.

But the finding was widely panned by the neuroscience community. The idea that adult neurogenesis was impossible “had really been embedded within the scientific literature”, says Fred “Rusty” Gage, a neuroscientist at the Salk Institute for Biological Studies in California.

Altman was apparently undeterred, replicating his findings in the brains of additional rats and then cats. Other researchers eventually joined in, finding adult neurogenesis in species such as canaries and monkeys, and discovering that it seemed to play a role in learning and memory – helping birds learn new songs, for instance.

But whether human brains also pump out new neurons remained an open question. You can’t ethically crack open a living person’s skull and dig around in their brain tissue.

Free newsletter

Gage and his colleagues found an ingenious workaround to that problem. In the 1990s, some people being treated for cancer received injections of a chemical called BrdU, which flagged dividing cells so that doctors could monitor disease spread. When five such patients had died, Gage and his colleagues were able to autopsy their brains. Lo and behold, they found BrdU in hippocampal cells – a sign of neurogenesis.

The trouble is that BrdU can sometimes flag cells undergoing repair, not necessarily division. And subsequent studies that used different markers yielded results all over the map. Some showed next to no neurogenesis in the adult brain; others, that the adult hippocampus adds 700 new neurons every single day, on a par with that of a much younger brain.

So, Song and his colleagues pioneered a different approach. Instead of looking for immature neurons with just one or two markers, they analysed the full genetic profile of individual brain cells, searching for the genetic characteristics of freshly generated cells. They discovered immature neurons in people who had died across all stages of life, even up to age 92.

But spotting a young neuron still isn’t enough to prove the adult brain is generating new ones. Neurons can linger in an immature state for a long time, perhaps even an entire lifespan. These Peter Pans of the brain aren’t necessarily created in adulthood; they just aren’t growing up.

The real challenge in proving adult neurogenesis occurs was to capture each stage of the process – and one remained elusive. “Nobody had identified the proliferating progenitors,” says Dumitru. “They could identify immature neurons, they could identify maybe stem cells – so the cells that are at the beginning and end of the trajectory – but nobody identified the proliferating ones.”

To identify these cells, which actually birth new neurons, Dumitru and his colleagues genetically analysed roughly 400,000 brain cells from the hippocampi of people who had died between infancy and adulthood. They used a machine learning model – a type of artificial intelligence – to pinpoint genetic patterns that resembled those seen in progenitors from animals and developing infants.

The overlooked power of diet for improving your mental health

The researchers almost couldn’t believe it when they spotted the first few progenitors. “It was so difficult to convince ourselves,” says team member Marta Paterlini, a molecular biologist also at the Karolinska Institute.

But after years of testing and re-testing, they finally felt confident their search was over. They found only about 350 progenitor cells – and they weren’t present in all the brains sampled. But by finding any at all, “we showed that there is active neurogenesis” in the hippocampus, says Dumitru. “That cannot be contested.”

Except that, well, some scientists still do. Developmental neurobiologist Arturo Alvarez-Buylla at the University of California, San Francisco, isn’t convinced that machine learning models can reliably categorise cell types. He says the only way to know for certain that adult neurogenesis happens would be to track a stem cell as it transforms into a neuron – a nearly impossible task to do in a living human.

But sceptics like Alvarez-Buylla are increasingly finding themselves outside a coalescing consensus. At least 38 clinical trials related to adult neurogenesis are now under way. “It’s there,” says Sandrine Thuret, a neuroscientist at King’s College London. “The new debate is, what is it for?”

One of the first clues to answering that question comes from the fact that adult neurogenesis appears almost exclusive to the hippocampus, the brain’s headquarters of learning and memory. This region is highly plastic, meaning it can easily reorganise itself and form new connections, helping us to take in and remember new information.

In a study from earlier this year, neuroscientist Orly Lazarov at the University of Illinois College of Medicine and her colleagues found that neurogenesis may play a role in this process. They examined post-mortem hippocampus samples from adults who had Alzheimer’s and adults without cognitive impairments, including “superagers” – people in their eighties or older who had outperformed younger adults on a memory test. On average, superagers had roughly twice as many immature neurons in their hippocampus as adults without cognitive impairments. People with Alzheimer’s had almost none at all.

In our efforts to keep our brains healthy, how do we know what is working? Helen Thomson explores a new generation of tests that can reveal whether our efforts are paying off

The finding suggests that neurogenesis is closely linked with cognition and may even stave off its decline. Some of the superagers with an abundance of immature neurons also showed signs of Alzheimer’s in their brains, including the condition’s characteristic plaques and tangles. It is possible that enhanced neurogenesis allows the brain to bypass or overcome what would otherwise contribute to cognitive decline, says Lazarov.

Several studies within the past year have also found neurogenesis is impaired in other conditions like Parkinson’s and depression. The latter finding comes from the lab of René Hen, a neuroscientist at Columbia University, New York, who has spent the past 20 years trying to understand the connection between neurogenesis and depression.

His interest began after coming across a study that showed rats dosed with antidepressants had increased rates of neurogenesis. Curious about whether this could explain how antidepressants work, Hen ran a follow-up experiment and found that if he manipulated rodents’ brains to stop producing new neurons, they also stopped responding to antidepressants. Hen was hooked and has been investigating the link ever since.

He and his colleagues have shown that, at least in animals, hippocampal neurogenesis seems crucial for pattern separation – the ability to distinguish between different objects, situations and emotions and remember them appropriately. This process is impaired in depression, as well as other psychiatric conditions in which neurogenesis may go awry, such as schizophrenia and bipolar disorder. It may explain why people with depression can tend to overgeneralise, for example, interpreting one bad day as evidence that things will always be bad, says Hen.

Like Alzheimer’s disease, these mental health conditions are also associated with smaller hippocampal volumes. While there are probably multiple factors that contribute to this, it is possible that impaired neurogenesis is one of them, says Hen.

Finding a way to stimulate neurogenesis could, therefore, be a promising treatment approach. Several studies have indicated that already available medications, such as antidepressants and the diabetes medication metformin, could stoke neurogenesis.

But there could be more advanced ways of manipulating the process. For instance, if we can pinpoint why superagers have increased neurogenesis, and why it seems to be protective, we could potentially develop therapies that mimic these effects. “We might be able to provide some kind of shield [against cognitive decline],” says Lazarov.

Harnessing neurogenesis could even treat conditions it isn’t directly involved in, such as traumatic brain injury or stroke. A 2025 study showed that transplanting neural progenitor cells into the brains of mice after a stroke led to the production of new neurons and helped the animals regain lost movement.

Still, it will take years to determine whether any neurogenesis interventions work, and even longer to bring them to market if they do. Song and his team are trying to speed up the process by developing miniature models, or organoids, of the human hippocampus. Because these organoids capture what happens in the living human brain more accurately than animal models, they could make it easier to identify therapies that boost neurogenesis, says Song. Other researchers are trying to develop non-invasive brain-imaging techniques to measure neurogenesis in living people, with similar goals.

There may be simpler interventions, too. “Lifestyle is an easy way of modulating, potentially, neurogenesis,” says Thuret.

Research has long shown that neurogenesis increases in rats when they are mentally stimulated, such as by having roommates or fun toys in their cages; people may similarly benefit from enriching activities like socialising or learning a new skill.

Exercise also shows promise, at least in rodents. Gage and his colleagues found that when adult rats run on exercise wheels, they produce more immature neurons than sedentary rodents. They also do a better job navigating a maze, signifying enhanced cognitive performance.

Thuret was curious whether the same could be true for humans. So earlier this year, she and her team exposed human hippocampal stem cells to blood serum taken from adults who had completed a three-month exercise programme and those who hadn’t. But instead of stoking neurogenesis, blood from the exercisers actually reduced the number of stem cells ready to become new neurons.

Thuret is still trying to unravel what this means. But given that it is well established that exercise benefits brain health, it may not necessarily be a negative outcome. It is possible that physical activity helps regulate the pace at which stem cells transform into neurons, reserving some for future development, she says.

It is intuitive to think that if impaired neurogenesis is bad, cranking it up to 11 would be good. But too much neurogenesis could backfire, says Thuret. Cancer, a disease of unchecked cell growth, is a prime example of how more isn’t always better when it comes to the human body.

This is just one reason why indiscriminately turning up neurogenesis probably isn’t a viable treatment option. It is more likely that therapies of the future will be targeted, tweaking neurogenesis in different ways and to different levels to treat various conditions, rather than having an across-the-board fix, says Thuret.

To gain the benefits of sleep, it was thought that the whole brain must switch off. But experiments suggest the right kind of rest can encourage our brain to improve memory and learning while we’re awake.

Plus, as far as researchers have been able to tell, neurogenesis is mostly confined to the hippocampus. Many cognitive and psychiatric symptoms originate there, but not all of them. For example, a completely different brain region mediates anhedonia – the inability to feel joy, which is a hallmark of depression. “I don’t think that a drug that stimulates neurogenesis is going to cure anhedonia,” says Hen. “The medicine of the future is probably going to be a medicine where we use multiple drugs, each one targeting specific symptoms.”

Unless, of course, neurogenesis isn’t limited to the hippocampus at all.

After finding progenitor cells in the hippocampus, Dumitru, Paterlini and their colleagues didn’t celebrate for long. Instead, they embarked on a new search, turning their attention to the subventricular zone, another part of the brain that some studies suggest is capable of neurogenesis well into adulthood. The work is in early stages, says Dumitru, but already they have spotted signs of progenitor cells in adult samples of this area – a new game of hide-and-seek has begun.

Satellites show some of the strongest evidence the AMOC is weakening

New Scientist October 26, 2026

Satellite measurements suggest the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) has been transporting less heat towards Europe, providing some of the strongest evidence yet of a slowdown in these ocean currents, which keep Europe’s climate mild.

The AMOC system of currents, which includes the Gulf Stream, brings warm, salty water from the Gulf of Mexico to the north Atlantic, where it cools and sinks, returning south along the sea floor.

The collapse of the AMOC would be catastrophic. How will we know when it’s coming?

As it cools, the water releases heat into the atmosphere. But based on the satellite data, Richard Allan at the University of Reading, UK, and his colleagues calculated that the heat flux out of the north Atlantic has decreased 18 per cent in 40 years.

Advertisement

Because the AMOC’s flow varies from year to year, the scientists used the first decade of data to estimate an average flow. They compared this to the following decades to find the circulation has declined 14 per cent in 30 years.

“We expect the AMOC to deliver heat northwards, and then that heat to come out of the top of the ocean into the atmosphere, and so if one of those things is changing, we expect the other one to change,” says Neil Fraser at the Scottish Association for Marine Science, who wasn’t involved in the study. “This is some of the strongest evidence so far that the AMOC has weakened over the last 40 years.”

Climate models suggest the surge of fresh water from the melting Greenland ice sheet will dilute the salty water of the AMOC and slow its sinking, weakening the circulation. Some research suggests the AMOC could collapse as soon as 2060, plunging Europe into “ice age” winters with stronger storms and widespread drought.

Free newsletter

Ocean buoys across the Atlantic have measured changes in water pressure corresponding to about a 10 per cent decline in AMOC strength since 2004, but because its flow can sometimes ebb for decades at a time, this doesn’t prove a long-term trend.

Scientists have looked for indirect evidence, like the “cold blob” in the north Atlantic, the only area of the world that has cooled since the 1800s. A 2018 analysis of these declining sea-surface temperatures estimated the AMOC had weakened 15 per cent since the 1950s.

But sea-surface temperatures could also be decreasing due to a shift in jet stream winds or increased shading by clouds. Heat flux from the north Atlantic to the atmosphere can be a better indicator as it is “one step closer to the thing that drives AMOC”, says David Thornalley at University College London.

Last year, a study calculated this heat flux from atmospheric reanalyses, which are essentially computer models that are nudged to match the spotty real-world observations on record. But the results didn’t show any decline in AMOC strength between 1963 and 2017.

The new study, which is undergoing peer review, is the first to estimate AMOC weakening with heat fluxes calculated in part from satellite measurements, according to Allan. For decades, the ratio between how much solar energy Earth receives and how much heat energy it radiates back into space has been growing more positive. The researchers combined satellite measurements of this energy imbalance with reanalyses and models to figure out how much less heat the north Atlantic has been releasing to the atmosphere.

“The resulting inferred net air-sea flux is of demonstrably better quality than other estimates, making this estimate more suitable to infer AMOC changes,” says team member Michael Mayer at the University of Vienna.

And because satellite measurements can be updated regularly, this method, if it holds up to scrutiny, could someday “provide a new early warning method for detecting changes in this vital current”, says Allan. The UK is investing £81 million in research to build an early warning system for AMOC collapse by 2030, although this study isn’t part of the initiative.

Stefan Rahmstorf at the University of Potsdam, Germany, argues that heat flux isn’t necessarily a better indicator of AMOC changes than sea-surface temperatures, which can be directly measured. But he says the two build on each other to increase concern that the AMOC could be approaching a tipping point.

Another recent study, which examined reanalyses of the ocean rather than the atmosphere, similarly found the AMOC has weakened 15 per cent in 30 years.

“The strongest evidence is the combination of several different lines of evidence, all pointing to a slowing AMOC,” says Rahmstorf.

What are microchimeric cells doing to our brain?

New Scientist October 26, 2026

We tend to imagine ourselves as having one brain that is entirely our own, built from our own DNA. Yet tucked away within this landscape are cells from other people – our mothers and, for those who have been pregnant, our children.

During pregnancy, maternal cells cross the placenta, while fetal cells travel in the opposite direction. Some remain long after birth, a phenomenon called microchimerism. I’ve always found this bidirectional cellular legacy fascinating, particularly now we know that some of these cells settle in the brain. My children, born via donated eggs, didn’t inherit my DNA, but microchimerism means that some of my cells may nevertheless live within them, while theirs may live within me.

I’ve always wondered what influence they might have, and a recent study prompted me to investigate. Are these cells simply passengers, or do they help shape the brains we grow up with?

Advertisement

Can you hack your brain to be ultra-productive?

In 2008, researchers first detected maternal cells in human fetal brain tissue. Four years later, another team found male DNA in women’s brains, probably acquired during pregnancies with male fetuses. Finding traces of another person is one thing. But establishing what those cells become, and whether they do anything useful, is another.

The new research, published this month and not yet peer-reviewed, brings us closer to answering those questions. Sami Kanaan at Fred Hutchinson Cancer Center in Seattle and his colleagues detected maternal DNA in samples of brain tissue taken from children with epilepsy. They then examined RNA from these samples, alongside data from people without epilepsy. This cellular instruction manual revealed that the maternal cells had developed into a diverse cast that included neurons, immune cells, blood vessel cells and supporting cells called astrocytes.

“It was a surprise to see naturally occurring microchimerism detected in the human brain with such highly diverse neuronal, glial, immune and vascular identities, in both healthy and diseased cohorts,” says Kanaan.

The results suggest that cells from another person can acquire characteristics of the brain itself – although why we may need these maternal cells instead of just our own isn’t yet clear. But we have some clues from animals.

In 2022, researchers compared mice carrying reduced numbers of maternal cells with those carrying typical levels, recording their brain activity and behaviour. The results suggested that maternal cells help regulate the brain’s resident immune cells, preventing excessive pruning of connections between neurons.

Mice with fewer maternal cells had disrupted communication between the prefrontal cortex and the hippocampus, regions involved in planning and memory. These mice also performed worse on tasks that involved recalling previously learned information.

This points to maternal cells possibly playing a role by helping the fetal brain wire itself during early development. “Whether comparable mechanisms operate in humans remains an open question,” says Kanaan.

However, he’s happy to speculate. Kanaan says there is already evidence in humans that maternal cells can influence the developing immune system, and that it’s reasonable to expect that the same might be extended to the brain.

He also says cells travelling in the other direction might have a role in healing: “In a mouse experiment, enhanced recruitment of fetal cells accompanied reduced brain injury and changes consistent with repair.”

Human organoids restore cognition in mice with half a brain

The idea that fetal cells are key to repair has been suggested in humans, too. In the 2012 study that detected male DNA in the brains of 37 of 59 women, there was a lower prevalence among those with Alzheimer’s. This could imply that fetal cells protect the brain. But the study couldn’t establish cause and effect, so we can’t rule out the possibility that the condition might have affected the persistence of these cells.

This is a common problem within the field. While microchimeric cells have been associated with Parkinson’s disease, multiple sclerosis, stroke and brain tumours, in each case it’s challenging to distinguish whether they are contributing to the condition or have been recruited to repair injuries.

Evolution offers some intriguing possibilities for their role too. David Haig at Harvard University argues that mothers and their children have a shared evolutionary interest in each other’s well-being, suggesting that natural selection may therefore tend to eliminate negative effects on health and favour beneficial effects of this cellular exchange.

However, Haig thinks their evolutionary “interests” don’t always align, particularly when it comes to how a mother’s resources are shared. “It is possible,” he says, “that offspring cells in a mother’s brain may promote care (and attachment) toward the offspring from whom the cells come, whereas maternal cells in offspring brains may favour cooperation toward the mother and with other siblings.”

For now, that remains a hypothesis. Still, all of these potential impacts on our health and behaviour raise a question. Why do some brains harbour more microchimeric cells than others? In Kanaan and his team’s study, for instance, despite maternal cells being found in the majority of samples, some had around 2.2 maternal cells per 100,000 cells, while others had up to 458.9 cells per 100,000. Do we know why?

“The answer is no, we do not know,” says Haig. He suspects there are genetic factors that contribute to this disparity.

For instance, cells carry proteins that help the immune system recognise whether a cell is “self” or “foreign”, but levels of recognition and tolerance vary, which may influence the number of microchimeric cells that survive.

Medical history may matter, too. For instance, pre-eclampsia, a dangerous condition characterised by high blood pressure in pregnancy, increases the permeability of the blood-brain barrier and may allow more fetal cells to cross into a mother’s brain.

What’s the world actually like, if what we see is just our brain’s interpretations?

Some differences may just be about sampling limitations – some brain regions can have more cells than another, meaning a negative sample doesn’t imply they aren’t present elsewhere.

Unfortunately, none of this allows us to say definitively that more microchimerism is better, or that we should be seeking ways to promote this cellular exchange to help protect brain health.

It may not be a satisfying conclusion, but it’s early days. The mere fact that the central nervous system can sustain, integrate and potentially benefit from genetically foreign cellular material at all goes against so much of how we thought our immune system worked. So, it may be a while before we truly get to grips with whether microchimeric cells contribute to resilience, vulnerability or repair – or all three in different contexts.

Until clearer answers emerge, I choose to take comfort in the possibility that some of my mum’s cells may remain within me. And although I can’t quite explain why (a genetic connection doesn’t define my concept of family), I also find something quietly moving about the possibility that my own cells have taken up residence in my children’s brains, potentially shaping their minds in unknown ways – and their cells possibly shaping mine in equal measure.

Personalised cancer vaccine expected to be approved next year

New Scientist October 23, 2026

A personalised mRNA vaccine for melanoma, the deadliest form of skin cancer, is expected to be approved for use in the US, Europe and the UK next year. The vaccine is designed to stimulate immune responses against genetic mutations that are unique to an individual’s cancer. When used alongside standard treatment in a late-stage trial, it substantially cut the risk of cancer recurrence or death within the next two years.

“I think approval could be quick, and next year sounds reasonable,” says Alan Melcher at the Institute of Cancer Research in London, who wasn’t involved in the trial.

Rare cancer spread between twins in utero

“It is a huge deal,” says Rebecca Lee at the University of Manchester, UK, who also wasn’t involved. Thousands of people in the UK alone could benefit from this, based on the trial’s patient population, she says. “It’s highly likely the US and Europe [including the UK] will approve it next year.” However, producing the vaccine is very expensive, and it may not be deemed cost-effective for use on the UK’s National Health Services (NHS), she says.

Advertisement

In August, drug-maker Moderna announced that the vaccine had positive results in a late-stage trial. More specific findings have now been released.

The trial recruited more than 1100 adults who had surgery to remove high-risk melanomas that were likely to recur or spread to distant sites. In the UK, 19,400 melanoma cases are diagnosed annually, of which about 25 per cent are deemed high risk.

Two-thirds of the participants were randomly assigned to receive a bespoke vaccine on top of standard immunotherapy, called pembrolizumab, which helps the immune system find and destroy cancer. Both were delivered every three weeks for up to a year. The remaining participants received placebo injections plus pembrolizumab.

The vaccine is made by genetically sequencing a small sample of a person’s cancer and comparing that sequence with the DNA in the individual’s healthy blood cells. This enables researchers to pinpoint mutations specific to the cancer.

Free newsletter

Based on the same technology used in covid-19 vaccines, the cancer vaccine contains mRNA molecules that encode for proteins with up to 34 of those mutations. “The jab contains a fingerprint of proteins specifically associated with the cancer,” says Lee. “This helps [immune] T-cells recognise the cancer better, and then pembrolizumab prevents those T-cells from becoming exhausted once they’ve started attacking the cancer cells.”

About two years after the start of treatment, 82 per cent of the participants who received the vaccine plus pembrolizumab were alive without their cancer recurring, on average, compared with 70 per cent among those on pembrolizumab alone. “It’s a really exciting result,” says Lee. Side effects were similar between the two groups.

The results combine cancer recurrence and death rates into one figure, but since a treated cancer has to recur for it to cause death, this combined measure should be interpreted mostly as a sign of the vaccine reducing recurrence, says Melcher. The participants haven’t been tracked for long enough to robustly determine whether the vaccine improves survival rates. These results should be available within a few years, says Lee.

We have long treated cancer based on its location in the body. But a whole new approach that analyses tumours differently is now helping people survive forms of cancer that were once considered a death sentence

But because the vaccine has to be tailored to and manufactured for each individual, it is expected to be very costly, which could affect NHS access. “If it was a cheap drug, I’d definitely say it will get approved [for NHS use], but it’s going to be expensive,” says Lee. In January, a report by Reuters suggested it would cost around $200,000 per treatment. Moderna and Merck (also known as MSD), which was also involved in the vaccine’s development, did not respond to a request about its cost.

Further research is needed to better understand who is mostly likely to benefit from the vaccine, says Melcher. Some people may have mutations included in their vaccine that fail to stimulate anti-cancer immunity as predicted, or pembrolizumab could work so well that the vaccine can’t lead to further improvement. “If we can find immune markers in the blood or tumour that predict patient responses, we could use those to determine who to give the jab to,” says Melcher.

James Larkin, also at the Institute of Cancer Research, says personalised vaccines could also work for other types of cancer, such as those affecting the lungs, bladder and kidneys, which are also routinely treated with immunotherapy. Further research is needed to verify this and explore whether the vaccines could work as standalone treatments.

Determining whether the discrepancies are deliberate is impossible because Meta’s systems are opaque, says David Nemer at the University of Virginia. “But when a technical glitch tends to repeat its outcome, it’s very hard to accept that this is just a technical failure.”

The comeback has been partly credited to Lula’s Army, an intensive online campaign in which 8 million WhatsApp channel subscribers receive daily tasks, such as posting photographs on Instagram posing with their fingers forming an L.

This year’s general election is Brazil’s first since large language models (LLMs) became widely popular, and it is awash with AI-generated content. Experts say Latin America’s largest democracy offers a glimpse of what is to come for AI in politics.

Do AIs already process information in a way that gives rise to consciousness?

Meta’s independent oversight board says the company’s election safeguards have failed.

“It’s very worrying,” says Nemer. “So much of our political campaign dynamics have been transferred to privatised companies that we have no idea how they operate.”

Regulating AI in political campaigns won’t be as simple as it seems, says Heloísa Massaro at InternetLab, a Brazilian digital rights non-profit that studied how eight major AI chatbots respond to questions about Brazil’s election.

Its report found that chatbots sometimes refused genuine questions about candidates, referring users to official electoral websites, but would agree to draft misleading claims questioning the integrity of elections for use in campaigning.

Massaro says clearer safeguards for LLMs are needed, but first their objectives must be defined.

“Are the safeguards working? That’s one question. But working for what, because it depends on what your goals are,” she says. “Is the solution to send people away without providing any kind of information? Is this what we want?”

Body temperature may drive the higher risk of autoimmune conditions in women

New Scientist October 23, 2026

The menstrual cycle and menopause mean that women’s body temperature fluctuates more than men’s, which could help explain why they are much more likely to develop autoimmune conditions. Our body temperature influences our immune response, and frequent fluctuations in women could affect their immune cells’ ability to differentiate between a dangerous invader and healthy tissue.

“If women’s immune cells are experiencing more changes in temperature, they might be getting more overwhelmed and dysfunctional, which could contribute to an increased risk of autoimmunity,” says Elizabeth Maloney at the Pasteur Institute in Paris, who presented the findings at the Immunology of the Exposome conference at the Royal Society in London on 12 October. “It could be one piece of the puzzle in understanding sex differences in immunity.”

We may finally have a cure for many different autoimmune conditions

Women generally mount stronger immune responses than men, making them less prone to infections. But this comes at a cost: women are up to four times more likely to develop autoimmune conditions, such as lupus or rheumatoid arthritis, which occur when the immune system overreacts to healthy tissue.

Advertisement

Such differences are due to several factors, including the genetics that determine sex. Most women have two copies of the X chromosome, which carries many immune genes, whereas most men have one X and one Y chromosome. This means women have greater genetic variation, strengthening their immune response.

Hormonal differences also play a role. Oestrogen, the main sex hormone in women, generally bolsters immune system activity in those of reproductive age, while declining levels during perimenopause and menopause seem to accelerate inflammation, which plays a big role in autoimmunity. Men’s main sex hormone, testosterone, generally reduces inflammation.

Now, Maloney and her colleagues have looked at the role of body temperature. They measured the core body temperatures of more than 900 adults, aged between 20 and 69, via a thermometer in the inner ear. The group was made up of a roughly equal number of men and women, none of whom had a known autoimmune condition.

Free newsletter

The researchers also collected blood samples, which they exposed to a powerful immune-stimulating protein from Staphylococcus aureus bacteria in a test tube.

The one-off temperature readings were similar between the men and women. But among the women’s blood samples, a higher body temperature was linked to suppression of T-cells in response to the protein. T-cells are part of the adaptive immune system, which responds to threats like viruses or – inappropriately – to molecules in the body. The latter response can bring about autoimmune conditions.

Among the women’s samples, the researchers found that every 1°C (1.8°F) increase in body temperature was linked to a 36 per cent decrease in these cells’ ability to produce interferon-gamma. This is an inflammatory protein that enhances the ability of T-cells to attack target cells, whether they are healthy or infected.

“This may be counterintuitive because we generally think of fever as stimulating inflammation,” says team member Darragh Duffy, also at the Pasteur Institute. But it seems there is also a mechanism by which high temperature can dial down the immune response to stop it getting out of hand, he says.

One interpretation of the sex differences in the results is that the more frequent temperature fluctuations experienced by women caused their T-cells to switch between suppressed and activated states more often, says Maloney.

Antibodies mistakenly attacking the brain are linked with conditions including schizophrenia, dementia and OCD, prompting a revolution in how we think about mental health conditions

The core body temperature of premenopausal women rises by about 0.6°C (around 1°F), on average, after ovulation, then falls a day or two before menstruation. Perimenopause and menopause can also cause sudden increases in body temperature, manifesting as hot flushes. “Maybe the adaptive immune system is having to constantly change its set point, which sort of wears it out, and then that contributes to autoimmune risk,” says Maloney.

“The findings add another dimension to sex differences in immune function,” says Sabra Klein at Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore. Future studies should examine whether body temperature affects immune responses between men and women independently of their hormonal differences, she says.

They could also track links between the menstrual cycle, body temperature and T-cell response, says Maloney. For now, the team is working with another group of researchers to implement body-temperature measurements in a vaccine trial starting next year, she says.

Labour leader Chris Hipkins said he was “happy” for Labour to commit to a “safe staffing model” for our hospitals.

Asked by Hosking whether Labour’s policy to improve New Zealand’s emergency departments with fixes like making better use of ward beds to discharge people would make a serious difference, Hipkins said every change would help.

Subsidising access to GLP-1s through Pharmac would be a “win win” for New Zealand, according to an Auckland University medical professor.

New research has found more than 80% of healthcare spending in New Zealand goes into treating chronic and long-term conditions.

A huge percentage of those conditions were tied to obesity, Professor of Molecular Medicine and Pathology Peter Shepherd told Newstalk ZB’s Mike Hosking Breakfast.

“We’ve now got these wonderful medications to reduce weight, and they’re showing massive effects long-term in terms of improved outcomes for heart disease, for Alzheimer’s, for diabetes ... we need to start proactively funding some of these solutions.”

Some 30-40,000 Kiwis were already paying for the medicines themselves.

“But if we funded it more widely, it'll benefit not just those people who are suffering, but also the rest of us by reducing healthcare bills.”

Illegal versions of the drugs cost around $100-$200 per month and Shepherd predicted official medications would cost a similar amount once patents ended.

Labour and National's education spokespeople have laid out areas where they can find common ground.

On Newstalk ZB's Early Edition mini education debate, Ginny Andersen and Erica Stanford mostly argued and talked over each other; however, they outlined some areas they hope to agree on.

Andersen said she wished to find common ground with Stanford on learning support.

"We know there's a really big amount of children increasing who need extra support for a whole range of reasons and I think that's one of the biggest challenges going forward for the education system."

Stanford said she hoped her Labour counterpart would agree to keep structured literacy in place.

"The issue we've now got is they [Labour] don't like the twice-yearly assessments, they don't like an hour a day, and they want to keep the, you know, the failing NCEA in place.

"Those things are core things that are part of the way we're going to raise achievement and close the equity gap in this country."

Labour leader Chris Hipkins said he wanted the ability to discipline ministers in his Government regardless of which party they come from.

Recently, Prime Ministers have sacked and disciplined ministers from their own party, but ministers from other parties often received an easier ride.

Appearing in a two hour segment with Mike Hosking, Hipkins said he wanted the Cabinet Manual written into any coalition agreement. The Cabinet Manual, which sets out the conduct of ministers, is referenced in the coalition deals that formed the current Government, with ministers in the Government agreeing to be bound by it.

“It’s just not being followed at the moment,” Hipkins said.

“I think we need to get back to enforcing the basic standards,” he said.

Hipkins said he would leave the option of a minority Government on the table.

Labour leader Chris Hipkins said Kerrin Leoni did not give a “full disclosure” to him and the party about the extent of her engagement with gangs.

Appearing in a two-hour segment with Mike Hosking, Hipkins also said he made it clear to Leoni that her position was “untenable” before she resigned.

Hipkins was asked whether Leoni lied about the extent of her engagement with gangs. He replied, “she didn’t tell us the full extent of her engagement”.

Asked whether he would have sacked Leoni if she hadn’t quit first, Hipkins said he “made it clear through the people speaking to her [Leoni] that her position was untenable”.

At that point, Hipkins said, Lenoi indicated she was withdrawing from the campaign anyway.

Hosking noted that Leoni has now said she will campaign as an independent instead of withdrawing from the race.

Hipkins said: “I don’t think she’ll win.”

King Country Rugby Union backs Mangakino sportsground lighting upgrade

New Zealand Herald October 26, 2026

Mangakino Sportsgrounds. Photo / Taupō District Council

Ballers and footy players in Mangakino hope for a brighter future now that Taupō District Council has applied for funding to extend and upgrade the lights.

Taupō district councillor Hope Woodward said she had heard of people using cars to light up the basketball court on Rangatira Drive when playing at night.

A local rugby player also reached out to her, saying basketball players weren’t the only ones jumping around in the dark as the Mangakino Sportsgrounds on Wairenga Rd didn’t have a full night-lighting set-up.

Aside from being the local rugby battlefield the Mangakino Sportsgrounds house the training barracks of the King Country Rugby Union youth and senior grade rep teams.

The union covers parts of the King Country, Taupō and South Waikato districts, which puts the Mangakino Sportsground roughly in the middle.

King Country Rugby Union community rugby manager Joshua Standen said they used the grounds often for age-grade and senior rep teams.

“We [also] have a lot of development days and coaching clinics out there.”

Standen said the grounds would benefit from night lights since training on weeknights was common, because the weekends were game days for the rep squads.

The council agreed that the current sportsground lighting was limited and uneven.

The council has been working with the Mangakino community on an upgrade proposal for the lights, which includes new poles and LED floodlights.

However, the upgrades weren’t included in Taupō District Council’s annual budget with council staff instead hoping for funding through the NZ Rugby Legacy Fund and Sports NZ Grassroots Spaces & Places Fund.

The council hopes to secure $122,550 needed to fund the lights project.

A council spokesperson confirmed their application to the Legacy Fund was endorsed days before applications closed this month.

The Sports NZ Grassroots funds are accessible through Sport Waikato and the council is also working with it to secure funding to light the sportsgrounds.

Standen said he wrote a letter supporting these applications because the upgrades would make the sportsgrounds, “a bit more user-friendly”.

Meanwhile, Woodward said she has an idea of how to solve the issue for the ballers.

“I’ve also asked that the existing rugby ground lights be considered for our basketball courts.”

She said the upgrades had been a long time coming and her community needed the upgrades.

“Our sportsgrounds are more than just places to play sport.

“They’re spaces where our people, particularly our rangatahi, find belonging, confidence and connection.

“In communities like Mangakino, these spaces are invaluable.”

The council said that if it was successful in securing the funding, new lights could be in place in time for the 2027 winter rugby season.
