WoolWorks: NZ’s biggest wool scouring factory rises from the flood

New Zealand Herald October 26, 2026

WoolWorks chief executive Rosstan Mazey stands surrounded by bales of freshly scoured wool, ready for export to manufacturers around the world. Photo / Penny Miles

By Penny Miles of RNZ

When shearing reaches its busiest period on farms around the North Island from December to March, the WoolWorks scouring plant in Hawke’s Bay will process about 165,000kg of wool each day.

It’s critical infrastructure for the farming sector, transforming fleece from hill country shearing sheds into the clean, dry, pressed product ready for manufacturers to make carpets and building products.

The factory south of Napier at Awatoto transforms greasy wool, packing it into bales using a new German wool press that exerts 600 tonnes of pressure.

The bales then start a long journey in shipping containers to manufacturers around the world.

“To put that back to sheep numbers, that’s around about 50,000 sheep.

“So that’s every day. It’s a lot of farms, so it’s big numbers,” WoolWorks chief executive Rosstan Mazey told RNZ’s Country Life.

Think about doing your laundry 10 times over – that’s roughly what happens to wool from thousands of sheep every day at the busy plant.

You can hear forklifts buzzing and beeping as they carry heavy bales around the floor.

Wash basins bubble, dryers rumble, and the wool press thumps.

Despite some rough times for the sector, Mazey believes there’s a bright future for the country’s wool exports.

He points to one innovative customer, Ngamatea Station, which sends its scoured wool to be made into tennis-ball felt, used on the courts of the world’s biggest Grand Slam tournaments.

“We’ve had a tricky last year with the amount of greasy wool that’s been taken out of New Zealand, primarily to China,” Mazey said.

“We’re seeing the situation change quite quickly over there just in the last couple of months.

“Their appetite for greasy wool from New Zealand is starting to reduce.

“We’re also seeing renewed interest for other scoured wool markets, particularly from Europe and India.”

Industry leaders are also hopeful that the India Free Trade Deal will strengthen ties with Indian manufacturers and, in turn, boost demand for New Zealand wool.

The vast majority of the wool scoured at WoolWorks – about 85% – goes to China, India, the United States and Europe, where it’s made into rugs, bedding, carpets and building materials.

About 15% stays in New Zealand.

Carpet and rug manufacturers Bremworth and Godfrey Hirst continue to manufacture fine wool carpets here.

Wool is also becoming more popular in building design; Auckland-based Autex makes insulation and acoustic panels.

Another Kiwi based in the South Island, Terra Lana, makes insulation, acoustic control and landscaping products using scoured wool.

You wouldn’t know it now, but three and a half years ago, the WoolWorks factory was inundated when stopbanks along the Ngaruroro River gave way during Cyclone Gabrielle.

During the cyclone, the water rose to about 2m.

Processing equipment was submerged and thick, silt-laden mud was left across the factory floor.

It was months before the water subsided, and the rebuild lasted more than a year.

WoolWorks Group Assurance Manager Tony Cunningham said the rebuild was significant.

There was a full rewiring of the plant.

New electronic monitoring equipment was installed, and damaged machines pieced back together by engineers.

Cunningham said it’s crucial that New Zealand maintains its wool-scouring capacity, despite some companies sending greasy wool offshore.

He said most of Australia’s wool is now scoured in China.

The manufacturer is also grappling with high energy costs and declining sheep numbers.

And while some sheep farmers have switched in recent years to Wiltshire sheep, which shed their fleece, many are sticking with traditional meat and wool breeds such as the Romney as wool prices inch up.

Christchurch street assault victim appalled as repeat violent offender walks free

New Zealand Herald October 26, 2026

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

This is a modal window.

Beginning of dialog window. Escape will cancel and close the window.

End of dialog window.

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

A Christchurch man who feared retaliation after being randomly assaulted in a daylight street attack says he was never given the chance to provide a victim impact statement before a repeat violent offender with 18 violence convictions was sentenced and released with no conditions.

In March this year, John (not his real name) was walking along Worcester St on his way home after work when he was attacked by Corey Whittaker.

Whittaker was biking towards John and, believing he had been “looking” at him a certain way, stopped and punched him repeatedly in the head.

John said he had simply been walking home and while he may have glanced in Whittaker’s direction, he did not even notice the man until the attack began.

“I was pretty shocked,” he said.

“He tried to kick and hit me a few more times, then he turned and walked off and circled back and circled back.

“There was something going on with him … and I remembered seeing an ankle bracelet on - that stood out to me.”

John managed to get away from Whittaker and a woman on the other side of the street called 111.

Whittaker fled and police arrived soon after.

“The police called me later and said that they had arrested him. A few days later I was contacted by a court victim adviser who told me he had been charged with common assault and pleaded not guilty.

“He had been remanded in custody and I said I wanted to be told if he was let out. My main concern was that it appeared he lived on the route I take to and from work and the gym and I was concerned for my safety.”

John told the adviser on March 16: “If he is released back into the community … I don’t want to be looking over my shoulder to watch out for retaliation.”

CONTACT SENIOR JOURNALIST ANNA LEASK

On May 25 the adviser confirmed that Whittaker’s next date in the Christchurch District Court – a case review hearing – was set down for June 8.

“You are not required in court,” she told John.

On June 8 another adviser told John by text message that the case had been resolved.

“Just letting you know the defendant in your case pleaded guilty today to the charge and was also convicted,” it read.

“He was sentenced to five months’ imprisonment but was released today on time served as the Judge takes into account how long he was in custody on remand.

When John queried Whittaker’s release, the adviser said: “Prisoners usually only do half of the time they are given if there have been no issues within the prison while they have been there.”

On June 10, John emailed the court asking for more information about the sentencing and the offender.

“As the victim of the offence, I am seeking these documents to gain clarity on the official facts accepted by the Court, the exact terms of the conviction, any safety-related orders put in place, and the timeline for any outstanding steps in the process,” he said.

On July 29, John was provided with the sentencing notes.

He learned that Whittaker had changed his plea and admitted the charge of common assault.

It appears he was sentenced immediately by Judge Greg Hollister-Jones.

The sentencing notes are short, comprising just three paragraphs.

The judge noted Whittaker wanted to proceed with the hearing without a pre-sentence report.

He briefly outlined Whittaker’s offending, wrongly stating that the victim was on a bike at the time of the assault, rather than the offender.

“You took objection to him looking at you. You punched him on the left side of his head and then punched him again on the right side of his head around the temple area.

“The charge has a maximum penalty of one year’s imprisonment. This is lower to mid-range offending for the charge of common assault.

“I take a starting point of five months’ imprisonment. I reduce that by 20 per cent for your guilty plea.

“You have 18 convictions for violence. So for that reason, there is a 20 per cent uplift and the end sentence is five months’ imprisonment and there are no release conditions.”

John was appalled that a violent offender could be sentenced without any input from a victim.

He said he had clearly indicated that he wanted to complete a victim impact statement; however, at that point police were yet to contact him about that process.

“It’s like the victim is just peripheral to the whole thing the whole way through,” he said.

To add insult to injury, John said a week later the police officer in charge of his case made contact to “update” him and confirm the offender had “been jailed”.

“I said to him, ‘he’s not in prison, he’s out’, and the officer wasn’t even aware of that,” he said.

“It just blew me away … and that’s why I decided to speak out.

John told the Herald he was disappointed and frustrated by his experience, and worried other people were going through a similar ordeal – or worse.

He has since met his MP to discuss his case.

“I’ve had a lot of time to think about my experience and the wider situation, which I suspect is more common than people realise. My concern is broader than my individual case,” he explained.

“I want to understand how New Zealand’s short-term imprisonment and release regime deals with repeat violent offenders, when release conditions are used, and what protection and information victims receive when an offender is released back into their community.”

John felt that as an offender with 18 previous violence convictions, Whittaker should have faced more serious consequences.

“I do believe in rehabilitation, and I don’t think one offence should define someone forever.

My concern is when violence becomes a repeated pattern,” he said.

“At some point, if someone continues to offend violently despite previous convictions, sentences and opportunities to change, I think the balance has to shift towards protecting the public.

“Every time a persistently violent offender is returned to the community, the system is making a judgment about risk. If that judgment is wrong, the next victim bears the consequences.”

John was not suggesting that “every repeat offender should automatically receive an indefinite sentence”.

“But I do think there has to be a point where repeated violent offending places real limits on how much discretion the system has to keep returning someone to the community,” he said.

‘Where someone has 18 previous convictions for violence and then commits another violent offence, I think it is entirely reasonable to ask whether that point has already been reached, and when public protection should become the overriding consideration.”

Ministry of Justice chief operating officer Carl Crafter said he was satisfied the court victim advisers (CVAs) had engaged with John appropriately throughout the court process.

He said the lack of a victim impact statement in John’s case was a matter for police.

“More generally, victims should be supported to understand the court process, the outcome of a case, and the options available to them if they need further information.

“The ministry regularly considers feedback and information about the delivery of victim services to identify opportunities for improvement. Where concerns are raised about a victim’s experience, these can also help inform improvements to the way services are delivered.

“We encourage any victim who feels they have not received the information or support they needed to raise their concerns with the agency involved.

“Where a concern relates to the court process, a CVA can help the victim understand the process, access available information and connect with appropriate support. Victims can also provide feedback or make a complaint if they believe their rights or expected standards of service have not been met. “

The Herald asked police why John’s victim impact statement was not completed in time for sentencing.

Canterbury metro area response manager Inspector Paul Reeves said: “Because the offender pleaded guilty and was sentenced at his case review hearing, there was no opportunity for the victim to address the court”.

Anna Leask is a senior journalist who covers Christchurch issues and national crime and justice. She joined the Herald in 2008 and has worked as a journalist for more than 20 years with a particular focus on family and gender-based violence, child abuse, sexual violence and homicides. She writes, hosts and produces the award-winning podcast A Moment In Crime, released monthly on nzherald. co. nz.

New Zealand Herald October 26, 2026

Volunteers from Coastguard Titirangi and Coastguard Waiuku responded with multiple rescue vessels. Photo / Coastguard

A major search continues this morning near the entrance to Auckland’s Manukau Harbour after a kayaker was reported overdue.

Coastguard’s National Operations Centre and emergency services were alerted about 3pm yesterday after a man who had been kayaking alone reportedly failed to return to shore.

Waitematā west area commander Inspector Simon Walker said an “extensive search operation” was conducted off Mill Bay in West Auckland with police Eagle helicopter and Auckland Westpac rescue helicopter dispatched immediately.

“Coastguard also assisted in the search as well as other vessels and boats operating in the vicinity at the time,” Walker said.

“We searched until dark, however the man was not located.”

Walker said the man was last seen on a blue and white kayak about 1km offshore between Mill Bay and Manukau Heads.

“Search efforts today will focus on aerial and coastline searches in the area.

“I would like to thank all the agencies that have assisted so far in the search.”

Volunteers from Coastguard Titirangi and Coastguard Waiuku also responded with multiple rescue vessels.

Volunteer crews searched the water and shoreline, covering the harbour entrance, the West Channel and areas east towards Cornwallis and the Papakura Channel.

In calm and sunny conditions, three rescue vessels, two helicopters and a hovercraft searched a large area of the harbour for about three hours, Coastguard said.

Contact the New Zealand Herald newsroom

Coastguard crews ended their search shortly before 6pm and returned to base, but said volunteers were prepared to assist again if required.

“Our thoughts are with the kayaker’s whānau at this worrying time,” a Coastguard spokesperson said.

Employment lawyer to lead review of Braydon Hepworth’s City Mission stay

New Zealand Herald October 26, 2026

The body of Braydon Hepworth was found in Linwood, Christchurch. A review of his care at the Christchurch City Mission is now planned.

By Adam Burns of RNZ

Further details of a forthcoming independent review into the care Braydon Hepworth received at the Christchurch City Mission have been revealed.

The 21-year-old father was told to leave the mission’s transitional housing less than two months before he disappeared.

His body was found buried in a shed in Linwood earlier this month.

Two Christchurch men have been charged in connection with the disappearance and death of Hepworth.

A 60-year-old man was charged with concealing his body and making a false statement to police.

A 34-year-old man also appeared in court on Friday on charges relating to the concealment of Hepworth’s body.

The mission’s board confirmed a fortnight ago that an independent review into Hepworth’s time with the mission and the decision-making involved in his care would take place.

On Monday, the board said the review would be led by Wellington barrister Andrew Scott-Howman.

Scott-Howman is an experienced employment lawyer and workplace investigator.

In a statement, board chair Jane Evans said Hepworth’s death had left the City Mission community deeply saddened.

“Our thoughts continue to be with his family and friends, and the staff who knew him. We’ve asked for a thorough and candid examination of Braydon’s time with the Mission and whether anything could have been done differently.

“The review will look at the Mission’s responsibilities in relation to Braydon. It will not consider the cause of death or any criminal matter, which are for the police and the courts.”

Scott-Howman was due to report to the board at the end of November with a summary of findings and response to be released soon after, “subject to privacy and legal limitations”.

Christchurch City Mission chief executive Corinne Haines earlier confirmed Hepworth was asked to leave the transitional housing complex Whakaora Kāinga in mid-July.

“Our services support many people with complex needs and there are occasions when we must ask someone to leave accommodation because important behavioural expectations have repeatedly not been met,” she said in a statement.

However, the circumstances surrounding Hepworth’s departure from the Whakaora Kāinga complex have raised concerns and questions from staff.

Former staff member Alex – who did not wish to use her surname – told RNZ that Hepworth’s death was the catalyst for her resignation because of serious concerns about the mission’s direction.

“I believe the shift towards a more rigid, business-oriented approach contributed to the loss of experienced staff and undermined the quality of support [Whakaora Kāinga] was established to provide,” she said.

In her resignation letter, seen by RNZ, Alex said Hepworth was given 15 minutes to pack his belongings and leave.

“A year of familiarity, relationships and a place to turn when life became overwhelming, reduced to 15 minutes to gather his possessions and walk away,” her letter said.

“I find it difficult to comprehend how this could be considered an appropriate way to exit someone whose circumstances called for compassion, careful consideration and trauma-informed practice.

“Braydon deserved better. His daughter deserved better. And every person who comes to Whakaora Kāinga seeking safety, stability, and support deserves better.”

RNZ understands that about 25 to 30 staff members have resigned from the City Mission within the past eight or nine months.

Severe winds and heavy rain are expected to lash parts of the country as Kiwis return to work this morning, although the wet weather is bringing welcome relief to firefighters.

Fire crews have been battling bushfires whipped up by yesterday’s strong winds, which also brought down power lines overnight.

A vegetation fire forced evacuations in Roxburgh, Otago last night, with firefighters working until 3.30am, Fire and Emergency southern shift manager Blair Walklin said.

The fire had been contained and rain had helped dampen it down. Crews from Dunedin were expected back at 7am along with heavy machinery to deal with remaining hot spots.

A blaze in Waiouru yesterday also sent large smoke plumes drifting over the Desert Rd, and another scrub fire spread across 3.7ha at a Waikato quarry yesterday, while six helicopters battled a blaze threatening telecommunications towers in Southland’s Takitimu Forest on Sunday.

In central New Zealand crews were called to deal with downed power lines and sparking street lights, according to a Fire and Emergency spokeswoman.

Powerco’s website shows dozens of properties with unplanned outages in the lower North Island, while an earlier Wellington Electricity outage has been resolved.

Another 650 properties are without power this morning in Urenui, northeast of New Plymouth, due to a crash.

MetService meteorologist Devlin Lynden told the Herald incoming rain and easing winds were good news for areas affected by the fires.

Winds were expected to ease in Canterbury overnight, while the Central Plateau could see rain from midday today.

Orange strong wind warnings are in place for Wellington, Wairarapa and Marlborough, with severe northwest gales forecast to bring gusts of up to 130km/h in Wellington early this morning.

The warnings expire at 8am in Marlborough, 9am in Wellington and 11am in Wairarapa.

MetService warns the winds could damage trees, power lines and unsecured structures, while motorists, particularly those driving high-sided vehicles, could face difficult conditions.

Fierce winds have already caused havoc in Wellington, where flights were cancelled and cyclists were reportedly blown off their bikes and wing mirrors ripped from cars yesterday.

An orange heavy rain warning is also in place for the Tararua Range until 11am, with between 90mm and 130mm expected.

Strong wind watches are also in place for Horowhenua, Kāpiti and Tararua, where northwest winds could approach severe gale force.

Lynden said the strongest winds would ease as the weather system moved north.

“By midday or early afternoon winds will have eased and turned to lighter and cooler southwesterlies.”

Further north, Aucklanders can expect a cloudy start with northerly winds and possible light showers.

Showers are expected to become heavier around midday before winds shift to cooler southwesterlies.

“[You] should start to see some fine breaks through the afternoon,” Lynden said.

Looking ahead, Lynden said the country was in for a cooler end to the week after a spell of relatively warm weather.

“I’d expect the general temperatures to drop from what we’ve seen recently.”

Western regions, particularly the West Coast, can expect more cloud and occasional showers as the country settles into a cooler westerly airflow.

Earth Sciences New Zealand is also forecasting another spell of rain later this week, with western regions expected to see the wettest conditions on Wednesday and Thursday.

Staff shortage leaves new Waitākere Hospital ICU ward empty

New Zealand Herald October 26, 2026

The union for senior doctors questions why ICU recruitment is only happening now. Photo / Health NZ

By Rowan Quinn of RNZ

A brand new intensive care unit at Auckland’s Waitākere Hospital sits empty, fully equipped, but with no money budgeted to run it yet.

No opening date has been scheduled, with no staff and no operating budget.

The unit was previously due for use by the end of this year.

The six-bed unit was heralded as West Auckland’s first ICU when it was announced as part of a $96 million, 30-bed urgent care ward building in 2021.

That Manaaki Hōhonu building officially opened last month, but only half the beds were used, because Health NZ had not employed enough nurses to staff every bed.

No staff were hired for the intensive care unit.

Health NZ advertised for a clinical lead – but on a one-year, part-time (0.4 FTE) contract.

Waitākere Hospital operations director Brad Healey said more staff would be recruited, once the “model of care” was confirmed.

“Intensive care requires a highly specialised workforce, and detailed clinical and operational planning, before services can safely begin.”

The union for senior doctors questioned why that recruitment was only happening now.

Association of Salaried Medical Specialists executive director Sarah Dalton said there had been more than five years to prepare.

“There are clinicians and patients who are eagerly awaiting these improved facilities,” she said. “They take years to plan and build.

“It is not like it’s a surprise when they open.”

The need for an intensive care unit for the area, which had a population of 250,000 people, had been discussed for years before it was even announced, she said.

“It’s just frustrating that, now it is open, there aren’t the people to staff it.”

Health NZ had a habit of building facilities, then not staffing them properly, such as the North Shore’s Totara Haumaru surgical centre on the North Shore, she said.

Healey said the new building provided the infrastructure to allow the delivery of more critical care services in a phased approach “over time”.

A Ministry of Health audit of Manaaki Hōhonu in July noted that, when the intensive care unit eventually opened, two beds would have to close at the North Shore hospital ICU.

North Shore and Waitākere hospitals are both part of the Waitematā health district, which serviced a population of 650,000 – the biggest in the country.

The audit noted, when the wider, 30-bed ward first opened, it would only use 11 beds, and said, if all 30 beds were used, extra staff would have to relocate from other medical wards.

The practice, known as a “lift and shift”, meant there would be no extra capacity across the hospital by opening the extra 19 beds.

Health NZ said 15 beds were now used in the new ward and there would be 25 by November 3.

West Auckland residents needing intensive care were normally either sent to North Shore or Auckland City hospitals.

Waitākere had 240,000 people and was expected to grow 25% in the next 15 years, a Health NZ document said.

When then-Health Minister Andrew Little announced the new development in 2021, he said the ICU was an important addition that would allow West Auckland people to get care closer to home, but would also boost capacity across the Auckland region.

Russell Brand had ‘insane sexual appetite’ and his bad behaviour was normalised, trial told

The Guardian Mon, 26 Oct 2026 20:08:45 GMT

Brand, charged with rape and sexual assault, was ‘sleeping with people day and night’, former assistant alleges

Russell Brand had an “insane sexual appetite” and his bad behaviour was “normalised and dismissed” by those around him, his former personal assistant has told a court.

Helen Berger alleged she had seen Brand treat women badly and that she once had to stop his mother and girlfriend walking in on him having sex with someone in his dressing room.

She also told the court she had overheard the comedian receiving oral sex in a toilet cubicle and once found a celebrity leaving his bedroom in the morning.

Brand, 51, faces three charges of rape, three of sexual assault and one of indecent assault against six women, in allegations spanning 10 years from 1999. He denies all the charges.

Wearing a grey suit and white shirt, Brand sat still in the dock as statements from prosecution witnesses were read to Southwark crown court on Monday.

Berger worked for Brand from June 2006 to February 2007, when he was at the height of his fame. She said the job was one of the hardest she had had because Brand had “non-stop energy”, and she left because she was “sick of him” and burnt out.

“Though I’d worked with celebrities before and seen a lot of people normalising bad behaviour, this was on another level. I think everyone else normalising and dismissing Russell’s behaviour made me think, I guess, this is just the way it is,” Berger said in a May 2024 witness statement to police.

Describing his behaviour, she added: “He was always in his underwear, he loved walking around in his underwear with no shirt on. I remember Sadie Frost came over to interview him. He did the whole interview in his underwear and no shirt and an open robe.”

At the time, Brand had filming commitments for Channel 4’s Big Brother as well as MTV and the BBC, a radio show, a national comedy tour, a weekly Guardian column, and was writing a book.

“In addition to his busy work, he had an insane sexual appetite and was sleeping with people day and night. He was very open about what his needs were,” Berger said in the statement, which was read out by the prosecutor, Riel Karmy-Jones KC.

“He never seemed happy after sex, more so depressed,” Berger alleged. “There were times when I was at his house and he would be on a deadline … and he would get antsy and joke with me: ‘May I go and have sex now?’”

She recalled Brand turning to the website Myspace to find random women to sleep with and how women, including an unnamed celebrity, would often be at his flat in Camden, north London, for sexual liaisons. “He was like a peacock, women always approached him,” she said.

When Brand was recording an MTV show, Berger alleged, he told her to ask women for their phone numbers, which she said made her feel uncomfortable.

She alleged that on other occasions she had to keep Brand’s mother and girlfriend away from his dressing room because he was having sex, and she overheard him receiving oral sex in a women’s toilet. Berger described overhearing Brand talking and recognising his trademark cowboy boots in the cubicle next door.

Berger recalled that when Brand was headlining the Edinburgh festival, he ended his show by asking that anyone with “a vagina and heartbeat” meet him at a pub afterwards. Many women showed up, Berger said, and she later found him having sex in the shower at the apartment he was renting.

“I never witnessed Russell doing anything against the law,” she said, before adding: “I did see Russell treat women poorly.”

She recalled how he was once “hitting on” a woman who revealed she had a boyfriend, before Brand “turned in a way” that startled his then PA. “He literally just switched off his charm and moved on to the next woman,” Berger said.

The court also heard a witness statement from the manager of a woman who said she was sexually assaulted by Brand when she worked at Channel 4 in 2009. The manager said she recalled the alleged victim telling her that Brand’s associates Jack Bayles and Gareth Roy had “told her she had to give Mr Brand a massage” or he would not continue with the day’s recording.

The manager recalled being told that Bayles and Roy “were both there the whole time and watched and laughed while Mr Brand sexually assaulted her right in front of them”.

The sister of a woman who alleges she was sexually assaulted and then orally raped by Brand at a Soho bar in 2004 told the court she was “upset and almost in shock” the next morning.

In 2023, the woman called her sister in tears and told the “full story” of what had happened, the court heard.

“It sounded like she was struggling to catch her breath,” the witness recalled. “She said his [Brand’s] eyes had gone completely black and he was possessed or had been a completely different person.”

The trial continues.

Netanyahu reportedly pressured military to attack Iran in run-up to election

The Guardian Mon, 26 Oct 2026 19:21:36 GMT

Israeli prime minister increases alarmist rhetoric as his far-right coalition narrowly trails in polls

Benjamin Netanyahu has resorted to increasingly alarmist rhetoric and reportedly put pressure on Israel’s military to take action against Iran as his far-right coalition narrowly trails in the polls ahead of Tuesday’s close-run elections.

The Israeli prime minister posted an AI-generated image of a nuclear mushroom cloud destroying Tel Aviv, telling Israeli voters to choose him or risk nuclear annihilation.

“Anyone who cares about their own physical existence, that of their family, and their loved ones should have a trembling hand before voting for [the opposition],” he wrote in a social media post about Iran’s nuclear programme.

Israel’s Channel 12 news reported that the prime minister and the armed forces chief of staff, Lt Gen Eyal Zamir, clashed in recent days over a directive to the military which could “potentially spark an immediate conflagration with Iran at a very sensitive juncture”, by provoking a miscalculation by Iran.

Zamir is reported to have requested the directive, the details of which were not specified, to be presented to him in writing.

Netanyahu denied the report, and the defence ministry later denied any intention to carry out military operations against Iran.

On Monday however, CNN reported that Netanyahu had tried to convince Donald Trump to launch a renewed assault on Iran in recent weeks, renewing the war both men started in February.

The report, confirming an earlier account in the Financial Times, said Trump had ruled out any such action until US congressional elections next week.

The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) issued a statement on Monday that stopped well short of a denial of the press reports. It simply insisted that its decisions were based exclusively on “security, professional, objective and national considerations”.

Netanyahu’s warnings were a marked contrast with his triumphalism in the immediate wake of the wars on Iran that launched last year and this spring.

In March Netanyahu said Israeli and US strikes had destroyed Iran’s ability to enrich uranium and produce ballistic missiles, and in 2025 he claimed a “historic victory” over Iran that would stand for generations.

Gadi Eisenkot, the leader of the opposition bloc and Netanyahu’s most likely challenger for the prime minister’s job, expressed his confidence in Zamir. “We won’t allow the IDF to be turned into a pawn in Netanyahu’s survival campaign,” said Eisenkot, who is a retired general.

Most polls suggest the mainly centre-right opposition bloc led by Eisenkot is poised to win more seats in Israel’s Knesset than the Netanyahu coalition, but neither would be able to muster the 61 seats necessary for a majority government.

The opposition would most likely be able to gather a majority and topple Netanyahu in coalition with parties representing Palestinians with Israeli citizenship, roughly a fifth of the population. But conservatives inside the Eisenkot bloc have ruled out such a coalition, raising the prospect of a minority government, another round of elections and a possible Netanyahu resurgence.

As the elections drew closer, Netanyahu framed the country’s choice as existential. He told Channel 14, which has acted as his lead cheerleader in the Israeli media: “There is a single fundamental issue here – our existence.”

He described the opposition bloc as the “left” in alliance with Palestinians, and enemies of the country. “We see what is happening in Europe. The alliance between the left and Islam might destroy the state of Israel,” he said.

The main opposition parties are rightwing or centre-right, sharing Netanyahu’s adamant opposition to the establishment of a Palestinian state, and who have largely supported the war in Gaza. Some opposition leaders have ruled out any kind of political alliance with Palestinian Israeli parties, who could emerge from the elections holding the balance of power in the Knesset. Palestinians in the occupied territories do not have the vote.

The opposition bloc is held together more by its shared antipathy to Netanyahu, who has dominated the Israeli political scene over the past three decades and veered increasingly towards authoritarianism, seeking to limit the independence of the judiciary and turn the police and Shin Bet internal security service into political tools.

The prime minister is also in the midst of a trial on corruption charges, and his legal jeopardy could increase if he loses his grip on power.

In the closing stages of the campaign, Netanyahu has also emphasised the overt support he enjoys from Donald Trump, who repeated his endorsement on Sunday in a social media post, saying “When you go to the Polls please remember that Bibi has been an outstanding warrior prime minister!”

The Israeli outlet Walla News reported that this repeat endorsement was a result of relentless pressure from Netanyahu’s office. It is unclear, however, whether Trump’s support will carry any weight with the electorate. The US president’s earlier “total endorsement” on 18 October made no visible difference to the polls.

In one survey, 64% of Israelis questioned said it would not influence their vote, and 17% said it made them less likely to back Netanyahu, against 12% who said it had deepened their resolve to support Netanyahu’s Likud party.

In the closing stages of the closely fought campaign, Netanyahu has also forecast growing financial isolation, saying billions of dollars in annual military aid from the US would dry up soon, and drew a rare public rebuke from the central bank for a repeated claim that Israel could use cryptocurrencies to dodge escalating global sanctions.

“Cryptocurrencies cannot serve as a means to circumvent sanctions,” the Bank of Israel said on Sunday evening. “The right course for the Israeli economy is to maintain economic relations with our primary trading partners and to focus on preventing sanctions and their negative impact on the economy.”

Netanyahu had already laid out a forecast for a bleak, isolated future a year ago, when he said Israel might need to become a militarised “super Sparta”, then rowed back again in the face of fierce criticism from a horrified Israeli public.

His return to this rhetoric and the tactics of fear, particularly after unexpected losses for far-right allies in Serbia and Brazil, raised questions about whether the ultimate political survivor may finally be on the ropes.

Few among his allies or enemies expected his government to survive long after 7 October, much less complete its term. But the majority of polls have been clear for more than two years that his current coalition looks set to lose its slim majority.

England Under-15s walk off pitch against Ireland in World Cup after racism allegation

The Guardian Mon, 26 Oct 2026 19:20:46 GMT

Match in new Fifa competition abandoned

England players refuse to resume match

England abandoned their Under-15 World Cup match against the Republic of Ireland on Monday after a player reported being subjected to a racist slur. Fifa confirmed it was investigating what happened in the final minute of the Group C fixture in Baku, Azerbaijan, when Ireland were leading 4-1.

Footage showed an England player approaching the bench after an altercation. He is believed to have alleged an opponent called him a “monkey” and raised a complaint with the coaching staff, prompting England’s head coach, Matt Thorpe, to approach the referee.

Thorpe was seen asking the referee to come over before instructing his players to leave the field. One of England’s assistant coaches subsequently told the referee: “We are reporting racism”, adding that the team did not want to continue playing.

When another official approached to discuss the next steps, the assistant coach reiterated that England’s players did not want to resume the match. He also said a player was upset by the incident. Footage later showed heated exchanges between members of the coaching teams, with representatives from each side saying they were seeking to protect their players.

“Fifa is aware of an incident at the Under-15 World Cup and Festival match between England and the Republic of Ireland,” said a spokesperson for world football’s governing body. “The match was abandoned by the referee following England’s refusal to continue.”

The spokesperson said the official reports were being collected and that the matter would be referred to Fifa’s independent disciplinary committee, which would decide on any further action.

The Football Association has not commented, but is understood to be waiting for more information. It is said to be taking the matter seriously and providing support to players and staff. The Football Association of Ireland has been contacted for comment.

The inaugural Under-15 World Cup involves 189 countries and territories. Games are played in an eight-a-side format on smaller pitches, with two 20-minute halves.

England, who had won their three previous matches against Cambodia, Montenegro and Nicaragua, faced Zimbabwe later on Monday, while Ireland were due to play Cambodia. Only the group winners will progress to the top-tier competition this week, with the rest of the teams divided into separate tiers depending on where they finished.

Middle East peace held back by US insistence that Iran is a threat, Oman’s foreign minister says

The Guardian Mon, 26 Oct 2026 19:12:09 GMT

Badr Albusaidi calls for security pact involving Gulf states, Iraq and Iran with US no longer primary provider of security

The Middle East’s ability to solve its problems has been held back by America’s 50-year insistence that the Gulf states should view Iran as a security threat, Oman’s foreign minister said on Monday in a significant speech designed to break the deadlock over the region’s future.

Badr Albusaidi called for a non-aggression security pact involving all six Gulf states as well as Iran and Iraq. The US would in future no longer be the primary provider of security, he said.

He was speaking on the day high-level defence and intelligence officials from Turkey, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia travelled to Tehran in an attempt to prevent a renewed outbreak of fighting between the US and Iran.

Tehran said the meeting also explored future security arrangements in the region. The high stakes were underlined by the sight of the Saudi defence minister, Khalid bin Salman, in Tehran weeks after Iran had struck Saudi infrastructure and as Iran-backed Houthis continue to send missiles towards Riyadh.

Albusaidi is the first Gulf leader to break ranks so explicitly by calling for the mainly Sunni Gulf states to form a security alliance with Iran, a long-term aspiration of Tehran’s.

Speaking at Girton College, Cambridge, he said the talks might be difficult and the proposal appeared counterintuitive, but “issues such as the strait of Hormuz have become impossible to resolve because external powers continue to define the terms of engagement, while regional powers are unable to take collective responsibility for making their own security arrangements and reach a consensus on them”.

He added: “What holds us back is that issues which ought to be handled at a regional level by the states of the Gulf themselves, are made more complex, more intractable and sometimes simply impossible to resolve because the region’s security arrangements are insufficiently developed.

“And they are insufficiently developed because they have relied for too long on the involvement of external powers.”

He said that for half a century Iran “had been systematically excluded from playing any meaningful role in the security arrangements of the region”. This had led to “profoundly negative consequences, not just for Iran, but for the region as a whole”, including the imposition of priorities on the region by external powers such as “the entirely false perception that there is a fundamental regional antagonism between Iran and the Arab states of the Gulf”.

He added: “Perhaps the most damaging of the priorities imposed on the region from the outside has been the requirement that Iran be excluded. Not just excluded. Worse. Positioned as the threat against which regional security had to be organised.”

Oman is on the southern side of the strait of Hormuz, with Iran on the northern shores. The two countries have reached a temporary agreement on how shipping traffic should be managed in the strait, but the plan is on hold until the US and Iran lift their respective blockades of the waterway.

Albusaidi also indirectly challenged Donald Trump’s case for a further attack on Iran by saying he believed the previous round of talks between the US and Iran in February, which Oman mediated, were “making significant progress, and that an agreement was within reach. We still stand by that judgment today.”

The Iranian foreign ministry has often proposed a security pact for the region in which Iran, as opposed to the US, plays a role. The US-Iran conflict may have reopened the debate among Gulf states about whether the heavy presence of US bases in their countries is a source of reassurance or insecurity. Oman is one Gulf state to have explored a regional security pact that includes Iran.

No Gulf state openly supported the US-Israeli attacks on Iran last year or this February, but some have covertly cooperated in the operations. Iran has sought to defend itself by attacking US bases and energy infrastructure in the Gulf states.

The meeting in Tehran was taking place against a backdrop of continued Pentagon briefings about a major US military buildup in preparation for a possible assault after the midterm elections. Qatari mediators spent much of Sunday in Tehran seeking terms for Iran to reopen the strait of Hormuz.

Israeli media reports claimed that the country’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, has been trying to browbeat the military into provoking a war with Iran before the Israeli elections on Tuesday.

Donald Trump’s repeated call for Netanyahu to be re-elected only adds to the mood in the region that the US and Israel have the potential to be a long-term source of insecurity.

The idea of a security pact with Iran will be resisted in large parts of the Middle East after the damage Tehran has been prepared to inflict on the economies of the region, either directly or through the use of intermediaries such as the Houthis. Iranian hardliners increasingly say Iran’s security best lies in trying to assemble a nuclear bomb.

A pact that is likely to take many months to negotiate may also not be a solution to Washington’s demand that Iran reopen the strait of Hormuz before US sanctions are lifted.

‘Autonomy, not flesh’: RAF chief outlines AI drone-powered future

The Guardian Mon, 26 Oct 2026 19:09:51 GMT

Air Chief Marshal Harv Smyth says technological advances will reduce need for human involvement in warfare

A future Royal Air Force will rely on “autonomy not flesh”, its chief said on Monday as he described plans in which Typhoon fighters are accompanied by four AI-enabled drones capable of patrolling hundreds of miles in the distance.

The technological shift would revolutionise warfare, limit the role of military personnel “towards the outside” and ease the pressure on recruitment, Air Chief Marshal Harv Smyth said in a speech in London.

The senior military officer was setting out a strategy for the RAF, which has been told it must be ready to fight against Russia by 2030, at a time when the use of artificial intelligence by the US, Israel, Russia and Ukraine has made warfare more deadly.

“AI will enable warfare that speeds well beyond human comprehension, meaning that our role will shift towards the outside, and it will shift towards controlling the activity and setting the guardrails,” Smyth said.

The aim, he added, was to mirror the Anglo-American second world war model of “steel, not flesh” – relying on tanks and combat aircraft rather than infantry – to avoid the bloody trench warfare that had led to millions of deaths in the first world war.

“Given today’s changing character of war, I would argue strongly that the modern paradigm must now become autonomy, not flesh,” the chief of air staff said in a lecture at the Royal United Services Institute.

Few examples were given about the future use of AI by the air force, but Smyth did point to the £300m Storm Fighter programme of “loyal wingman” drones announced in July as part of the delayed defence investment plan. “Crewed platforms are no longer enough,” Smyth said.

Four armed, AI-enabled uncrewed craft would work alongside every RAF Typhoon, with the first tests to be conducted next year. The aim is for the drones to be in service by the end of the decade, in line with a Nato directive for the UK and other alliance members to be ready to fight Russia if necessary by 2030.

Over the weekend Wes Streeting, the defence secretary, said the UK had “a little over 1,000 days to complete our mission: to be ready with our allies to fight and win”.

The drones would “provide force multiplier function and the affordable mass we so definitely require” and, Smyth added, would be “placing sensors, weapons, and united warfare capabilities well within contested airspace”.

One possibility would be to use the drones to track Russian aircraft seeking to cross the Greenland-Ireland-UK gap into the north Atlantic, controlling them from a cockpit of a Typhoon flying over Scotland, several hundred miles away.

AI has been used by the Israeli and US military to dramatically increase the pace of target selection in the wars in Gaza and Iran, allowing them to run more bombing missions.

The IDF used two databases, Lavender and Habsora (or the Gospel), to increase the pace at which it could attack people and buildings during the war in Gaza. The US’s Maven Smart System, developed in conjunction with Palantir, was used to identify and strike 1,000 targets in Iran in the first 24 hours of the war this spring.

Russia and Ukraine have begun to use AI to identify and strike targets on the ground, eliminating the need for satellite or radio communication as they descend on their bombing mission. In July, Ukrainian investigators concluded that a drone that killed a person near a Zaporizhzhia gas station in July was relying on AI for its attack.

“Autonomous air systems penetrate Russia’s perceived sense of sanctuary on a routine basis,” Smyth said, describing how Ukrainian drones conduct long-range strikes against targets inside Russia, such as oil refineries.

Drones would allow the RAF to increase its ability to strike at a time when recruitment has been challenging. The RAF’s fully trained personnel numbers have fallen from 29,800 in 2020 to 27,850 today, and the total has only begun to increase over the last 18 months.

As students we never sought power – here’s how we reclaimed Serbia

The Guardian Mon, 26 Oct 2026 19:04:33 GMT

After freedom, we want to give our people something radical: a normal, functioning state

Two years ago, I harboured no political ambition whatsoever. I was a student at the faculty of technical sciences in Novi Sad, my home town, pursuing a PhD in human resources and simply living my life. That was until the canopy collapse at the newly renovated train station in Novi Sad in November 2024, which killed 16 people. I took part in street protests and rallies in response to this shocking event, and like many others, realised that it needed to be a turning point.

This was not an unavoidable tragedy. Systemic corruption and a culture of entrenched impunity were obvious factors in the collapse. But instead of ordering a full and impartial investigation and coming clean on official failings, the authorities began pushing back against us for demanding justice. We were vilified and attacked in the streets but law enforcement did nothing. So we took refuge in our lecture halls and schools, barricading ourselves inside faculty buildings, ready for a long haul.

Democratic principles have long been ignored in Serbia but we made sure we observed them in our gatherings. As our coordination developed, we made sure we had the same clear goal for every demonstration we organised: pressuring a corrupt government to meet our demands. And these were demands that in any free country would have been accepted automatically. We wanted, for example, all the documentation concerning the renovation of Novi Sad railway station to be made public, without redaction, and that everyone responsible for the works be held to account. We demanded that those who assaulted us in the streets be arrested and prosecuted. Instead of agreeing, state officials began branding us fascists and traitors.

I was personally targeted for speaking out. As I handled media relations and communications, this often meant giving interviews to the country’s few remaining independent outlets. For this, I was accused by the regime’s propaganda machine of money laundering “millions” and conspiring with foreign powers. Others had to leave the country after being accused of high treason; some spent months in detention on manufactured, illegally obtained evidence. Many of us were placed under surveillance, our parents threatened, and many were fired from jobs and dragged through the mud in the pro-government popular press.

But none of that intimidation broke us; rather it hardened our resolve. And eventually, when it became clear the regime would never concede, we opted to enter the electoral arena ourselves. That was the genesis of the Student List. Through open, democratic plenary sessions, we nominated individuals of integrity and competence, people who were committed to justice and freedom for a silenced society.

Our aims were clear and never wavered: we wanted Serbia to be governed by the rule of law, independent public institutions, transparency and solidarity in a fractured nation. We marched thousands of kilometres across Serbia, campaigning relentlessly and in doing so helped, I believe, to rekindle hope among the broader public. State propaganda could not hope to drown out that much unfiltered grassroots momentum.

Now the regime has fallen, our collective effort to rebuild Serbia begins. True, sceptics may argue that we have filled parliament with political novices. The truth is that we have filled it with people eager to serve and willing to learn. Our newly elected representatives are professors, doctors, lawyers, farmers and scientists, all experts in their fields. Each has an established record of honest work and civic integrity. They may lack traditional political backgrounds, but they have spent the past two years studying the realities of governance and public trust. That very lack of direct political involvement is why the Serbian people have placed their faith in us: they did not vote for slick rhetoric or cynical manoeuvreing. They voted for clean hands.

We are neither promising, nor expecting overnight miracles as a result of this victory; rather we hope for something fundamentally radical for Serbia: normal, functioning institutions.

This mandate must first of all dismantle the culture of impunity. That requires verifiably independent prosecutors, fully transparent public procurement processes, and legal accountability for anyone who treated state resources as private spoils. For too long our teachers, healthcare workers and civil servants have seen their expertise subordinated to party loyalty cards. We want to restore the dignity of these dedicated public servants.

Sign up to This is Europe

after newsletter promotion

We have taken our country back, and are proud to stand as free citizens of Serbia. If this historic turning point proves anything, it is that this country does not belong to an untouchable ruling elite. It belongs to all of us. We have proven that dignity is non-negotiable. Now, the real work begins. This victory marks the end of institutional fear. For the first time in years, we can breathe freely.

Novak Simin is a member of Serbia’s Student List movement

The Guardian view on Lula’s comeback: a victory for Brazil and the world, as well as a Trump rebuff

The Guardian Mon, 26 Oct 2026 18:40:14 GMT

A fourth presidential victory gives Lula another chance to defend democracy, protect the Amazon and deliver for Brazil’s working people

Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s win in Brazil’s presidential election is a triumph for him, his country and the world. The 80-year-old incumbent snatched victory from the jaws of defeat, blocked the rise of the far right and saved the planetary air-conditioning system of the Amazon from irreparable destruction. Known universally as Lula, he made history by becoming the first candidate to win a presidential run-off after finishing second in the opening round. In triumphing against Flávio Bolsonaro, the leftist stopped what could have been the most dangerous consolidation of authoritarian rule in Brazil since military rule ended. A Bolsonaro presidency could have used a rightwing Congress to extend presidential terms and pack the supreme court, entrenching power for generations.

Lula seemed to have been energised by his first-round defeat by Mr Bolsonaro. The three-time president initially pitted his extraordinary life and record against a 45-year-old senator married to controversy. But voters wanted answers to economic insecurity, rising prices and poor public services. Lula reversed course in the second round, offering immediate relief from everyday costs and indebtedness – including to the rising number of self-employed voters whom his rightwing opponent had been courting. Popular mobilisation transformed the runoff into a race to stop a Bolsonaro restoration with student protests, mass demonstrations and a 10 million-strong “Lula’s Army” WhatsApp channel. It seemed to work. Nearly 5 million more people voted in the second round of the Brazilian election than the first.

Mr Bolsonaro’s desperate refusal to concede follows his father’s playbook. In 2022 then-president Jair Bolsonaro did the same, claiming fraud. The elder Bolsonaro’s attempted coup saw him jailed for 27 years. This time Lula’s margin of victory – 4.4m votes – over the younger Bolsonaro was twice that achieved over the father. His win has also been recognised by rightwing regional leaders, conservative newspapers and even a prominent evangelical ally of the Bolsonaros. It may be significant that defeat denied Mr Bolsonaro a presidential shield from allegations of corruption and money laundering. Whether he remains in Brazil after his term as senator expires in February remains to be seen.

After the Bolsonaro clan, the next biggest loser from the results of the Brazilian election is Donald Trump. Lula’s win broke a run of seven rightwing presidential wins across Latin America, a regional advance for which Mr Trump had claimed credit. While rightwing leaders in Chile, Paraguay and Peru congratulated Lula on his victory, the White House remained silent. The US president has only himself to blame: he tried to use tariffs to pressure Brazil over the elder Bolsonaro’s prosecution and its courts’ enforcement actions against American tech companies. Mr Trump’s meddling handed Lula a winning argument for Brazil’s sovereignty.

Brazil remains divided, with a rightwing Congress ready to obstruct Lula – particularly on the environment. But few are better placed to negotiate than the former trade unionist who founded the Workers’ party. Lula’s victory provides an elected counterweight and that matters for labour rights, public services, Indigenous communities and global climate policy. The win shows the wider democratic left that a broad coalition can defeat the right. Can governing produce the secure livelihoods, strong state provision and meaningful opportunities that make that coalition durable? The next four years in Brazil may provide an answer.

The Guardian view on Serbia’s student revolution: from principled protest to power

The Guardian Mon, 26 Oct 2026 18:38:53 GMT

Two years after the Novi Sad tragedy gave birth to a youthful political movement, Sunday’s remarkable election has taken the country into a new era

This weekend it will be two years since the collapse of a shoddily constructed train station canopy in Serbia’s second city, Novi Sad. The tragedy, killing 16 people, was swiftly attributed to state corruption and failures of regulation, sparking student-led protests across the country.

Some of those demonstrators dared to imagine that they could become the catalyst for a democratic revolution.

On Sunday, that is more or less what happened. After sustaining their protests and turning them into a political movement, the students resoundingly defeated Aleksandar Vučić’s autocratic government in a snap legislative poll called by the president himself. Their victory constitutes one of the most remarkable election outcomes in recent European history.

For well over a decade Mr Vučić and his Serbian Progressive party (SNS) have exerted a domineering grip over civil society and the media, ruling through a combination of cronyism, patronage and bullying authoritarianism. As a report by international observers confirmed on Monday, the government made full, unscrupulous use of such tactics to ensure there was no level playing field for the vote. That it was nevertheless routed by a leaderless movement of 20- and 30-somethings will have been noted across a continent in which youth protest is challenging political priorities.

As in Hungary, where a focus on corruption helped the opposition to unseat Viktor Orbán after 16 years in office, the students’ campaign for basic democratic renewal struck a deeper chord than perhaps even they thought possible. Posing the choice for voters as “Serbia or mafia?”, they put forward a Student List of civic candidates dominated by academics, but also featuring farmers and well-known athletes. A turnout of almost 70% – the highest in a Serbian election since the breakup of Yugoslavia in 1992 – delivered them a comfortable majority.

What comes next will necessarily be an experiment in doing things differently. By standing apart from established structures of politics, the student insurgents embodied a freshness of approach and won the trust of the public – including in rural areas presumed to be bastions of Vučić support. In the immediate future, the new government is likely to function as a kind of constituent assembly, dedicated primarily to cleaning up civil society and rolling back the abuses that saw Serbia plunge towards the bottom of European corruption rankings.

Politically, the priority will be to consolidate this domestic agenda by winning the forthcoming presidential election. which is due by late December. But in the longer term there will be less straightforward debates to be had. Mr Vučić’s defeat is good news for the western Balkans as a whole, where he has been a consistently disruptive presence. But on foreign policy issues such as joining the European Union and relations with Russia, opinion across the student movement is divided.

As a new government seeks to re-establish the rule of law and a properly functioning and accountable state, Brussels must do all it can to assist that process while outlining a plausible and attractive path to EU membership. Mr Vučić’s Serbia, like Mr Orbán’s Hungary, became a soft autocracy where power was so entrenched that it was hard to imagine how it could be dislodged. But now there are new and better possibilities. In extraordinary fashion, the students’ inspiring journey from principled protest to power has shown just what the art of politics can deliver.

Bookies fear budget hit but gaming machine self-harm killed off the old-fashioned shops

The Guardian Mon, 26 Oct 2026 18:35:33 GMT

A wholesale plunder of local communities via casino-gaming took place and racing was content to sit on sidelines

Has it really been almost a year since racing’s last bout of Budget-related anxiety? Apparently so, because having successfully persuaded Rachel Reeves to exempt racing from a (modest) hike in betting day in 2025, here we are again, nervously anticipating Wednesday’s budget amid warnings that John Healey could effectively sound the death-knell for high-street betting shops.

Healey is widely expected to raise the rate of Machine Games Duty (MGD) in the budget, a move which could, according to some predictions, lead the closure of thousands of high-street shops with significant knock-on effects for racing’s income from off-course gambling.

The prospect of a significant hike in MGD this week was initially floated by a report from the Social Market Foundation (SMF) thinktank in June. The report recommended doubling the duty rate on the profits from high-street gaming machines, from 20% to 40%, to reflect the significantly higher rates of harm associated with machine gaming compared to traditional betting on racing and sport.

The gambling industry’s response was swift and indignant. Citing a report from the consultancy firm Regulus Partners, the industry warned that if Healey took the SMF’s advice, up to 4,000 of the UK’s 5,500 betting shops could be forced to close over the next three years. That, in turn, could cost the racing industry an estimated £92m in annual income – a third of its total from betting.

The British Horseracing Authority also expressed its concern. “This would have devastating consequences for British racing,” Greg Swift, the BHA’s director of communications and corporate affairs, said in a statement earlier this month, “hitting prize money, Levy funding and our ability to continue investing in our world-leading equine welfare and veterinary research projects.”

Subsequent rumours ahead of Wednesday’s budget suggest that Healey is considering a less dramatic rise in MGD, from 20% to 25%. Yet even this, according to the gambling industry, could lead to hundreds of shop closures and tens of millions in lost revenue for racing.

So, is the end really nigh for the high-street betting shop? Its demise has, after all, been forecast with some regularity over the last couple of decades since the advent of online gambling, and above all when the campaign to cut the maximum stake on the high-street FOBT machines, from £100 to £2, was at its height.

Suggestions at the time that most or all of the UK’s shops would be shuttered within months if the cut were imposed proved to be a long way short of the mark. The current total of around 5,500 shops is well below the 9k around a decade ago, but that also reflects the fact that the gambling market as a whole, and among younger generations in particular, is increasingly moving online.

At the same time, though, there can be little doubt, however, that racing remains painfully exposed to a major reduction in the number of shops. The sport’s income from the retail sector is tied to media rights contracts for live pictures and data agreed on a “per-shop” basis. The Regulus report suggests that racing receives around £27k in media rights and Levy payments from the average shop’s total annual revenue of £440k.

If a sport that derives a significant chunk of its income via betting is caught up in the fallout from a tax rise on casino-gaming, however, there is an extent to which it can only itself to blame.

The BHA took offence when, shortly after being installed as prime minister, Andy Burnham lumped in betting shops alongside vape shops and adult gaming arcades as undesirable presences on the high street. But if an outlet cannot absorb a five per cent rise in MGD, there is an argument that it is no longer a betting shop at all. It is a mini-casino, with betting on the side.

At the turn of the century, a betting shop (or maybe two) was a familiar and largely accepted part of the high street landscape. But that consensus was swept away in the headlong rush to squeeze as many shops as possible into areas of high population density, in order to instal the maximum number of four FOBTs in each one.

It was the bookies themselves that killed off the old-fashioned betting shop, amid a cynical and deliberate orgy of corporate greed that sucked hundreds of millions of pounds from what were already the UK’s most deprived areas. They did not want or need five or six “betting” shops in a row, but they got them anyway. At one stage in the mid-2010s, there were 18 on the main high street in Hackney alone.

Catterick Bridge 12.40 Cyberspace 1.10 Bladey Lady 1.40 Barmyblade 2.10 Knicks 2.40 Marching Mac 3.10 Havana Rum 3.40 Corsican Caper 4.10 Pol Roger

Newcastle 12.56 Wilde’s Legacy 1.26 Royal Time 2.01 Cawthorne Cracker 2.31 Silver Hill 3.01 North Of Richmond 3.31 Rule Me In (nb) 4.01 Mon Missel

Bangor-On-Dee 1.46 Glance Of Glory 2.16 Rattlin Home 2.46 Hornica 3.16 Just Golden 3.46 Inedit D’Amour 4.16 The Big Breac

Wolverhampton 4.30 Sant Alessio 5.00 Show Me Glory 5.30 What A Go I’ve Had 6.00 On Key 6.30 Distillate 7.00 Bessie Wallis 7.30 Pulsar Star 8.00 Kaaranah (nap) 8.30 Gustav Graves

It was a wholesale plunder of local communities via casino-gaming, and even as the campaign to restrict FOBT stakes gained irresistible momentum, racing was largely content to sit on the sidelines and keep counting the cash from its media rights deal. While Matt Hancock, the culture secretary in 2018, was consulting on whether to cut the maximum FOBT stake to £2, the BHA’s actively supported the gambling industry’s warnings of imminent disaster – including wholesale shop closures – if the cut was imposed.

So while the rise of online gambling was always going to see a steady decline in the number of betting shops, it is thanks to the FOBTs that there will be very few in the general public to mourn their passing, if or when they close their doors. And racing, which did little or nothing to stand up for betting while the FOBT scandal unfolded, can have few genuine grounds for complaint if, after Wednesday’s budget, it continues to pay the price for its complicity.

England fret over Fin Smith’s fitness for looming Australia match

The Guardian Mon, 26 Oct 2026 18:30:01 GMT

Borthwick responds by calling up Charlie Atkinson

Guy Pepper and Benhard van Rensburg also doubts

England are fretting over the fitness of the fly-half Fin Smith in the lead-up to the Nations Championship home opener against Australia on 8 November. The Northampton player ­damaged a calf in the second half against Leicester on Saturday and will be unable to join the national squad who have a three-day training camp in Bagshot this week.

Losing Smith so close to the ­Wallabies game would be a significant blow given the 24-year-old started at 10 in all three of England’s Tests in July and was instrumental in Saints’ domestic title triumph last season.

England’s management say they remain hopeful he will be back in time to face Australia but, with limited preparation time available, there will inevitably be some disruption to Steve ­Borthwick’s plans.

Borthwick has responded by ­calling up ­Gloucester’s Charlie ­Atkinson as cover, with Marcus Smith and George Ford the other ­specialist 10s in the squad. Since deposing Ford after England’s defeat against Ireland in the Six Nations, Fin Smith has staked a firm claim and is very much the man in possession of the 10 jersey. Marcus Smith’s last start at fly-half for England was against Ireland in ­Dublin in the opening round of the 2025 Six Nations.

There will be an official update on Smith’s condition on Tuesday with injury doubts hanging over several other players. Bath’s Guy Pepper appeared to be in pain as he limped off against Gloucester on Friday, while Benhard Janse van ­Rensburg has not featured since sufferingsustaining a heavy concussion in Bristol’s second Prem game of the season.

The inside centre Seb Atkinson is also unable to train this week but has not ruled out playing for Gloucester at Northampton on Saturday. It leaves Borthwick and the squad’s other specialist centres – Henry Slade, Joe Marchant, Max Ojomoh and Fraser Dingwall – waiting to see what will unfold before the formal squad announcement next Monday.

Marchant, for one, is delighted to be back in the frame for the first time since the 2023 World Cup. He then moved to Paris to play for Stade Français, ­having previously been told his England career was over, but is now back and eligible again after joining Sale Sharks.

Major clean-up under way after two storms cause havoc in Britain

The Guardian Mon, 26 Oct 2026 18:25:07 GMT

More strong winds forecast after Austen and Boelo kill two people and bring travel disruption and flooding

Tell us: have you been affected by Storm Boelo and Storm Austen

A major clean-up operation was under way on Monday after weekend storms caused havoc, with forecasters warning of more strong winds to come.

Two men were killed by falling trees after two named storms, Austen and Boelo, struck parts of the UK, and there was widespread travel disruption, flooding, power cuts and event cancellations.

The Energy Networks Association, which represents operators in the UK and Ireland, said 90,000 customers were still without power on Monday morning. That figure was later down to 39,000.

The association’s chief executive, Lawrence Slade, told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme that disruption had been widespread, with operators having to restore power to about 700,000 customers over the weekend.

He said Friday, Saturday and Sunday had been particularly challenging. “It certainly was a tough one. One of the problems was how quickly Boelo followed after Austen,” he said.

Another issue was that there was no letup in the strong winds, widely 50-70mph and up to 85mph in northern Scotland. “Until that weather system passes we can’t safely get engineers out to replace poles, to get wires back up etc,” Slade said.

The weather was much milder on Monday but the Met Office said more strong winds were on the way and issued two yellow weather warnings. One is in place from 6pm until 3am on Tuesday, covering western coastal areas from Cornwall up to south-west Scotland. Gusts of up to 65mph could hit exposed coastal areas, accompanied by heavy rain at times. The Met Office advised people to take care near cliffs and be aware of strong waves.

The second warning will be in place from 3am to 9pm on Tuesday and covers most of Scotland. Forecasters said winds of 50-60mph were likely to be quite widespread, with gusts up to 70mph in the far north. It warned of possible travel cancellations, road closures and more power cuts.

The weekend storms led to two deaths, authorities said. A 60-year-old man was hit by a falling tree in Dumfries and Galloway, while a man in his 20s died in Finchley, north London.

The 60-year-old was named on Monday afternoon as Richard Baines, the curator of Logan Botanic Garden near Port Logan.

David Knott, the director of horticulture at the Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh, said Baines would be remembered for his “passion and enthusiasm for plants … significantly increasing and expanding the plant collection at Logan”.

There was flooding in several parts of Scotland, with dramatic footage from Largs showing flood water cascading through the town centre. One resident said it was the highest she had ever seen in 36 years of living there.

Staff at the Thai restaurant Tha-Tien-Thai shared a video of their kitchen overrun by water with the desperate caption: “There is nothing left.” They said its doors would be closed for the foreseeable future “due to larger flood restoration than originally planned”.

Robyn Cryans, an executive assistant from Renfrew, is on holiday in Cyprus and woke to see pictures taken by a neighbour of her Nissan Micra Sport submerged back at home.

“It is very upsetting, a bit stressful,” she said. “It was unexpected considering we’ve got a £10m flood barrier literally just down the road which is supposed to activate if the Clyde bursts its banks.”

She is scheduled to fly back on Tuesday and fully expects to find her flat damaged. “I’m obviously very upset about it, but at the end of the day it’s material objects. It could have been a lot worse.”

In Aberdeenshire, 13 primary schools without power were shut on Monday, and Ellon academy was closed because of storm damage. Ten primary schools were shut in the Highlands.

Scotland’s first minister, John Swinney, met senior politicians, emergency teams and forecasters on Sunday to discuss the ongoing response to the weather.

Emergency services were called to a flooded care home in Saltcoats, North Ayrshire, on Sunday evening. Police Scotland said everyone at the care home was accounted for, road closures were in place and officers were expected to remain on site overnight to assist.

There was also travel disruption, with flights diverted from landing at Leeds Bradford, England’s highest airport, and others cancelled. Most train services were getting back to normal but operators advised customers to check before they travelled.

The storms brought a number of event cancellations including the Sunday racing at Aintree, abandoned because of the high winds. The Guardian’s live blog of the terrible tea-time Sunderland v Leeds goalless draw summed up the action: “And the winner is … the wind.”

No 10 clarifies Andy Burnham’s stance on freedom of movement

The Guardian Mon, 26 Oct 2026 18:03:46 GMT

Clarification comes after PM fuelled speculation about EU-UK relationship in series of interviews at weekend

Downing Street has been forced to clarify Andy Burnham’s stance on whether the UK would return to having freedom of movement with the EU after the prime minister said an “honest discussion” was needed on the issue.

Burnham fuelled speculation about a return to freedom of movement in an interview at the weekend, prompting questions about how close the UK could become to Brussels.

Confusion deepened after further interviews were interpreted as leaving the door open to an eventual return to freedom of movement and another referendum on the issue.

It forced a Downing Street spokesperson to say the prime minister was not proposing a return to freedom of movement, or any particular option.

“He is saying that it’s time for us to discuss what kind of long-term relationship with Europe is best for Britain and he is referring to the types of areas that that agreement and long-term future could cover,” she said.

“He is crucially not leaning either way, and that will be for the British public to decide. And his focus for now is on next month’s summit and the practical arrangements that we hope to make there, which will add billions to the economy.”

She said the government was not yet at the stage of confirming whether the public would decide on proposals for the UK to move closer to the EU.

Asked whether Burnham accepted that returning to freedom of movement would mean Britain lost control over legal migration, the spokesperson said: “He’s not setting out a concrete position either way. What he’s saying is that he wants to have a conversation with the British public about what our long-term future with the European Union looks like.”

In an interview with the Sunday Times, Burnham indicated that staying out of free movement would no longer be a red line in discussions about how the UK can move closer to the EU.

On Monday, Burnham ruled out the possibility of rejoining the EU within this parliament and indicated he could fight the next general election on a promise to take the UK back into the EU. He said: “I’m not going to move away from the red lines that were in the Labour manifesto.”

Hours later, Burnham told journalists “no” when asked if he would allow the UK to join the EU freedom of movement scheme without a referendum.

When asked whether he wanted Britain to rejoin the EU, he said: “I’ve said I’m going to be honest and say, in my lifetime I would like to see that happen, but I am not going to move ahead of the public. I am not going to dictate in terms of my own opinions here, you have to make sure that the British public are the bosses.”

Challenged on how his constituents in Makerfield would feel about his discussions about the EU, given 65% of them voted to leave, Burnham added: “I said we wouldn’t rerun the referendum and that’s not what I’m doing.

“The British public, the people of Makerfield, will be the bosses here. They will decide what happens in relation to Brexit.”

Burnham even ruled out an early general election on a manifesto change on this issue. He told GMB: “There is no election coming anytime soon. People may as well put that out of their mind.” However, he left the door open to a future fight on a promise to fully rejoin the EU.

Burnham will be in Brussels for the UK-EU summit on 20 November, as he seeks to strike a better deal with the bloc. He believes the Brexit deal has “weakened our economy [and] weakened our control of immigration” and is not good enough for the country.
