The best heated clothes airers in the UK to save time and money when drying your laundry – tested

The Guardian Mon, 26 Oct 2026 15:00:18 GMT

Guardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more.

Heated airers claim to dry your clothes without costing the earth in energy. We put 19 to the test over two years, from covered options to winged racks

The best electric heaters

Rising energy bills and perma-drizzle are conspiring to keep the nation’s laundry damp, not least by making it such a turn-off to turn on the heating. No wonder heated clothes airers are having a moment. These modish appliances sell out within hours of reaching shops and inspire evangelistic fervour among owners, who call them “life-savers” and “gamechangers”.

Can a hot clothes horse really change your life, let alone dry your soggy washing as fast as a tumble dryer for a fraction of the cost and, in most cases, with none of the noise? After testing 19 bestsellers over the past two years – during which time I took my tumble dryer to the dump and slashed my dependency on radiators – I can confidently say yes.

Not every airer I tested made the final cut. A few, though, impressed me so much I’m now fully converted to the belief that the heated clothes airer is the best thing in laundry since the clothes peg.

Best heated clothes airer overallLakeland Dry:Soon Deluxe 3-tier heated airer and cover

Best budget heated airerBlack+Decker Heated winged clothes airer

Best heated airer for fast dryingMinky SureDri Heat Pod Pro

I’ve spent three decades testing products from Sky boxes to mattress toppers, and it’s made me professionally sceptical of manufacturers’ claims to magically solve domestic problems. I also have a solid background in procrastinating by doing laundry, hanging laundry and folding laundry, so I couldn’t resist the Filter’s offer to pay me to watch clothes dry.

Heated airers all do much the same thing in much the same way. There are small differences in design – some have triangle frames, some are winged and some have covers – but they’re basically all clothes horses that you plug in. I had to find clear distinctions between them, and this chiefly meant devising fair, quantifiable tests to measure how quickly, evenly and cheaply each airer dried clothes.

The key test was a half-hourly laundry weigh-in to measure how quickly each airer dried an identical load. Actually, two identical loads – one small (4kg) and one big (8kg) – 19 times, once for every airer. I removed and weighed the clothes every 30 minutes to see how much moisture had evaporated until the fabric was dry, and this gave me an overall drying time. Room temperature remained at a steady 19-20C throughout. For more behind-the-scenes insights into weighing knickers, check out the Filter’s newsletter.

I took other measurements too, not least to give me something (anything) to do while the laundry dried, such as the dimensions of each airer and the length of its heated bars. I used an infrared thermometer to take the bars’ temperature every 30 seconds to compare heat-up times, and a wattage meter to check power usage. I then used the October 2026 electricity price cap (26.32p a kWh) to work out running costs an hour.

After testing, I donated the airers to two organisations that do important work in and around Southampton. The first is Scratch, which provides services and furniture for families and individuals experiencing poverty, and the other is Yellow Door, a charity offering support for people affected by domestic abuse.

Here’s my guide to the 10 best heated clothes airers based on my tests.

This airer is for anyone who’s fed up with choosing between the expense of a noisy tumble dryer, the mess of clothes on radiators, and the rank stink of laundry slowly drying on a conventional clothes horse. With its ventilated heat-retaining cover in place, it’s the most efficient barred airer I tested.

Why we love it Lakeland’s Dry:Soon Deluxe three-tier heated airer arrives ready to use. It took me only two minutes to unfold the tiers, position the cover, plug in the cable and switch it on. The airer is a handsome chrome rack on its own, but the light grey embroidered cover makes the whole thing look rather gorgeous.

The bars warmed up faster than most of its rivals, reaching 27C within 30 seconds before maxing out at 50C. When I laid a 4kg load of damp T-shirts across them and closed the cover, the lot was dry in two hours. That’s no faster than a tumble dryer, but it’s much more energy-efficient, costing about 8p an hour compared with 79p for my 3kW tumble dryer.

The Dry:Soon Deluxe has some excellent user-friendly details. In particular, a timer lets you set it to switch off in hourly increments up to 12 hours ahead. All Lakeland’s airers come with a three-year warranty compared with the basic statutory guarantees for most heated airers.

It’s a shame that … this airer costs almost as much as a tumble dryer. Deluxe by name, deluxe by price. But it’s many times cheaper to run, so it might be worth it to keep your bills down.

Suitable for: families who want to give up their expensive tumble dryer habit Available drying space: 21m (up to 36 hanging T-shirts) Dimensions (open): 73 x 75 x 137cm (DWH) Dimensions (folded): 10 x 75 x 137cm (DWH) Max capacity: 15kg Time to dry small load: 2 hours Running cost: 8p/hour

The Black+Decker doesn’t get particularly hot, which helps if you have curious toddlers and delicate clothes. It still managed to dry my small load of T-shirts in an afternoon, and at £50 with a 6p-an-hour running cost, it’s a decent budget buy. It’s also one of the easiest airers to fold down and slip under the sofa when not in use.

Why we love it The Black+Decker winged airer has a small footprint, taking up about 50 x 50cm on its beam supports, yet it boasts a capacity of 10kg when unfolded, thanks to its ironing-board-style shape. It warmed up to 33C in its hottest spots and dried my small load of T-shirts in just over four hours, with a little help from me flipping them and moving them around.

I also like that the wings fold inwards to double up the heat when drying thicker garments, albeit not very large ones, and the dryer is so light (about 3.5kg) that I could move it around using one hand.

It’s a shame that … it warmed up slowly and failed to get hotter than 33C even after three hours. That’s great for delicates and damp towels, but not hot enough to dry thick fabrics.

Suitable for: drying light fabrics and warming up towels Available drying space: 11.5m (up to 20 hanging T-shirts) Dimensions (open): 54 x 148 x 93cm (DWH) Dimensions (folded): approx 54 x 100 x 20cm (DWH) Max capacity: 10kg Time to dry small load: 4 hours 15 minutes Running cost: 6p/hour

Heat pods turn your old unheated airer into a heated version. This one has a cover that fits a standard three-tier clothes horse, plus an electric heater that sits underneath to fill the space with hot air.

Why we love it Minky’s pod system is a damp-blitzing machine. With the fan heater emitting plenty of heat and the cover trapping it, even its lowest setting blasted my laundry dry faster than most of the conventional airers in my test. It’s good value, too, even though you have to provide your own airer (this Minky model from Argos is £35), and the zipped cover is excellent quality and looks smart.

The Minky Pro’s lowest, middle and highest settings all have a similar energy consumption according to my readings (between 970W and 1,067W), costing roughly 27p an hour. That’s a significantly higher running cost than a barred heated airer, but only about a third as much as running a 3kW tumble dryer.

Given that I dried a large 8kg load in less than three hours using the Minky’s highest setting, albeit with a fair amount of rearranging clothes, this gadget could genuinely replace your tumble dryer.

The air inside the cover gets very hot, especially when it’s on the highest setting. That’s great for fast drying, but Minky says you should only use the Heat Pod Pro to dry fabric that can “endure temperatures up to 85C”. Save your delicate smalls for a conventional barred airer.

It’s a shame that … the Minky’s fan noise is annoying compared with the blissful silence of a barred airer. At 60dB, it’s significantly quieter than a tumble dryer, but a little too loud to have in the same room while you watch TV. I also found the power button liable to get stuck, but that may be my own heavy-handedness.

Suitable for: work clothes and school uniforms that need a fast turnaround Available drying space: about 21m, depending on your clothes horse Dimensions (heat pod unit): 60 x 68 x 135cm (heat pod unit, DWH) Max capacity: about 10kg Time to dry small load: 1 hour 30 minutes (setting 1); 40 minutes (setting 3) Running cost: 26-28p an hour

Best for: runners and dog walkers who need to dry soggy shoes and socks

Heated shoe stands are a simple addition and work well on this airer, drying my thick walking socks faster than if I’d laid them across the bars. The A-frame design also makes this among the sturdiest smaller airers I tested, and it stood firm even when I threw a large load of washing at the top tier.

It didn’t make the final cut because … my small 4kg load needed an unusually long five hours, even after I’d moved things around and flipped them over. I also hated risking my fingers in the metal-hinged supports each time I folded and unfolded the airer.

Available drying space: 17m, including shoe stands; dimensions (open): 54 x 91 x 146cm (DWH); dimensions (folded): 18 x 91 x 146cm (DWH); max capacity: 15kg; time to dry small load: 5 hours; running cost: 9p/hour

Best for: solo households and small living spaces

Argos’s three-tier airer took several minutes to heat up and maxed out at a reasonable 45C – hot enough to dry my small load in about four and a half hours (after a bit of rearranging). The pivoted frame makes it feel less sturdy than airers with feet at each corner, but it’s a breeze to fold and unfold.

It didn’t make the final cut because … the Argos Home airer feels less robust than similarly priced rivals.

Available drying space: 17m; dimensions (open): 73 x 70 x 144cm (DWH); dimensions (folded): 13 x 70 x 144cm (DWH); max capacity: 15kg; time to dry small load: 4 hours 20 minutes; running cost: 8p/hour

Best for: heavier items such as towels and jumpers

With 17.2m of drying space and a 298W power rating, the VonHaus isn’t as big as the Lakeland or the Dunelm XL, but it claims it can support a mammoth 30kg of damp washing. That’s also more than three times the maximum capacity of my washing machine, and indeed of my arms.

Hyperbolic capacity claims aside, this airer has some clever ways to max out its drying space and efficiency, such as adding an unheated top rack (ideal for delicates) and a cover to trap the hot air. The plasticky cover isn’t a patch on those from Lakeland and Minky for quality or aesthetics, but it gets the job done, helping my small load dry in under three hours.

It didn’t make the final cut because … the airer doesn’t look as smart as its similarly sized rivals, not least because of the plastic feet that remained defiantly clumpy when I folded down the frame.

Available drying space: 17.2m; dimensions (open): 69 x 73 x 139cm (DWH); dimensions (folded): 15.5 x 73 x 139cm (DWH); max capacity: 30kg; time to dry small load: 2 hours 45 minutes; running cost: 8p/hour

Best for: drying all your smalls in one place

This is the new, “extra large” version of the dinky Dunelm ladder airer I tested in 2025 (see below). Its 133cm height and 12 heated bars (58cm each) add up to a much more generous drying capacity than its mini cousin, but it’s still not very powerful. I measured up to 185W energy consumption and an average 30C bar heat. That’s not exactly hot (for comparison, the bars of the Dunelm XL 3-tier airer reached 55C in places) and not warm enough to dry jeans or a jumper fast enough to avoid that slightly stale smell, but I found that it dried lighter T-shirts, hand towels and undies efficiently. As with the smaller version, I love the look of this airer.

It didn’t make the final cut because … this won’t dry a whole load, even a small one, but it’s a great wardrobe assistant that doesn’t hog space.

Available drying space: 6.96m; dimensions (with feet attached): 49.5 x 67.5 x 133cm (DWH); max capacity: 10kg; time to dry small load: 6 hours (all small items, after swapping some); running cost: 5p/hour

Best for: sizeable wardrobes that contain delicate fabrics

This is one of the biggest and most feature-rich airers I tested, with a ventilated cover, timer and digital temperature controls that I found fairly easy to use. The top setting reached nowhere near the claimed 70C but did manage 52C in places, and I love having the lower-temperature settings for drying flimsy fabrics on the bars. You can attach peg hangers to dangle your smalls in the heat, but they don’t allow much dangle room. As with all the airers I tested, you get a much quicker dry if you lay items across the bars.

It didn’t make the final cut because … it doesn’t dry clothes quite as fast as the Dry:Soon Deluxe, and it’s a right old jigsaw to put together the first time you use it. After that, though, I found it easy to open and close.

Available drying space: 30m; dimensions (open): 73 x 70 x 147cm (DWH); dimensions (folded): 15 x 70 x 147cm (DWH); max capacity: 16kg; time to dry small load: 3 hours 30 minutes; running cost: 8p/hour

Best for: drying undies and other small items

Beldray’s winged airer is a good buy at £50, but don’t expect it to dry a week’s worth of laundry. Hanging clothes from its 18 bars doesn’t dry them fast enough to avoid mild stinkiness, and there wasn’t enough room to lay more than four of my T-shirts across the bars. It blazed through underwear, though. The bars get surprisingly warm given the airer’s modest 230W power rating, so it made fast work of my damp socks, knickers and boxer shorts, as long as I gave each item its own spot on the bars. It folds up small for storage, too, although you have to wrestle the heated bars off the X-frame stand – not something I managed without a little light swearing.

It didn’t make the final cut because … it’s a great helper, but not big or powerful enough to dry a load of clothes.

Available drying space: 12.4m; dimensions (open): 54 x 148 x 91cm (DWH); dimensions (folded): 54 x 105 x 7.5cm (DWH); max capacity: 15kg; time to dry small load: 3 hours 30 minutes (all small items); running cost: 6p/hour

Best for: keeping in the hallway to dry damp socks, shoes and gloves

The smallest airer in my test and by far the cheapest to run, Dunelm’s 90W aluminium ladder uses a mere 2p an hour under the October energy price cap, and takes up very little space. Its plastic feet are a pain to attach and add about half a square metre to its footprint when they’re open, but all in all this is a great little gizmo for taking the soggy edge off hand towels, tea towels or even rained-on hats and gloves.

It didn’t make the final cut because … it’s not big or powerful enough to dry a load of washing.

Available drying space: 3m; dimensions (with feet): 53 x 34 x 87cm (DWH); max capacity: 5kg; time to dry small load: 3 hours 30 minutes; running cost: 2p/hour

Heated clothes airers are such a simple and smart idea that it’s weird they haven’t been around longer. They’re wildly popular, too: Aldi’s winged heated airer sold out within days of going on sale in 2025, and I’m feverishly awaiting news of this year’s model. But do they deserve the hype – and how can you get the best out of yours?

Minimal running cost is the biggest selling point of heated airers. Their packaging bears promises that they’ll dry your clothes for as little as 6p an hour, dramatically undercutting all rival methods other than blazing sunshine. With electricity prices marginally lower than a year ago, while gas prices have risen, heated airers are certainly a more cost-efficient way of drying clothes than using your radiators.

Six pence an hour was a little optimistic, though. I found that standard barred airers, running at about 320W, worked out at 7p an hour in September 2024 and 8p an hour now. It’s cheaper than putting on the central heating, but it does add up, because most heated airers take a whole afternoon or more to dry a full load of washing, and those 8p hours will add up. Airers that dry clothes faster, such as the fan-heater-based Minky SureDri Heat Pod Pro, cost more to run. At 1kW, the SureDri costs about 26p an hour, adding up to 78p for three hours of drying.

That’s still significantly cheaper than running a tumble dryer or, indeed, a washing machine. Under October 2026 energy prices, a tumble dryer running at 3kW costs 79p an hour to run, and it can cost even more to switch on the central heating.

A standard T-shirt, laid flat and unfolded across several bars of a 300-320W barred heated airer, should dry in about two hours. If you’re drying a whole load of clothes, though, it’ll take a whole afternoon – or about eight hours if the air feels cold or humid. You will need to flip and rearrange items during this time to give the fabric equal access to the bars.

Airers that contain a fan heater dry clothes more quickly. The fastest-drying airer in my test, the Minky SureDri, blew out enough hot air to dry my small load of washing in less than two hours. With a large load, I found it easier to halve it and dry it in batches.

There are ways you can speed up the drying process. My best tip is to ignore the marketing photos that show airers draped like Christmas trees, with clothes hung from every bar. As I discovered while running this test, your clothes simply won’t dry that way unless it’s a warm day, which rather defeats the point. Instead, lay individual items across the bars.

Covered airers cut drying times by almost half, but I’d recommend removing it as soon as your clothes are dry. Covers are vented to avoid condensation, but I found that some moisture crept back in if I left my clothes inside.

However powerful your airer, always spin your clothes to remove as much water as possible before laying them on it. Wet clothes won’t dry, and water and electricity are not a happy combination.

On that note, don’t use a heated airer in the bathroom. Electric peril aside, bathroom air is notoriously damp. I had the best results when using my test airers in the bedroom with the window ajar – and the faint fabric softener scent was a sweet bedtime bonus.

When you dry clothes on any warm surface, whether it’s a heated airer or a radiator, the moisture rises from the clothes – to where? I asked a range of experts about this, and they broadly agreed that the key is to let the moist air escape from your home.

“It’s not the drying method alone but the combination of moisture and lack of ventilation that leads to damp problems,” says Dr Anastasia Mylona, technical director at the Chartered Institution of Building Services Engineers. “You can manage this by ensuring good ventilation when drying clothes indoors; for example, by opening windows or using extractor fans.”

A dehumidifier can help avoid damp, as well as speed up the drying process, says cleaning expert Nancy Emery of bathroom retailer Drench. “If you’re investing in a heated airer, my advice is to invest in a dehumidifier as well, and always run them together.”

I’ve found heated airers much less likely than radiators to cause damp walls, and property expert Phil Spencer explains why. “Airflow is key, so if you want to use a heated airer, put it in the middle of the room rather than next to the wall,” says Spencer, who, among other things, founded the property advice website Move iQ. “This is why heated airers are preferable to wall-mounted radiators.”

However, radiators can heat up the room, and heated airers can’t, at least not significantly. That’s an important factor in the battle against damp, says Emery. “Maintaining your home’s temperature above 18C helps because condensation can’t settle on warmer surfaces.”

I put these tips to the test using an affordable humidity meter. I measured the moisture in my spare room’s air before doing any laundry, and then again at various stages of drying a medium load on a large heated airer – with and without opening the windows and using a dehumidifier.

It had rained all week, so perhaps it’s no surprise that my house boasted a base humidity level of 70%, 10 percentage points higher than the recommended UK maximum. I was surprised, though, when this only rose to 72% once I’d loaded the airer with damp clothes. Running my dehumidifier brought the room’s humidity down to 70%. When I opened the windows, it dropped to 65% – even before the load was completely dry. I’ve now defaulted to leaving the windows open whenever possible, whether or not I’m drying clothes.

“Opening windows regularly is the best way to allow humid air to escape, though it may seem counterintuitive in colder weather,” says Nicholas Donnithorne, UK technical services manager at Rentokil Property Care. “Leave quarterlights ajar or trickle vents open. Dehumidifiers can help, but they require regular emptying and aren’t a substitute for proper ventilation.”

For more autumn and winter home essentials, read the Filter’s guides to: The best electric blankets and heated throws The best electric heaters, tested

Jane Hoskyn is a features journalist and WFH pioneer with three decades of experience in rearranging bookshelves and “testing” coffee machines while deadlines loom. Her work has made her a low-key expert in all manner of consumables, from sports watches to solar panels. She would always rather be in the woods

The date of an article’s most recent update can be found in the timestamp at the top of the page. The horse that ushered in Manchester United’s 21-year tragic arc

The Guardian Mon, 26 Oct 2026 14:43:51 GMT

There’s plenty of blame to go around at Old Trafford. Like all downfalls it started with a seemingly small, unconnected moment

Sign up for our free newsletter here

And so here we are again, at that point as the nights draw in and Manchester United prepare to sack a manager. Autumn: season of mists, mellow fruitfulness and a crisis at Old Trafford. Sunday’s 3-0 home defeat to Bournemouth, coming on the back of last week’s 4-1 reverse against Como, made clear what many had feared from the moment Michael Carrick was given the job on a permanent basis: that he isn’t up to it.

But then, who could be? When you’ve burned through a long list of managers in 13 years, it’s perhaps worth considering whether the manager is really the problem. Could some blame perhaps go to the director of football, Jason Wilcox, or the chief executive, Omar Berrada, the people making the appointments? Or perhaps to Sir Jim Ratcliffe, the cost-cutting tax exile and minority shareholder with responsibility for sporting operations? Or to the Glazer family, who plunged the club into debt with a leveraged buyout in 2005 and have since made calamitous decision after calamitous decision, reducing the most successful club in English league history to a mid-table laughing stock with a roof that leaks symbolically?

It’s worth remembering where all this began. The United story has taken on the aspect of a classical tragedy and, like all good tragedies, it begins with a small, seemingly unconnected moment, amplified by pride, that ends up bringing the whole edifice crashing down.

In 1999, Mull of Kintyre, a horse owned by the Irish millionaire John Magnier, won the Gimcrack Stakes at York. Traditionally, the winning owner would give a speech at the Gimcrack Dinner, but Magnier was a shy man who hated public speaking so he asked his friend, the United manager Alex Ferguson, to give the speech on his behalf. The racing establishment, though, refused: it had to be the owner. To spite them, Magnier named Ferguson as the owner of another horse, Juniper. The following year, Juniper was narrowly beaten in the Gimcrack Stakes. Magnier, though, was determined. So the year after that, he made Ferguson the owner of Rock of Gibraltar, which had won its first three races. Rock of Gibraltar won the Gimcrack easily and Magnier, waving a metaphorical two fingers at the racing authorities, watched Ferguson give the speech.

Magnier was largely making mischief, but he was also happy to do a favor for a friend, to give Ferguson a better experience of racing, and he benefited from the association of the horse with such a famous name. In addition, Ferguson did not get on well with the United chairman, Martin Edwards, and had a sense that football clubs were becoming good investments. Accordingly Magnier and his associate JP McManus bought shares in United. (The full story is explored by the journalist David Walsh here).

It turned out, though, that Rock of Gibraltar was a much better horse than anybody had realized, winning seven Group One races in a row. The stud fees would be worth tens of millions of pounds. Ferguson believed the verbal deal was that he could choose 50% of the prize money won by Rock of Gibraltar (about £800,000) or 50% of the stud fees, which ended up being worth tens of millions. He went for the latter. Magnier’s recollection was rather different: 5% of the prize money or one stud nomination a year.

Ferguson sued and, with his name on the ownership documents, probably would have won had it gone to trial. But then rumors started to spread about some of Ferguson’s financial dealings at United. Paid actors at United’s annual general meeting raised awkward points, then Magnier and McManus sent a list of 99 questions to the United board, which mysteriously found their way into the Daily Mail. United were highly embarrassed. Fans began to demonstrate against Magnier and McManus at race meetings. A settlement was reached, with Ferguson paid £2.5m to drop the action. But the damage was done.

Magnier and McManus had decided to sell their shares in United, and another shareholder was ready and waiting: Malcolm Glazer. Ferguson backed Glazer, who launched his leveraged buyout. Magnier and McManus sold up in 2005 for £260m, a profit of a little under £100m. Had they waited for Ratcliffe, who bought a similar stake in 2024, they would have received roughly £1bn more than that. For Ferguson, a threat had been dealt with.

The problem was that Glazer and his family would prove some of the worst club owners in English history. For 20 years, United have been addled by debt and have made consistently terrible footballing decisions. Ferguson’s team was good enough, and his personality big enough, that United won five league titles and a Champions League after the takeover, but once his genius had gone, there was nothing left.

A mismatched squad built up over seven flawed managerial appointments and a multiplicity of conflicting approaches will not readily be sorted out. Carrick is the latest victim of a crisis 21 years in the making. For the want of a horse a club was lost.

‘My death was reported in Rolling Stone’: how the Zombies made Time of the Season

The Guardian Mon, 26 Oct 2026 14:35:51 GMT

‘A year after we broke up, we heard that two bands had started touring the US as the Zombies. One group said they were the originals but with a new singer – because I’d been killed in a car crash’

Our first single, She’s Not There, was one of the first songs I wrote, when I was 18. It remained our only hit in the UK by the time we recorded our second album, Odessey and Oracle, in 1967 – this was only three years later but it felt like a lifetime. We’d recently signed to CBS and had been given £1,000, which even then was not a huge amount of money. We recorded pretty quickly in a few sessions spread over six months, producing ourselves for the first time.

Time of the Season was the last song I wrote for the album. I was sharing a flat with our bass player Chris White, and we were going to each other’s rooms and playing the different things we had. I said: “I think I’ve just written a song that could be a hit.”

The lyrics reflected the mood of the time. In 1967 there were pictures of war on TV, and people were seeing what a devastating thing it was and saying: “I’m not going to be part of this.” The “Who’s your daddy?” line was, in a way, going back to Gershwin’s Summertime, one of the first songs we performed together, but “Is he rich like me?” had kind of a double meaning: “rich” in the sense of understanding how to live.

We recorded at EMI Recording Studios, later known as Abbey Road. The Beatles were in before us making Sgt Pepper’s Lonely Hearts Club Band – we had the benefit of some of the same recording engineers, in particular Geoff Emerick. He found this special way of marrying the bass and the tom-tom sound. I suggested the clap before the beat and a vocal sound after, which became the exhalation.

We soon used up our £1,000, but because of the tight timeframe we were working to, there was a spontaneity and freshness that was very valuable. It’s a method I try to preserve. It’s just much more fun.

I was learning Time of the Season while we recorded it. Standing where the vocal mic had been set up, I was looking at this big red recording light with a clock underneath it while I tried to get it right. The studio was very strict about sessions finishing on time, and there were these guys with long brown coats moving equipment about. On one occasion, we were standing around a piano working out harmonies and they wheeled it out in the middle of a take.

Rod always has an overview of his songs in his head – he can hear the drum track, what the bass should be playing and what the lead vocal should be doing. He’s extremely good at phrasing, so he was in the control room saying: “No, this phrase should be on the beat but the next phrase should be pushed …” Meanwhile, all the time I’m watching the big hand creeping towards five o’clock.

Things got a little bit heated. I was saying, “If you’re so bloody good, you come in here and sing it,” and he said, “You’re the bloody lead singer, you stand in there until you get it right!” The language was probably richer than that. It makes me smile now to think I was breaking off from saying the most terrible things to Rod to sing these angelic lines: “It’s the time of the season for loving …”

Rod likes to think I disliked Time of the Season, but I just thought there were more commercial songs on the album. Care of Cell 44, to me, sounded like the epitome of a hit single, but obviously I was wrong – it was released ahead of Odessey and Oracle and wasn’t successful. By the time the album came out in Terry Quirk’s misspelled sleeve, the band had split.

The following year, Al Kooper left the American band Blood, Sweat & Tears and became a staff producer at CBS. He’d just visited London where he bought about 80 albums that weren’t available in the US, and later said Odessey and Oracle was the one that really stood out. On his first day at CBS he went to see the label’s president, Clive Davis, and said: “Whatever it costs, we have to get this album.” And Davis said: “We already have it. We were going to pass on it – it’s not commercial.”

Al fought for it, and CBS released two singles that disappeared without trace. I think Time of the Season was only put out as a favour to Al, but one DJ in Boise, Idaho, would not stop playing it, and that was where our luck turned. It gradually picked up huge radio interest.

By then, it was well over a year since we’d broken up and we were all doing other things, but we soon heard that a couple of other bands had started touring the US as the Zombies – one included two members of ZZ Top. The manager of one of these bands claimed they were the original members with a new singer, because Colin Blunstone had been killed in a car crash. It turned out my death was reported in Rolling Stone.

The original Zombies didn’t play together again until 1997, when a box set was launched at the Jazz Cafe in London. I was singing with my solo band, but the other guys came up on stage and let it be known they wanted to play – we hadn’t planned it or rehearsed. We did She’s Not There and Time of the Season and it sounded really good. I thought: “You know what? There really was something special about that band.”

Can you say a song’s got legs? Time of the Season wasn’t a success in the UK charts, but people know it. It’s often used in films set in the 1960s but also appears in commercials, where it sounds really current. I’ve never quite worked out how it can be both of its time and timeless.

The Zombies release Continue Here, an album of remastered mono B-sides and singles, on 30 October. Their Begin Here festival is in St Albans, 30 October to 1 November.

I used to think I had impeccable taste in music. My kids taught me to stop being a snob

The Guardian Mon, 26 Oct 2026 14:00:44 GMT

Music may not define them in the way it defined many of my generation, but my children still know a good tune when they hear one

There was a moment, some years ago in a St Kilda summer, when our family was driving along a busy street, the car windows down, belting out Eric Carmen’s Make Me Lose Control. I had one of those out-of-body experiences parents sometimes get, where you get a clear view of your younger, cooler self looking on in a state of acute embarrassment and despair.

How the hell had this happened?

There is no better way to examine your own prejudices than attempting to raise children engaged in cultural things. Taking their lead has led me to strange territories, including ballet, medieval festivals and the Gruffalo stage show. But as we enter the hinterland of adolescence, music continues to be the most revealing and unpredictable of journeys.

Full disclosure – I am a recovering music snob. My introduction to journalism was being a “rock journalist” (imagine the thrill of that business card) for Cream magazine in the early noughties. Having misspent much of my youth behind the counter of record stores, I was one of those (mostly) young men who saw High Fidelity as a kind of secondhand memoir. Oh, how we judged you for your love of mainstream pap.

And yet. The wonderful thing about kids and music is they like what they like. No child is born with an innate sense of cool or cringe. And, being kids, they tend to like fun things. When ours were of an age to move on from Play School records, we let them roam free at local op-shops and choose CDs for their cheap boombox at home. For $1, we ended up with an eight-disc set of Best of the 80s. This proved to be life-changing.

I had no nostalgic love for 80s pop. When I was developing my own music taste, my idea of upbeat pop was Morrissey imagining his girlfriend in a coma. Good times! But suddenly our lives were soundtracked by Tears for Fears, A-ha and Bananarama. I knew it was serious when our eldest chose the Beach Boys’ Kokomo as the soundtrack to her final kindergarten presentation.

I am grateful for the new music and artists our kids have since discovered. Their ever-changing playlists (a source of much conflict on car journeys) have introduced me to diverse acts from Chappell Roan via Raye to sea shanties and modern folk. But the greatest gift has been the chance to realise how wrong I was about music I already knew.

It turns out Queen isn’t tacky and overblown but joyous and extraordinary. Belinda Carlisle didn’t perform disposable fluff but some of the most perfect pop songs ever written. Likewise, the Bangles. Cyndi Lauper? Genius. Cheap Trick? Actually quite good.

And who knew that Bowie’s richest period wasn’t the albums Hunky Dory to Low but the first three tracks of Let’s Dance? (With an honourable mention for his and Jagger’s drunken singalong version of Dancing in the Street.) Who knew? The kids knew.

What is interesting about this generation of kids is how omnivorous and eclectic they are when it comes to music. The streaming age means almost all of music history is available to everyone, all of the time.

New music no longer dominates the old. It’s no harder to hear Eddie Cochran’s Twenty Flight Rock than the Weeknd’s Blinding Lights.

The tastes of their parents no doubt play a part – there’s no getting away from how many 80s-themed parties and discos our kids have attended – but their musical world seems far wider than that of my parents, whose music library fitted neatly on to a single, narrow shelf.

The algorithm also plays its part, of course. Given our family shares a streaming library, I am long resigned to my recommended listens and favourites being corrupted by the children’s choices. But I try to remind myself they are not polluting the river so much as widening the banks.

Outside the house, I am conscious that other algorithms are influencing their listening habits in the same way radio and television once influenced mine. Our kids aren’t yet on social media, but their current playlists are informed by music heard at various sporting events (the Killers, MGMT and Summer of ’69 tend to be on high rotation).

I certainly wasn’t listening to music from 40 years earlier when I was 13. More nostalgically, I miss the musical subcultures that were so important and so rigidly defended when I was coming of age. The contained bubbles of popularity allowed by social media enclaves don’t seem quite the same.

But that was my journey, not theirs.

Our kids have been able to build musical identities out of the very best pop, rock and, uh, however we’re classifying sea shanties without being pinned to the zeitgeist. Sometimes that involves Olivia Dean, sometimes Eric Carmen, sometimes a forgotten track from The Transformers: The Movie soundtrack.

Music may not define them in the way it defined many of my generation, but they still know a good tune when they hear one.

So, yes, listening to music through the ears of my kids has taught this old snob to listen without prejudice or embarrassment. Because it turns out that serious and important music doesn’t always last, but the fun stuff goes on for ever.

Myke Bartlett is a writer and critic

Liam Dawson reveals England are ‘gutted’ after ODI series setback against Pakistan

The Guardian Mon, 26 Oct 2026 13:15:49 GMT

‘We were desperate to win’

Spinner believes defeats are useful learning experiences

Liam Dawson has revealed England’s disappointment after the two ­agonising defeats to Sri Lanka and Pakistan that have left making the ODI tri-series final in serious doubt. “That ­changing room is gutted, we’re desperate to win,” he said.

To reach the final, England need Pakistan to beat Sri Lanka on Tuesday and then they have to thrash Sri Lanka on Thursday, but Dawson is optimistic the losses can help them in the World Cup in 12 months’ time in southern Africa.

“If you look at the last two games, we’ve been in positions where we should have won, so that is a ­massive positive as a group,” he said. “To lose those two games from a position we’re in is frustrating because we should have won those games.

“If, in a year’s time, we do get to those situations again and bank on our previous experiences then we’ll look back at this tri-series as a huge positive.”

The 36-year-old said he is not drawing any conclusions from ­usurping Adil Rashid. For more than a decade, the leg-spinner has been the No 1 spinner for England in white-ball formats and he needs 26 more dismissals to become their all-time leading one-day wicket-taker.

After missing September’s home series win over Sri Lanka because of an injury, Rashid has been overlooked for the defeats to Sri Lanka and ­Pakistan.

The explanation given is Dawson’s skiddy slow left-armers are more suited to the conditions in ­Rawalpindi and Lahore, with Rashid expensive in his only tournament outing against Pakistan last week.

In Rashid’s absence, ­Dawson has impressed, but a ­bowling unit light on experience has been exposed as England let seemingly surefire wins slip away.

The former England captain Nasser Hussain told Sky Sports last week that Rashid’s recent performances had “dropped off”, although Dawson believes the double World Cup winner remains a stellar operator.

“I don’t think I can be compared to Adil, he’s a phenomenal bowler,” he said. “You don’t play 165 ODIs and become a bad bowler. I don’t think you can compare us at all because we’re so different in our roles in the team. He’s a fantastic bowler, he’s been exceptional for England and I think he still will be.”

Without an express paceman or mystery spinner, England let ­Pakistan off the hook from 154 for nine chasing 242 in Lahore on Sunday as Shadab Khan and the No 11, Haris Rauf, sealed an extraordinary win for the hosts.

‘I laughed so hard my Tampax fell out’: Michael Gambon’s pranks revealed by the stars he cracked up

The Guardian Mon, 26 Oct 2026 12:15:41 GMT

He made Daniel Radcliffe’s Harry Potter fart, left Judi Dench unable to control herself and told a fry-up fantasy about Helen Mirren. A new biography details the star’s mischief

Jasper Rees’s authorised biography of Michael Gambon, published three years after the great actor’s death, has nuanced accounts of his performances in Shakespeare, Beckett and Pinter as well as The Singing Detective and the Harry Potter films. There are even chapters devoted to his hands (“the biggest you’ve ever seen on anybody” – Brian Cox) and similarly enormous feet. But, Gambon being Gambon, there are also dozens of accounts of tomfoolery on and off stage …

David Hare’s 1995 play Skylight is set in a draughty flat where a dish of spaghetti is cooked up on stage. Those kitchen cupboards proved useful for Lia Williams to hide when Gambon’s goofing got to her at the National Theatre. Gambon would adopt a different accent or speak in tongues during a scene and “when he made me laugh it was hell on Earth because there was nothing I could do about it” said Williams, who called him “one of the funniest people I’ve ever met”. She continued: “One time I laughed so hard that my Tampax fell out and I had to deal with that for an entire act.”

Ibsen’s Ghosts was a hot potato when it was first staged in 1882 thanks to its scandalous plot involving syphilis and incest. Gambon had some fun with the spuds when playing the self-righteous Pastor Manders in an 80s BBC TV version. Director Elijah Moshinsky envisioned a tense, sombre dinner scene and Gambon sat alongside Judi Dench and Kenneth Branagh. The potatoes were duly passed around by Natasha Richardson. “I’ll just have the usual eight,” requested Gambon. His co-stars’ corpsing led them to leave the set. “We couldn’t control ourselves at all,” confessed Dench.

Not every actor’s biography includes “fart machines” in the index but toots fake and real are let off in several chapters. When Gambon took over the role of Dumbledore in Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban, he and Alan Rickman pranked Daniel Radcliffe by triggering a fart machine during a closeup of the young star when he was in a sleeping bag alongside fellow Hogwarts students. “I was initially really annoyed,” said Radcliffe, before concluding that if Rickman and Gambon had engineered it then “that is pretty funny”.

When Gambon played King Lear for the RSC in 1982, Antony Sher sported a red nose as the clownish Fool. The poster presented them as a sort of double act and Sher was widely seen as stealing the limelight. Rees likens it to Gambon taking on what is often referred to as an “actor’s Everest” only to find another climber “clambering frantically up the same rope”. Adrian Noble, who directed the tragedy, said Gambon “joshed [Sher] mercilessly”. During the storm scene he reportedly bellowed: “Come on out, you little red-nosed fucker!”

When he was appearing on stage in Arthur Miller’s A View from the Bridge, Gambon kept a signed photo of Robert De Niro – with words of admiration for Gambon’s work – on his dressing room table. The pair would appear together in the film The Good Shepherd in 2006 but had never even met by the time he was doing A View from the Bridge. The fake autograph and note – “I loved working with you Mike, you’re great – love Bobby” – were apparently written by Gambon himself.

One festive season in the late 60s, Gambon found himself starring in the Christmas show Hans, the Witch and the Gobbin at Birmingham Rep – much to his annoyance, remembered co-star Anthony Higgins. A prodigious swearer, Gambon decided to add to his stage makeup for a performance. “One night he’d written on one eyelid ‘fuck’ and on the other ‘off’,” said Higgins. Gambon blinked each eye to deliver the message to Higgins. Artistic director Peter Dews had to give him a word of warning.

When Gambon played the tramp Davies in a 2000 revival of Harold Pinter’s play The Caretaker, he revelled in repelling theatregoers – as well as the brothers played by Douglas Hodge and Rupert Graves. One night, according to Rees’s book, Gambon had his back to the audience and buried his hand in his trousers, where he had stowed away a serving of chocolate cake. He withdrew his smeared fingers and sniffed them, causing his co-stars to crack up. “Rupert was in terrible trouble,” remembered Hodge. “Rupert wet himself regularly.”

Gambon loved to supply journalists with tall tales and see who believed him. He treated one interviewer to an “insight” into how he and Helen Mirren prepared while in the wings for their roles as Antony and Cleopatra for the RSC. Mirren, he assured the journalist, got into character by performing a mime in which she prepared a dish of ham and eggs for Antony. “Absolute rubbish,” Mirren told Rees, though added: “It’s a lovely story.”

Michael Gambon: The Authorised Biography by Jasper Rees is published by Century (£30). To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop. com. Delivery charges may apply.

‘We don’t have inflation’? Five charts show the US economic reality of Trump’s second term so far

The Guardian Mon, 26 Oct 2026 11:00:42 GMT

As the US midterm elections approach, we take a look at data to see a true picture of the US economy under Trump

With the midterm elections fast approaching, many Americans have the economy on their minds.

US voters are exhausted by years of higher prices. Donald Trump won the presidency in 2024 on promises to lower inflation and undo the damage he said the Biden administration had inflicted on the economy.

In Trump’s view, his plan is working. At a recent rally in Montana, Trump boasted about the current economy, framing it as a booming time for Americans. “We’re richer now,” he said. “We don’t have inflation.”

Economic data paints a different picture. Inflation, especially gas prices, has soared over the last year. The job market has been in stasis, and higher interest rates have meant it’s more expensive for Americans to borrow money for loans and mortgages.

These fluctuations have a concrete impact on the lives of Americans. A recent Harris poll for the Guardian found that a majority of Americans, including some Republicans, disagree. Nearly two-thirds said they believe the country is experiencing a recession, and many said higher prices had been a pain point. Americans are reporting having trouble saving, and a third polled said one surprise bill could sink them financially.

Here’s what the data shows us about Trump’s second term so far.

The rate of price increases has dramatically cooled since its peak in 2022, when the pandemic’s economic stimulus packages found their way into consumer prices. Inflation peaked at 9.1%, a 40-year high, in June 2022.

In January 2025, the month when Trump started his second term, inflation was down to 3%. By April 2025, it would be 2.3% – the lowest rate since 2021.

That’s when things start to get bumpy. After Trump placed tariffs on nearly everything that the US imports, inflation started to heat up again, climbing back up to 3% in September 2025. After many of his tariffs were paused and eventually found to be illegal, prices started going down again. In January and February 2026, inflation was back down to 2.4%.

The Iran war, specifically its impact on oil prices, has brought inflation back up to levels not seen since 2023. In May, inflation reached 4.2% and has hovered above 3.4% since.

It’s been nearly six years since Americans have seen inflation at a manageable 2% level. Price increases build up over time and can put a squeeze on budgets, which is why it’s such a sensitive point for voters during a crucial election.

In the Guardian’s recent poll with the Harris Poll, gas prices were the most common pain point for Americans, with 83% saying they are making a dent in their current finances.

Soon after the war in Iran began, the strait of Hormuz, a key route that a fifth of the world’s oil typically passes through, was blocked off. Its closure has pushed up prices all around the world. Though the US itself is a major oil producer, prices have still surged since the war. The average price of gas was $4.32 per gallon in mid-October, according to AAA, nearly $1.30 a gallon higher than a year ago.

Even for an oil-producing state like Texas, a gallon of gas is $3.81 compared with $2.64 a year ago. Meanwhile, drivers in California, a state that imports much of its gas from overseas, are paying $6.21 per gallon.

The labor market is another metric used to measure the health of the economy, and while the US job market has seen some growth since Trump took office again, figures have fluctuated over the last year. In 2025, altogether 181,000 new jobs were added to the economy, compared with 2.2m jobs in 2024.

Employers have been dealing with a mixed landscape for hiring: harsher immigration policies, uncertainty from tariffs and higher prices for supplies have all meant slow job growth. The unemployment rate has remained low, though, at just over 4%. Economists call this a “low-hire, low-fire” economy, in which employers are neither hiring nor dismissing workers.

Though many Americans report struggling in today’s economy, a small group have never been wealthier. The stock market has continued to soar since Trump took office, recovering from dips seen during his initial tariff announcement and the early days of the Iran war.

Economists largely see AI investment as the leading factor in the stock market’s acceleration. Tech companies are spending billions of dollars investing in datacenters and for chips that are needed to power AI.

While many Americans are invested in the stock market through their retirement and pension funds, this growth has really been a boon for the top 1% wealthiest Americans, who own nearly half of the stock market investments.

Economists say higher prices paired with an exuberant stock market have led to a K-shaped economy, where the wealthier have never felt richer while everyday Americans continue to deal with tightened budgets from high prices.

Interest rates are often not as noticeable to consumers as gas or grocery prices, which they come across every day. The impact that higher interest rates have on the economy takes longer to appear and runs deep. Interest rates shape how much Americans pay to borrow money – to run their businesses, pay off car loans and buy their homes.

For the Federal Reserve, shifting interest rates is the tool it uses to balance the economy. Raising rates can cool the economy, bringing prices down, though at the risk of hurting the job market. Lowering rates can stimulate the economy at the risk of leading to more inflation.

When Trump entered office in January 2025, the Fed was in the middle of a series of interest rate reductions. Officials said they were seeing inflation cooling and slower growth in the labor market. Interest rates were at a range of 4.25% to 4.5% – 1% lower than they were a year ago.

Uncertainty around Trump’s new tariffs would ultimately lead officials to pause the reduction, though the president was still demanding lower rates. As tariffs proved to have less of a long-term effect on prices, the Fed started lowering rates again in fall 2025.

For months, the Fed held off on changing rates as the economic impacts of the war of Iran bore out. But in September, the Fed hiked rates for the first time since 2023, by a quarter point. The Trump-appointed Fed chair, Kevin Warsh, said that “inflation is too high and has been for too long”.

Higher interest rates have already had an impact on mortgage rates, which had dipped down to below 6% (for a 30-year mortgage) for the first time since 2022, in February, but are now up past 7%.

Harry Styles says his laptop has been dead for six years. Is he just showing off?

The Guardian Mon, 26 Oct 2026 11:00:39 GMT

He is either being insincere – knowing he could buy an entire Apple store if he wanted – or he is genuinely overwhelmed by tech. If it’s the latter, he has my sympathy

Clips of the “epic conversation” (rambling, blokey chat) Rolling Stone orchestrated between Harry Styles and Thom Yorke keep appearing online, and none more often than the one in which Styles declared his laptop has been dead for about six years. “I don’t know where the charger is,” Styles laughed, prompting a predictable rash of “his computer is NOT OK” jokes from 6 Music dads everywhere.

Is this charmingly relatable, or … not? One personal finance influencer declared it “a deeply unlikeable clip”, seeing it as the kind of tech-free flex you can get away with only if you are rich and famous. It’s true that the ability to protect your peace by withdrawing from the brain-liquefying churn of online life is a privilege inaccessible to most people, who need tech to function and earn a living. Opting out means delegating digital drudgery to other people: Christopher Nolan’s determination not to have email must be a massive pain for his entourage. I bet Ed Sheeran not having a smartphone is extremely inconvenient, too – someone else must always have to put the hotel into Google Maps, arrange the Deliveroo dinner and order the Uber.

This dead laptop business does feel slightly disingenuous – Styles could have an entire Apple store delivered if he fancies a tech upgrade. But I’m inclined to feel more tolerant. He says he uses his phone to write songs, and maybe there is an element of overwhelm at play? I’m always losing cables and procrastinating over tech issues. “I don’t understand why you’re waiting for it to die when you’ll really be in trouble,” my husband said crossly to me this morning as I fought to turn off my ancient phone, which had decided once again that typing was forbidden. But I’m filled with dread and confusion at the thought of replacing it (what model, how many GBs, must I engage with the Cloud?) and my life isn’t too busy or demanding; I can’t imagine what it’s like when you are a global icon on a world tour.

So, in case he is floundering not flexing – Harry, check your sock drawer. That’s where I found my charger last time I lost it.

Emma Beddington is a Guardian columnist

If the PM reboots the UK for working-class people, unions will be with him. But the time for talking is over

The Guardian Mon, 26 Oct 2026 10:00:27 GMT

Andy Burnham has railed against neoliberalism – the historic shift must start with this week’s budget

Andrea Egan is the general secretary of Unison

After Keir Starmer, things could only get better inside Labour. But Andy Burnham’s arrival as party leader and prime minister didn’t just clear that low bar. It was a cause for hope, especially for those of us in the trade union movement. That’s less because Burnham is streets ahead of his predecessor as a politician – although he is – and more about just how radically the new prime minister has framed his project for the country.

I’ve been active in the labour movement for almost four decades. In that time, I cannot count how many times I’ve heard talk of reversing the devastation wreaked by Margaret Thatcher. For socialists and grassroots trade union activists, this kind of political thinking is bread and butter. But not so much for a Labour prime minister.

Tony Blair, between torching the Middle East and taking a hammer to our civil liberties, infamously came to build upon Thatcher’s legacy rather than bury it. Gordon Brown and Starmer were more set against the Thatcherite fracturing of our society than Blair. But they both continued to inhabit the political cage she built: the idea that there is no alternative.

Before now, the only major party leader ideologically opposed to neoliberalism in a remotely serious way was Jeremy Corbyn, who drew up a programme that would have started to undo the rule of the market. But it wasn’t to be. So in beginning his premiership by insisting that there is, in fact, an alternative way of organising our economy and society to the neoliberal one, Burnham marked a historic shift.

This kind of talk isn’t cheap. How the prime minister has articulated his vision really matters, both because it has challenged the assumptions that have shaped our politics for decades and because the analysis is fundamentally correct. Virtually every aspect of this country’s malaise, as Burnham powerfully explained to Kemi Badenoch, can be traced back to the “wrong turns” taken in the 1980s.

But the flip side for Burnham is that his diagnosis doesn’t leave any doubt about what Labour must do in government. To measure up to his own ambitions, the party will have to implement changes to the structure of our economy unseen since the immediate postwar period. At a minimum, that means bringing sectors into public ownership and investing on a huge scale to rebuild a social fabric – our public services, infrastructure and collective life – that has been shredded.

Many of the Burnham government’s measures so far have been welcome. Banking quick wins that don’t require wrangling with the Treasury but signal you are on the side of the people was a sensible approach for the early days. Labour’s steady improvement in the polls reflects that. But four decades of neoliberalism won’t be ended through Google Maps updates of petrol prices, or even with measures to provide breathing room in the face of the cost of living crisis.

Following up a bold, historical diagnosis with piecemeal measures just isn’t politically sustainable. From US wars to the climate crisis, the factors making essentials ever more unaffordable are out of control. Without the radical action the prime minister has called for, then, the lives of our people and communities are going to keep getting worse, rapidly. And the stakes remain high: it’s the far right that will benefit if this project fails.

So the budget must be the moment that the prime minister’s programme starts to match his rhetoric. Unison is clear about that, and so are my colleagues across the trade union movement. We’re not expecting neoliberalism to have melted away by the time John Healey finishes reading out his statement. But we are demanding serious measures that actually begin to improve workers’ lives.

We expect a big, multiyear funding plan to restore investment and wages in our public services – alongside kicking profiteering vultures out of the public sector through bringing services back in-house. These measures should be funded by finally making the wealthy few pay their fair share of tax. It’s imperative that the prime minister and chancellor defy pressure from the business lobby and the rightwing media to reject changes such as equalising income and capital gains tax.

after newsletter promotion

The decades-long political settlement the prime minister has rightly defined himself against might have impoverished the vast majority, but there were some winners. And those who have profited handsomely from neoliberalism will fight tooth and nail against any attempt to actually break with it.

So, if the prime minister sticks with his historic ambition to remake Britain in the interests of the working class, it won’t be easy. But the trade union movement will be by his side. There’s no dodging a battle with the vested interests committed to keeping things as they are – and the budget is the place to begin.

Andrea Egan is the general secretary of Unison

Wolff was at pains to point out the considerable efforts made by a number of other people in bringing the young Italian to the verge of a record-breaking title.

If he seals the title in Mexico City he will become F1’s youngest world champion at 20 years old.

Antonelli led from pole position on Sunday with a controlled, ­dominant run largely at the front of the field, for his ninth success of the season.

“On Kimi’s side, the main headline is that [it is] for me the best race that he’s delivered,” Wolff said. “Getting off the start with the ­inferior tyre and then controlling it at all times. ­Exceptional. I think he’s ­outperformed the car.”

Wolff believed it was all the more impressive given how difficult Antonelli’s rookie season had been in 2025 when at times he struggled with the car and made mistakes that caused some to question whether Mercedes had been correct to promote him to the team so soon.

Those are doubts he feels Antonelli has comprehensively silenced. “There are many ­people that said last year after nine races ­without points he shouldn’t be in a ­Mercedes,” Wolff said. “People in other teams that said he shouldn’t even be in Formula One.

‘He was like 10 men after taking cocaine‘: how Britain’s drug habit is fuelling domestic abuse

The Guardian Mon, 26 Oct 2026 09:00:27 GMT

Home Office figures show nearly two-thirds of drug tests carried out on arrested abuse suspects detected use of a drug that ‘boosts confidence but increases paranoia’

During lockdown, Charlotte and her ex-partner would spend evenings cooped up in their flat, listening to music, watching YouTube videos and chatting until the small hours. Those nights would be fuelled by alcohol and lines of cocaine.

“I wanted to be loved, and when he told me he loved me like nobody ever would and nobody ever will, I drank the Kool-Aid,” Charlotte says. “I wanted to believe that. And there’s a point when you’re with somebody and you’re drinking, you’re doing coke, where you think you have this bond, you think it’s just you two in the world.”

But that emotional high would be fleeting. “Without a doubt, without any exception, it would never end peacefully. My ex-partner would get so ridiculously paranoid once he was using cocaine. It was just crazy,” she says. Charlotte’s partner would accuse her of taking more than him, messaging men and hiding things from him. When she denied it, he would subject her to brutal physical assaults.

“And then the next day it was all apologies and it’ll all be fine, it’ll all be different.”

Data suggests it is a common scenario. Home Office figures sent to the Guardian show nearly six in 10 police drug tests carried out on people arrested on suspicion of domestic abuse were positive for cocaine between July 2025 and June this year.

It is not possible to see the whole picture, as some of the tests were carried out after the police suspected drug-taking, but it tallies with a 2023 pilot study that found 59% of domestic abuse suspects tested positive for cocaine or opiates.

A wider Guardian investigation has found that Britain’s record-breaking cocaine habit is also driving crimes from assault to dangerous driving. The stimulant is increasingly ubiquitous, fuelling situations ranging from fights on nights out to violence at football matches.

Cocaine has featured in a number of domestic murder cases in recent years. Victoria Thomas, a 45-year-old mother-of-two from Cardiff, was strangled to death by her husband, Alcwyn Thomas, who was “argumentative and moody”, having been filmed on CCTV taking cocaine shortly before he killed her on 19 August 2024.

On 13 June last year, 32-year-old Izzy Knight was murdered by her husband, Paul Knight, in the house they shared in Northamptonshire while their two daughters slept upstairs. In a note, he blamed “having an addiction to cocaine and spending money I don’t have”.

Both men were sentenced to life in prison.

Cat Chappell, a BACP-registered therapist specialising in domestic abuse who previously volunteered on the National Domestic Violence Helpline, says cocaine boosts confidence but increases paranoia, “and so much of abuse is around paranoia”. “It’s taking what’s already there, making it like 10 times worse,” she says.

It can also make it more difficult to leave, she says, because perpetrators will often offer to get help with their cocaine problem. “And [for victims], that’s what you want to hear in those moments.”

Charlotte and her ex-partner got together just before the pandemic and, though it was not the first time she had taken cocaine, it was not something she had done regularly. Her ex, on the other hand, was a habitual user.

“My ex was a really small man, and after cocaine use he’d be like 10 men. He was like the Incredible Hulk, it was like there was this beast in him and he would get this strength. And I can’t tell you where it was from. Then he would come at me and he would absolutely beat me to a pulp. It was absolutely terrifying,” she says.

He would routinely trap her in the bedroom. “I remember one night he got really paranoid that somebody was in the house and he brought knives upstairs. He would pace about all night. It was really, really horrific.

“For somebody who’s already [controlling and abusive] it’s like adding fuel to the fire, it really is, with coke.”

He often stole from her to fund his habit, using her phone to take money from her bank account, including times when he had knocked her unconscious.

Charlotte remembers police visited their flat about 19 times, as a result of her own calls and those made by neighbours, but she would always cover up her ex’s cocaine use.

“I would deny a lot of it because I didn’t want to say, ‘Yes, I’ve been doing it as well’, so you’re in this absolute no-win situation because you’re then sticking up for them all the time.”

She began to abuse alcohol to cope with the situation she was in. “I didn’t want to be there,” Charlotte says. “I was just drinking because I didn’t want to feel anything. I’d wake up, drink all day. I just wanted to feel numb, numb, numb, numb, numb.”

She was finally able to leave on Boxing Day in 2021 when her ex went out to score drugs and she wrote an email to her father asking him to pick her up. She has been free of alcohol and cocaine since.

After initially attempting to pursue her ex for knocking her teeth out, police later decided to take no action against Charlotte’s abuser. She fears he will go on to abuse someone else.

It was Women’s Aid that helped her get her life back on track and she is now an advocate for the charity in her home city of Leeds. She also works for another charity, Smart Works, which helps women get into employment.

Nik Peasgood, the chief executive of Leeds Women’s Aid, says Charlotte’s story is increasingly common. She thinks cocaine is having an effect on the levels of violence perpetrated by abusers and she is calling for more research to help understand the relationship between cocaine, domestic abuse and mental health.

“If they’re already abusive and the relationship’s abusive, [cocaine] might lower their inhibitions, it might make the frequency worse, it might make the severity worse, it might mean that they can’t control how they normally control the relationship and the situation. But it doesn’t make somebody abusive or violent if they’re not already. It’s not an excuse for that violence.”

Peasgood says that cocaine, unlike a lot of other drugs, is used by a broad range of people, including middle- and upper-class people and those who are well-respected within society and do not fit the stereotype of what people think domestic abusers looks like.

The drug can be a barrier to people seeking help, particularly for victims in professional jobs who feel they have a lot to lose if they are caught using illegal substances.

“[Contacting the police] has ramifications away from just the perpetrator when there are drugs involved, and [there is] fear around that,” says Peasgood. “Especially if people have got children, it’s something they wouldn’t necessarily want others to know about.”

Through her work, Charlotte has now met many others who faced similar situations. “I’m in recovery now and it’s alarming how many people tell the same tale of drinking, doing coke, and it just becoming an absolute explosion of rows and just horrific violence,” she says.

“I think it’s not a problem that’s actually going away. If anything, it’s getting worse. You only have to speak to people in the rehab or recovery world and they’ll tell you this is going nowhere. It’s really scary.”

She believes the figures don’t show the true scale of the issue. “I think this is much wider reaching than we realise, due to the stigma of reporting it and the shame of the victim using the drug.”

For many people, she says, cocaine use is “very much seen as our weekend thing”. “It’s very much behind closed doors and not spoken about. People would be gobsmacked at how many people actually do it. It’s so widespread, it’s unbelievable.”

In the UK, call the national domestic abuse helpline on 0808 2000 247, or visit Women’s Aid. In the US, the domestic violence hotline is 1-800-799-SAFE (7233). In Australia, the national family violence counselling service is on 1800 737 732. Other international helplines may be found via www. befrienders. org.

As mega-hit Into the Woods wows the West End, what’s the secret weapon of this Sondheim spectacular?

The Guardian Mon, 26 Oct 2026 08:00:26 GMT

With its shimmering forest and its plunge into darkness and destruction, this fairytale romp bagged an Olivier for its lighting – and, reveals designer Aideen Malone, it wasn’t even finished

For a minute I worry that Aideen Malone might return her Olivier award. “It’s funny that I won an award for it, because I would say Into the Woods is one of the most unfinished pieces I have ever done,” declares the lighting designer. “There was a lot of detail we never got a chance to finish. We ran out of time – big time!”

Luckily, the judges and audiences disagreed. If you want to see enchantment, take yourself to Stephen Sondheim’s musical set in the twisted world of fairytale. Cinderella, Red Riding Hood and others bounce into the forest, which shimmers in a weave of powdery, gleaming branches and light angling through all the trees. Now transferred to the West End from London’s Bridge theatre, it’s a breathtaking piece of design for a seriously playful musical.

“This is a stunning piece, but it’s a monster,” Malone declares. “There was a lot of problem-solving.” From a lighting point of view, it is “about the passing of time, day and night. The woods are very luscious and inviting initially, and then become darker and more mysterious.” As tales old and new collide, and characters stumble far beyond their happy ever afters, design signposts the journey. After the initial quest into the woods, the characters return to find that arcadia has collapsed into “destruction and wasteland”.

Rangy and witty, the Irish designer arrives for our interview convinced that I’ll be chatting to all the “absolutely stunning” creatives behind Into the Woods; Jordan Fein (director), Tom Scutt (set) and Roland Horvath (video). “It’s a great team effort,” she insists. She previously sent light through Scutt’s wheat fields in their Olivier-winning Fiddler on the Roof. Into the Woods offers a series of smoke and mirror surprises, for which Malone uncages a whole spectrum of smoke and haze: “A fog that’s quite dense but rises, and then a cool fog that stays low on the ground.” Light pierces the layers, especially when characters experience an epiphany (Red Riding Hood plucked from the wolf’s belly, Jack dismounting the beanstalk).

What was her own career-setting epiphany? “Was I a little theatre kid?” she considers. “Not really.” A Dublin pantomime at an impressionable age was a turning point, while at her all-girls secondary school, the annual musical cast the tall Malone as swaggering blokes in Oklahoma! and The King and I. Acting beckoned – but her degree at Dublin Trinity and then Goldsmiths in London also covered backstage roles. “I fell upon lighting, and was definitely more comfortable with not being on the stage, collaborating with the whole team. I enjoyed how lighting is very technical and creative at the same time. I haven’t looked back since.”

Her career in lighting began on the fringe and working on dance shows. She toured with dancer and choreographer Akram Khan, enjoying how dance let her “play with beautiful bodies in space. It’s very sculptural. Often you don’t need to worry about the faces, and you can play with angle.”

Theatre then became her home turf. Do all directors understand lighting? “Not to name any names,” she grins, “but some are very visual, and some aren’t.” She prefers “somebody with nerves of steel who is prepared to try stuff” – like Sally Cookson, with whom she devised hit shows such as Jane Eyre and A Monster Calls. “Devised work is nerve-racking,” says Malone, “because you don’t know what you’ve got till the last week of rehearsals. You have to figure it out once you’re in the space.” Their 2016 Peter Pan at the National was touch and go, she admits: “But we always get there for press night.”

The pandemic prompted a long-contemplated masters in light and lighting at University College London. “I thought I knew a lot about colour,” Malone says, “but I learned so much about the detail of a light source, which makes a huge difference when you’re lighting skin tones.” This fascination carries back into her stage work. “Two people in daylight might look the same, but put them under theatre light and they’re quite different. One person needs 1% more magenta, and one needs 1% less. It’s a challenge.”

Malone has always been drawn to “the cool and warm natural colours of daylight” – a favourite venue is the Open Air theatre in London’s Regent’s Park, where she and Scutt designed Carousel and Fiddler. She also embraces projects blending architectural and theatrical knowhow, such as Sadler’s Wells East, which opened last year. A neon sign above the entrance proclaims: “You are welcome” – but glowing lighting through the building must sustain that welcome from morning to night.

Although she is broadening her work, theatre retains its essential appeal for her. “You have a work light on and the space looks flat – then you put a spotlight on and it’s transformed. It’s a bit of magic.”

Into the Woods is at the Noël Coward theatre, London, until 9 January
