‘It’s collective punishment’: nearly 2,000 Palestinians in Hebron displaced as Israeli forces take over homes

The Guardian Mon, 26 Oct 2026 07:00:25 GMT

Families forced to flee as Netanyahu tries to prove security credentials after two Israeli soldiers killed days before election

Hebron, the biggest city in the West Bank, had paid little attention to Israel’s looming elections until it found itself suddenly in the midst of them, a proving ground for Benjamin Netanyahu’s security credentials in the run-up to Tuesday’s vote.

A gun attack on an Israeli military checkpoint on Friday in which two soldiers were killed brought immediate televised visits from Netanyahu and his finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, whose ruling coalition is narrowly trailing with two days of campaigning left.

They vowed abrupt and sweeping retribution, and the prime minister warned of imminent military operations on a scale the West Bank has not seen in nearly 60 years of occupation.

Within hours, the whole city of 250,000 people had been sealed off and the neighbourhood of Farsh al-Hawa, closest to the site of Friday’s attack, had been flattened. By Sunday morning, there was nothing left but rubble of an industrial area that had been full of car workshops, a big ceramics plant and other enterprises.

As the bulldozers were at work there, another district a few kilometres away was being systematically emptied. Ein Deir Baha was allegedly home to at least one of the two men involved in the attack (both of whom were killed on the spot), and on Friday its residents paid the price.

The imam from the local mosque, Fahed Ahmaro, was woken at about midnight by the loudspeakers from military vehicles patrolling the street, telling homeowners to vacate their homes immediately for their own safety.

Ahmaro had 30 members of his family living in his house. He rushed his frail mother and some of his grandchildren to his daughter’s house in another part of Hebron, and was on his way back in the hope of picking up some of his possessions when his neighbour phoned him.

“He told me not to come back, and the army had blown up the gates to the house. I don’t know what they have done to it by now. I heard they destroyed the furniture,” Ahmaro said. “You don’t know what you have until you lose it. Now I realise how devastating it is to lose your home.”

At midday on Sunday, he was in a Hebron market shopping for a change of clothes for his grandchildren, uncertain how long the family’s exile would last.

He had heard that the house was being used as a base by Israeli soldiers and looking up at the house, perched on the side of a steep hill, he could see some lights on but no sign of life.

The Hebron municipality said that 370 families, nearly 2,000 people, had been displaced by the army sweep through Ein Deir Baha. In its official comments, the Israeli army had said that the displaced population had left voluntarily, that “civilians who wished to evacuate were permitted to temporarily leave the area”.

Ahmaro was outraged at the suggestion that he had any choice about fleeing.

“Never, never, never. Why should I leave my house?” he asked.

Abdul Halim al-Tamimi tried to stay put when the military came at 1.30am. The 77-year-old was told his family had only 10 minutes to vacate their home.

“An intelligence officer told me if we didn’t go, they would displace us the same way they have done it in Gaza,” he said. “We stood there in front of the house, and we refused to leave until we were faced by three military vehicles and they forced us out.”

By the time the Tamimi family left, it was 3am on Saturday morning. On Sunday morning their home was festooned with large Israeli flags and ringed with military vehicles. The army had turned the substantial villa into its headquarters.

In its statement, the Israeli military claimed that 2,000 local people were from the Jaba’a clan, from which the gunmen were allegedly drawn, and which the army claimed was “associated with Hamas”.

The claim drew consternation and derision from people in Ein Deir Baha. They numbered the extent of the Jaba’a clan at 150 at most, with no known reputation for radicalism.

“We are from a completely different family. We are innocent people. We have nothing to do with the whole thing,” Tamimi said. “I don’t know what they are using it for, other than maybe election publicity.”

Palestinians in the occupied West Bank have no vote in Tuesday’s elections, but their lives could be deeply affected by the outcome.

By Sunday evening, all roads in and out of the city remained closed to cars, with heavy steel barriers swung across them. The only traffic was on foot, with taxi drivers squabbling for fares. The driver of a delivery truck, Wasam Sadi, pulled in at one checkpoint with the cab windshield smashed and glass fragments in his eyes. He had been attacked by settlers at a nearby junction, he said.

“It’s collective punishment,” said Hebron’s mayor, Yousef al-Jabari. “They have dragged people from their houses, and they have prevented the media from getting into the district in order to cover up what is happening.

“Netanyahu and his gang are using Palestinian land to displace Palestinian people, closing the city, closing the mosque, in order to achieve their political goals.”

We’ve made Oxford Street traffic-free – and that’s just the start. Soon there’ll be green spaces for arts and music too

The Guardian Mon, 26 Oct 2026 06:00:24 GMT

We’ll revive the in-person shopping experience with a transformation of the area, inspired by the John Lewis and Selfridges founders who first set up there

Sadiq Khan is the mayor of London

At around 8pm on Sunday evening the last car made its way down Oxford Street, marking the start of a momentous new era for our nation’s high street. Today, after decades of discussions and deliberations, the action we’ve taken means almost one kilometre of Oxford Street is now officially traffic-free – just in time for Christmas. But this is only the start of a much bigger transformation, and the first step towards a bright new future for this historic thoroughfare.

Walk down Oxford Street, and you’re passing through hundreds of years of British history and culture. In 1864, an ambitious young draper called John Lewis opened his first shop on the street. Forty-five years later, the American entrepreneur Harry Gordon Selfridge arrived with a radical idea: to transform shopping from a mundane necessity into an unforgettable experience. He filled his store with dazzling window displays, world-class entertainment, restaurants and lounges. He even installed women’s toilets – a rarity in Edwardian England – giving women a newfound freedom to make the most of the city. As he opened the doors to his first customers, he told them “everyone is welcome”.

That spirit has been at the heart of Oxford Street’s success ever since. We love it because it feels as if it belongs to all of us. It’s where teenagers come for their first shopping trip with friends. Where families marvel at the magic of festive lights and decorations. And where generations of Londoners and visitors have come to discover the latest music, fashion and trends. It’s also the beating heart of British retail – pumping billions into our national economy, with the surrounding area accounting for an incredible 1% of the UK’s total economic output in 2022.

But in recent years this iconic street has started to lose some of its sparkle. Changing consumer habits and the legacy of the pandemic have taken their toll. Footfall has fallen. Some of our best-loved stores have closed their doors, only to be replaced by vape shops and candy stores. And, too often, the experience of visiting a chaotic, congested Oxford Street has felt more like an ordeal to survive than a day out to enjoy.

If we’re to restore this beloved street to its former glory, we must rediscover the pioneering spirit of Harry Gordon Selfridge and create a space for everyone to enjoy, breathing new life into the high street and bringing back big brands. And that’s what our bold plans – backed by the overwhelming majority of Londoners and businesses – are all about. And with household names like Ikea, Puma and Clarks investing in new stores, there’s already excitement for what Oxford Street can become.

People need a reason beyond simply buying something to visit their high street. And in an age when almost anything can be delivered right to our door, that principle matters more than ever. Coming to Oxford Street should feel like a positive experience. Somewhere you want to spend time, as well as your hard-earned money. A place where you’re not choked by tailpipe fumes or deafened by the noise of passing motorists. And that starts with reclaiming it for pedestrians, not traffic – rebalancing the relationship between cars and people in the centre of our city.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

That’s why I’m so delighted that, thanks to our efforts, the road stretching between Orchard Street and Great Portland Street is now officially traffic-free. But removing cars is just the beginning. Imagine an Oxford Street where you can stroll at your own pace, take a break from shopping with a coffee under the trees, or stumble across some live music, a fashion show, a sports exhibition or a cultural event. We’re determined to put Oxford Street not just on par with top global shopping destinations like Times Square, the Champs-Élysées and La Rambla, but make it even better.

And while it’s a process – we’re deliberately keeping disruption to a minimum over the busy Christmas period – by next spring, visitors can expect to see new trees, new seats and new public plazas, alongside improved lighting and signage. This ambitious project has been far from straightforward or easy. As usual, we’ve had to overcome opposition from a vocal minority, and 14 years of a previous government that didn’t back the plans. But with seven in 10 Londoners expressing support for our vision, after extensive consultation, I knew we owed it to our city and to our businesses to deliver these improvements, which will help to boost jobs, growth and investment as we build a fairer, safer, greener and more prosperous London for everyone.

Of course, we’ll continue to listen to Londoners. Many of the initial changes are temporary, and we’ll use real-time feedback to help refine the final designs in a test and review period throughout 2027. But for centuries, Oxford Street has reinvented itself, adapting to changing times and helping shape British culture along the way. And now it’s in need of its next great transformation. One that honours its extraordinary past while creating new possibilities for the future. A future where new memories are made, new businesses flourish and new chapters of British history are written.

Today marks the beginning of that journey – and I encourage everyone to come to explore this newly transformed street, as we work together to ensure its best days are still to come. In the words of Harry Gordon Selfridge – everyone is welcome.

Sadiq Khan is the mayor of London

Could Europe’s autumn of discontent threaten the survival of the EU?

The Guardian Mon, 26 Oct 2026 05:00:23 GMT

Anger on the streets could increasingly turn against the EU itself if it can’t show why cooperation makes people’s lives better

Europe is living through an autumn of unusual discontent. What protesters from Paris to Milan to Madrid share is a deepening anxiety about the future and a growing anger at the gap between what they expect from their governments and what they feel governments are delivering, whether the issue is unaffordable housing, stagnant wages, the spiralling cost of living or failing schools.

The electoral consequences of the failure to get a grip on this public anger are already with us. Spain goes to the polls next month in a snap election called after parliament voted down key housing reforms. France begins the process of electing a new president in April, while Poland, Italy and a string of smaller states will vote before the end of 2027. The stakes could not be higher.

At the same time, national leaders face mounting pressures from abroad. Issues such as Ukraine, uncertainty over US security guarantees and economic competition with China demand more European cooperation, even as national politics makes this increasingly difficult. Governments face popular demands to deliver security and prosperity, just as their capacity to do so independently is shrinking. This leaves Europe with a difficult question: how can countries whose leaders are increasingly struggling at home find the common ground needed to act together abroad?

If the EU did not exist, Europeans would have every reason to invent it. Together, its members form a market of 450 million people and an economy of almost €19tn, the third largest after the US and China. No individual EU country comes close to that weight on its own. Germany, the largest, has 84 million people and an economy about a sixth the size of the US’s. Twenty of the 27 member states have fewer than 12 million inhabitants, less than half of Shanghai’s. In a world of tariffs and export controls, it is scale that secures a seat at the table.

But this rationale for cooperation does not make the EU’s survival inevitable. This political project has often been declared on the brink of collapse; the most recent crises include Brexit, the pandemic and energy shocks. Yet it has proved remarkably durable, responding with improvised solutions that previously seemed impossible.

The very traits that infuriate Eurosceptics – slow decision-making, endless negotiations and messy compromises – are, counterintuitively, sources of strength for Europe. The dispersion of power between governments, parliaments, courts and EU institutions makes the system hard to capture and compromises tend to stick.

The EU’s staying power lies in its capacity to adapt despite disagreements, while helping countries achieve what is termed “effective sovereignty”. Nominal sovereignty is the right to decide alone, even when deciding alone – as the UK has discovered to its cost since it left the club supposedly to regain its sovereignty – changes little. Effective sovereignty is the capacity to shape outcomes on energy, trade, migration or defence that no European state can control by itself. And the EU has itself adapted: its fully paid-up members remain the core but non-members such as Norway and Switzerland participate on defence, security, energy and economic policy. The EU has an interest in bringing Britain back into closer cooperation too, even if not exactly as it looked pre-Brexit.

But the EU’s resilience should not be taken for granted. Negotiations over the next seven-year budget, worth almost €2tn, show just how hard it is to achieve consensus. While everyone agrees on the need for greater European security and economic competitiveness, countries can’t agree on who should foot the bill. France, for example, is pushing for new EU-wide taxes, which others resist.

Even so, growing domestic political instability does not necessarily mean there will be paralysis in Brussels. Quite the opposite – it creates an impetus to act. With France’s presidential election approaching, Emmanuel Macron has urged fellow leaders to strike a budget deal by Christmas, warning that political room for manoeuvre would shrink in the new year if Marine Le Pen succeeds him.

Le Pen no longer talks about taking France out of the euro or a Brexit-style referendum. But her platform would undermine the union from within, turning the EU into a “Europe of Nations” and threatening cuts to France’s contribution to the EU budget.

Whether political change comes through elections, protests or new compromises in Brussels, public discontent cannot simply be negotiated away. This brings us back to the streets. French, Italian and Spanish citizens want functioning public services, affordable housing, economic and national security, and a sense that they have some control over their futures.

Sign up to This is Europe

The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment

after newsletter promotion

Younger Europeans, in particular, face growing uncertainty about their economic prospects, from finding affordable housing to securing stable employment. So far, this pessimism has not translated into widespread rejection of the EU. Recent polling suggests that young Europeans remain among the EU’s strongest supporters, with 90% favouring greater unity among member states and 78% wanting the EU to have more resources to act.

This gives Europe an opportunity, but also a responsibility, to turn that support into tangible improvements in their lives. That is the real test in the years ahead. Decisions about defence, industrial policy and social protection will involve difficult trade-offs, and not everyone will benefit equally. But if European cooperation becomes better at preserving institutions than at responding to citizens’ concerns, the discontent now spilling on to the streets could increasingly turn against the EU itself. The EU has repeatedly shown that it can survive political crises. Now it must ensure that the people living through them can do more than merely get by.

Catherine De Vries is professor of political science at IE University in Madrid. She is the co-author with Alexandros Kentikelenis of How Europe Survives

7 Numbers That Explain Anthropic’s Business

The New York Times October 26, 2026

Artificial Intelligence

Advertisement

Supported by

We broke down the A. I. company’s key figures, which give insight into the health of its business, its future plans and who’s in charge.

By Sri Muppidi and Lauren Hirsch

Sri Muppidi reported from San Francisco, and Lauren Hirsch from New York.

Anthropic, the San Francisco company that makes the Claude chatbot, fully revealed its financials for the first time on Monday as it races to go public in a blockbuster listing as soon as next month. In a filing, the company provided rare insight into the business of a “frontier” A. I. lab that makes cutting-edge A. I. models.

Here’s what stood out in Anthropic’s business.

Anthropic generated $16.3 billion in revenue for the first half of this year, up nearly 14-fold from the same period a year ago — a stunning rate of growth. The company generates revenue primarily through selling subscriptions and use of its A. I. models and Claude A. I. products.

Net loss was $80.7 billion for the first half of this year. The loss appeared large because it includes a one-time charge of $72.4 billion related to convertible notes, a type of debt that will later convert into equity, and other financial instruments.

Anthropic had raised billions of dollars from major backers like Amazon and Google in the form of convertible debt. As Anthropic’s valuation skyrocketed, the value of the convertible debt also rose. Because that debt is considered a liability, it was logged by Anthropic as a loss.

Anthropic has committed to various contracts for computing power and other infrastructure that it needs for building and running its A. I. The contracts listed in its financial prospectus could total up to $807 billion, according a tally by The New York Times.

Not all these contracts are the same. One deal to lease computing power from SpaceX through 2029, for example, can be scrapped starting in 2027 with a 90-day warning. Others are longer term, such as a $110 billion deal with Amazon that lasts until 2036.

For contracts that cannot be canceled, Anthropic is on the hook to pay whether it uses the computing power or not. That could pose a major risk if its growth does not keep pace with its commitments.

Anthropic had about $132 billion in cash and readily accessible investments at the end of June, already an enormous well of capital it can tap to fuel its growth. The fact that it is going public to raise even more money underlines how aggressively the company is spending. In fact, Anthropic has so much money that the interest it earned on its cash pile alone was worth more than $1 billion in the first half of the year.

Five customers made up roughly 25 percent of Anthropic’s revenue in the nine months that ended on Sept. 30, which means the company is dependent on just a few major clients. (Anthropic did not disclose the names of the customers.) Many customers are not locked into long-term contracts and could reduce or cancel spending anytime.

This number refers to the proportion of voting control that will be held by Dario Amodei, Anthropic’s chief executive, and the company’s six other co-founders after the public listing, which would continue the founding group’s influence in the A. I. lab. The structure is common with founder-led technology companies, allowing founders to run their firms with some protection from the day-to-day whims of public investors.

Of the 335 pages of Anthropic’s filing, 94 were dedicated to explaining the company’s risk factors. Among them was how A. I. models could pose “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity,” which could also expose the company to product liabilities and reputational harm. Anthropic also cited “intense competition” and its inability to secure enough computing power as major risks.

Sri Muppidi is a business and technology reporter for The Times and DealBook, covering artificial intelligence. Contact her securely on Signal: @srimuppidi.13.

Lauren Hirsch is a Times reporter who covers deals and dealmakers in Wall Street and Washington.

For Senegalese Street Vendors in New York, ‘Work Is Worship’

The New York Times October 26, 2026

Arisa Haboshi for The New York Times

Most days, Canal Street in Lower Manhattan teems with licensed and unlicensed street vendors peddling purses, watches, sweatshirts and all manner of tchotchkes. Many of the vendors are Senegalese.

Many spend their days on the sidewalks, selling everything from coffee to knockoff designer handbags.

Despite the fear stoked by the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown, they are sustained by their faith and an unwavering belief in the American dream.

Supported by

Struggling to find steady work, many migrants who have arrived recently from Senegal have adapted with a relentless sidewalk hustle, sustaining their families through street vending.

By Aimee Ortiz

Visuals by Arisa Haboshi

Most days, Khadim Ndiaye wakes up in the apartment he shares with five people in the Bronx and heads down to Canal Street, where he sets up shop on the sidewalk. Cat-eye, oversize and aviator frames bearing familiar logos — Prada, Gucci, Fendi — are among the sunglasses he hawks to passers-by.

Some days are better than others, but the worst are the days when he comes “back home the same way I left in the morning,” which is to say, with no money.

Mr. Ndiaye, 33, is among the thousands of Senegalese migrants who have made their way across the Atlantic from Dakar, Senegal’s capital, followed by a perilous overland trek through South and Central America to New York with one goal: to create a better life for themselves and their families in Senegal.

For many, that means spending days on the city’s sidewalks, selling everything from coffee to knockoff designer handbags. They are sustained by their faith and an unwavering belief in the American dream, even as fear has swept through New York’s Senegalese community over the Trump administration’s mass-deportation campaign.

While Senegalese immigrants have long had a foothold in the city, a recent surge of newcomers, many of them young men seeking asylum, have found themselves struggling to find work and adapt to their new surroundings. The Trump administration’s immigration crackdown has made life even harder for the new arrivals, many of whom are members of the Baye Fall, a subgroup of a Sufi Muslim brotherhood called the Mouride, for whom labor and prayer go hand-in-hand. Unable to find work, many turned to vending.

A 2024 report by the Immigration Research Initiative, a nonpartisan think tank, found that 55 percent of general merchandise vendors in New York City are from Senegal. The work comes with its own risks. The police frequently seize counterfeit merchandise, forcing vendors to essentially start over from scratch. At least five vendors from Senegal were arrested in an ICE raid on Canal Street in October 2025.

To guard against the risks they face, vendors have banded together, Mr. Ndiaye said, using WhatsApp to text the locations of law enforcement operations, for instance, or warn others when a block is teeming with ICE agents.

It’s hard “leaving your home birthplace and going to a new place,” he said, adding that “being mistreated in that new place makes it harder to bear.”

Despite the hardships and discrimination he’s faced, Mr. Ndiaye said that he and other newcomers like him just want to support their families and contribute to the building of this nation.

“We believe in the American dream,” Mr. Ndiaye, who has applied for asylum, said. “We believe in a country that has opportunities.”

Jeanne Batalova, a senior policy analyst at the Migration Policy Institute, a nonpartisan think tank, said it’s not surprising that Mr. Ndiaye and other Senegalese migrants have turned to street vending, particularly “in a country that doesn’t really provide much support to people who arrive.”

“It’s a younger population and it’s a working-age population with a strong work ethic,” she said. In addition to supporting themselves and their families back home, she added, many asylum seekers arrive owing considerable sums to smuggling networks.

Got a confidential news tip? The New York Times would like to hear from readers who want to share messages and materials with our journalists.

“There is a significant pressure on people to work,” she said.

Amadou Ly, an activist and founder of the Amadou Ly Foundation, which assists immigrants in New York, said the city does not provide enough support for new arrivals, particularly for Senegalese migrants and other “communities that do not tend to have a loud voice or a loud representative.”

“Instead of the NYPD utilizing its resources towards over-policing people who are selling counterfeits, we can actually use resources towards employment and things that benefit our economy,” he said.

Ousmane Diop said he started AFRIC’A. R. T., a grass-roots organization based in Harlem, about five years ago to support the African immigrants, including Senegalese migrants, as they arrived in New York, many speaking only their native Wolof. After an initial surge early in the Biden administration, he said, about 10,000 Senegalese migrants crossed the Southern border between March 2023 and March 2024.

“We were facing a housing crisis, employment crisis, integration crisis,” he said, “and we had to come up with some plan.”

Mr. Diop, who was granted asylum in the United States in 2018, is now the chief executive and president of AFRIC’A. R. T. The organization offers English classes and helps newcomers navigate the asylum process and find a safe place to live.

As President Trump has taken a harder line on immigration in his second term, Mr. Diop said, people have skipped hearings in immigration court, fearing that they could be arrested and deported. Among those who turned to street vending as a way of making ends meet is Abdoul Azez Kasse, who said he started selling wallets on Canal Street after the work permit he received as an asylum seeker expired. Under the Biden administration, his paperwork was renewed like clockwork, but under Mr. Trump, “the immigration procedures have been dragging now, and taking too long.”

With nearly 20 people in Senegal relying on the money he makes, Mr. Kasse, 35, said he leans on his faith as a Baye Fall to get him through.

“Even if I have to sell water and make 50 cents out of every bag that I sell, I will do it,” he said. “I will do it because I believe that here, work is worship.”

Even as organizations like Mr. Diop’s help Senegalese migrants settle in New York, tensions have surfaced with more established members of the city’s Senegalese community, which has historically been based along a stretch of 116th street in Harlem known as Le Petit Sénégal.

Having arrived in the United States when she was 8, Marie Ndiaye, 36, is what the newcomers call an “ancient.” Some of the more recent migrants, she said, felt that “the ancients, people like myself, did not truly embrace them and did not help them the way they felt like they needed to be helped.”

Ms. Ndiaye, who has helped organize “know-your-rights” workshops for new migrants and has even let a few of them stay with her to help them get on their feet, said that sense of entitlement was frustrating.

But she credits the newcomers with rejuvenating Le Petit Sénégal and restoring some of its flavor after years of gentrification.

“They’re not diluted like people like myself,” Ms. Ndiaye said, referring to the nearly two decades she has spent in the United States. “They are very authentic from what they wear, how they talk. I mean, my Wolof improved.”

Malamine Bamba, 33, who survived a dangerous trek through South America to reach the United States a little over two years ago, believes he is on a holy mission. Dressed in colorful patchwork clothing that identifies him as a Baye Fall, and with a smile on his face, he walks around Le Petit Sénégal selling small cups of café touba, coffee made from beans ground with djar, a musky black pepper, which he pours from a 10-liter container. On good days, he can make $80 to $90. He uses the money to support himself and his family back in Senegal, and to pay off the $10,000 he owes to the smugglers who helped him get to the United States. Mr. Bamba said he’s paid off about half.

The spiced coffee is a sacrament, he said, one that his faith implores him to share with the world. Mr. Bamba walks until he sells out, and then he goes home to brew another batch.

“Everybody knows that if you sweat, you’re going to get the benefits,” he said. “I strongly believe in that so that’s why I be always smiling because I know that a better future is ahead of me.”

Aimee Ortiz covers breaking news and other topics for The Times.

Brazilian Markets Convulse After Unexpected Election Result

The New York Times October 26, 2026

Brazil’s Presidential Election

Advertisement

Supported by

President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s re-election victory prompted a sharp reversal in financial markets that had expected his opponent to win.

By Joe Rennison

Stocks in Brazil plummeted on Monday after President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s re-election victory and his opponent’s early dispute of the results.

The Bovespa Index, Brazil’s benchmark stock index, quickly fell more than 10 percent as trading began, triggering a 30-minute circuit breaker — a tool that pauses trading to prevent runaway sell-offs. The index ended the day 14 percent lower, its worst fall since the onset of the pandemic in March 2020.

The country’s currency, the real, weakened significantly, down more than 8 percent against the dollar, on course for its sharpest single day weakening against the dollar since early 1999.

The new government’s cost of borrowing rose sharply, with the yield on Brazil’s dollar-denominated 10-year government bond rising more than 0.2 percentage points to around 6.45 percent. Its local-currency 10-year bond yield rose even more, up more than two full percentage points to around 15 percent.

The moves were a sharp reversal, after stock prices rose over the past few months and bond yields trended lower, as investors began to bet on Mr. Lula’s opponent, Flávio Bolsonaro, clinching victory. Mr. Bolsonaro, the right-wing candidate, had aligned himself with President Trump and had been seen as the more market friendly of the two candidates.

“Brazilian assets are likely to face immediate pressure and heightened near-term volatility as market unwinds positions built on expectations of a Bolsonaro victory,” said Dev Ashish, an economist focused on Latin America at Société Générale, a French bank.

There was little early sign of the moves affecting markets in the United States. Major indexes ended the day higher, and the 10-year Treasury yield moved slightly lower.

Argentina did appear to feel some spillover. Argentina’s dollar-denominated 10-year yield rose 0.4 percentage points. Mr. Ashish noted that much of the ferocious volatility on Monday reflected the rapid unwind of pre-election bets.

“Once the initial volatility subsides, market attention will likely shift to cabinet appointments,” he said, “particularly whether Vice President Geraldo Alckmin assumes a leading economic role, the influence of centrist congressional parties within the governing coalition, and the administration’s broader fiscal strategy.”

Joe Rennison writes about financial markets, a beat that ranges from chronicling the vagaries of the stock market to explaining the often-inscrutable trading decisions of Wall Street insiders.

The Massachusetts bar, which catered to lesbians, lifted its Covid mask requirement once a week to attract more patrons. The decision brought criticism and national attention, but did not save the business.

By Mark Arsenault

A Western Massachusetts bar at the center of a Covid masking controversy last month is moving toward closing down, according to a message it posted Monday on social media.

The bar, the Last Ditch, said on its website that it was founded for lesbians, as well as “transexuals, gender freaks, workers and their friends,” an oasis for safe and happy drinking in the tiny city of Greenfield. It became internationally known for the backlash to its owners’ decision to relax a mandatory face mask policy. The hope was that making masks optional on Saturdays would increase business. But opponents of the change argued the bar was abandoning its goals to be welcoming to everyone.

People posting online accused the owners of being ableist and risking the lives of immunocompromised customers. A backlash to the backlash quickly emerged, with people mocking customers and their Covid concerns.

A Boston Globe story in September on the masking dispute went viral, and the travails of the Last Ditch were published by media around the country and overseas.

The publicity appeared to draw dozens of potential customers to the first mask-optional Saturday night after the local controversy became widely known. But the burst of attention was apparently not enough to save the bar in downtown Greenfield, a city of about 17,000 people.

A message on the Last Ditch Instagram page said that the bar needed “new owners ASAP.”

“We are SOFT CLOSING effective immediately, all BOOKED events will CONTINUE, otherwise we are CLOSED,” the message read. “Love and solidarity to all.”

“We have put our lives on hold to foster networks of care, resources, and a home base for organizing,” the posting said. “It’s time we pass it on.”

The bar’s social media listed several scheduled events this week, including an open mic night and karaoke.

Three housemates, Asa Rosario, Jackie Matellian and Sage Territo, opened the bar in 2025, hoping to fill a need after two queer bars in the region had closed in recent years.

A message to the bar’s email account on Monday returned an automated response saying, “We are community run for the community, so we are slow to reply.”

Amy Cahillane, the community and economic development director for Greenfield, said Monday that “it is always a shame to lose a small business,” especially one that was a valuable part of the city’s downtown.

Anthropic’s I. P. O. Prospectus Spells Out a Future of Promise and Peril

The New York Times October 26, 2026

Artificial Intelligence

Advertisement

Supported by

The A. I. company took great pains to describe the many benefits that can come from using its Claude chatbot and technology, but also offered up a heavy dose of gloom.

By Mike Isaac

Mike Isaac covers Silicon Valley and artificial intelligence from San Francisco.

For years, Dario Amodei, a founder of the start-up Anthropic, has been painted as the pre-eminent doomsayer of artificial intelligence, often making sweeping statements about how the technology could wreak havoc on the world.

On Monday, as Dr. Amodei presented his company’s paperwork for what could be the biggest ever initial public offering on Wall Street, he painted a more nuanced picture: Even with its many risks, A. I. has the potential to bring about untold benefits to humanity.

From the very top of the founder’s letter — a kind of mission statement typical of many I. P. O. prospectuses — Dr. Amodei and his six co-founders set the stakes.

We believe that AI is one of the most consequential technologies in human history.

This is a view on which Dr. Amodei has long been consistent. Since Anthropic’s earliest days, he has argued that the technology has the capacity to profoundly change the world. Often, Dr. Amodei would harp on the negative consequences those changes may bring. Lately, he has more frequently been playing up some of the benefits.

It is in line with a change in tone Anthropic has recently pitched to its investors. Across the industry and even among Anthropic’s backers is a view that Dr. Amodei’s vocal concerns about the technology have overshadowed what many believe are its upsides — an important sales pitch as the company seeks to raise billions on the stock market.

In closed-door meetings, the company has said it plans to emphasize more of the positive aspects of A. I., from increased productivity for workers to curing the world’s worst ailments.

First, we believe that AI will profoundly accelerate the rate of progress in biology and medicine, potentially curing diseases that have plagued humanity for millennia, including cancer, Alzheimer’s disease, heart disease, rare genetic diseases, and the major infectious diseases.

It could bring about a sustained acceleration in economic growth, with all the benefits for human wellbeing that growth can bring.

Anthropic is accused of focusing on economic disruption rather than benefit. Specifically, critics argue, the company more often stresses monumental job loss while peers focus on the many ways the technology will empower workers. In his letter, Dr. Amodei allows for a future of unprecedented growth, which could bring about worldwide prosperity.

He goes on to cite examples such as giving people access to the knowledge and skills of a lawyer, an accountant or a farmer.

More broadly, AI can help to strengthen markets where they are currently weak. Mobile phones did this in the developing world in the 2000s, giving people access to critical information on prices that allowed trade to flow.

And finally, Dr. Amodei notes that advancements in A. I. could unburden us from needless bureaucracy. He sketches a future where DMV lines are shortened, job seekers can find can receive services to find employment more easily and Medicaid systems are navigable. Perhaps most of all, he claims the technology can help “democratic governments deliver on their promises to citizens.”

Alongside our customers, we intend to apply our AI models to revolutionize these and dozens of other areas of human endeavor. Doing so may well represent the greatest economic opportunity in human history.

Though the prospectus is front-loaded with sweetness and light, the paperwork has all the hallmarks of Anthropic’s anxieties. In page after page, the company lists the many risks that A. I. poses to its business — and society.

AI can be misused by those who wish to do harm, for example to conduct cyberattacks or to design biological weapons.

At least some of this is already happening. Over the summer, a series of cybersecurity breaches from Anthropic, OpenAI and other leading A. I. labs kicked off an industrywide discussion on how to safeguard advanced systems.

Dr. Amodei and the company go on to list the flip sides to all the positive possibilities laid out at the beginning of the document. With economic prosperity comes the potential for great upheaval.

The incredible economic value of AI may come with economic disruption, similar to what has happened with previous technologies but greater in magnitude.

And Anthropic suggests that just as democratic governments may be empowered, so too could autocratic regimes. Dr. Amodei continues:

Authoritarian governments may use AI to create high-tech surveillance states, deepen repression, and make themselves much more difficult to dislodge.

No I. P. O. prospectus from Anthropic would have been complete without Dr. Amodei’s biggest concern, and what some might call the ultimate “risk factor” — a disclosure companies are required to make to investors about issues that could adversely affect their business.

Sufficiently advanced AI systems could, if not developed, deployed, and operated with appropriate safeguards, oversight, and security measures, pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity.

Put more simply: Yes, Anthropic believes its technology could bring about conditions for human flourishing the likes of which have never been seen. The company also believes it could bring about the end of the world.

Most normal companies do not tend to address such weighty philosophical matters when filing to go public. But Anthropic is far from a normal company.

Mike Isaac is The Times’s Silicon Valley correspondent, based in San Francisco. He covers the world’s most consequential tech companies, and how they shape culture both online and offline.

Walter Koenig, Chekov From ‘Star Trek,’ Has Died

The New York Times October 26, 2026

As the baby-faced Russian navigator of the U. S. S. Enterprise, he was a mainstay of the original television series and seven films. He was 90.

Walter Koenig as Pavel Chekov in a 1968 episode of “Star Trek.”Credit... CBS, via Getty Images

Supported by

By Anita Gates

Walter Koenig, a mainstay of the “Star Trek” franchise as Pavel Chekov, the Russian navigator aboard the U. S. S. Enterprise, died on Sunday at his home in the North Hollywood neighborhood of Los Angeles. He was 90.

The death was confirmed by his agent, Zachery McGinnis.

Ensign Pavel Chekov — who arrived at the beginning of the show’s second season, in the fall of 1967 — was conceived as a solution to a demographic problem. Gene Roddenberry, the creator of “Star Trek,” had been told that young viewers considered the show’s leads, William Shatner (Captain Kirk) and Leonard Nimoy (Mr. Spock), who were both 35 when the series began, practically middle-aged.

So Chekov was positioned as a younger type — Mr. Koenig was 30 when he was cast — complete with a mop-top haircut that the producers hoped would remind adolescent girls of Davy Jones of the Monkees, the popular TV-generated rock band.

His character also represented a future beyond the Cold War’s balance of atomic terror, one in which a Russian officer could be serving under a captain from Iowa as a unified humanity explores the stars.

Mr. Koenig (pronounced KAY-nig), whose parents were Russian Jewish immigrants from Lithuania, was born in Chicago; his onscreen accent was theatrical. Over the show’s remaining two seasons on network television, before “Star Trek” ascended into a multimedia pop-culture phenomenon, Chekov appeared in 36 episodes, most often just doing his job and making practical pronouncements like “Warp speed 2, Captain.”

How The Times decides who gets an obituary. There is no formula, scoring system or checklist in determining the news value of a life. We investigate, research and ask around before settling on our subjects. If you know of someone who might be a candidate for a Times obituary, please suggest it here.

His favorite episode, Mr. Koenig said, was “Spectre of the Gun” (1968), in which the Enterprise crewmen were forced by aliens to participate in a Wild West gunfight. In that episode, Chekov took a bullet to the chest from Wyatt Earp (as it turned out, it was all an illusion) and enjoyed lavish physical affection from a saloon hostess.

Mr. Koenig was irreverently honest about the technological shortcomings of “Star Trek.” Before being cast, he said, he had never watched a full episode because, while channel surfing, he had noticed that in an outdoor scene the rocks looked like Styrofoam. Asked by one interviewer about the show’s special effects, he shook his head and said, “The triggers didn’t even pop.”

Of the “Star Trek” movies in which he appeared, released between 1979 and 1994, he considered “Star Trek IV: The Voyage Home” (1986) “the best film we did,” he told Yahoo Entertainment in 2016. A time-travel story centered on recovering whales from the 20th century to save Earth from certain doom some 300 years later, it represented, Mr. Koenig said, Mr. Roddenberry’s vision of telling “sociopolitical stories that spoke to what was happening in the world at the time.”

In that film, Chekov was interrogated by F. B. I. agents who were curious about his Russian accent and his phaser, and he confused San Franciscans by asking where the “nuclear wessels” were kept.

Walter Marvin Koenig was born on Sept. 14, 1936, in Chicago, the son of Isadore and Sarah (Strauss) Koenig. (The family name was changed from Königsberg when his father immigrated to the United States.) His mother had worked at a millinery shop in England on her family’s way to the United States. His father worked as, among other things, a musician, a nightclub owner and, just before World War II, a traveling translator for RCA Victor.

The family moved to New York, and Walter grew up in the Inwood section of Manhattan. He attended Grinnell College in Iowa as a pre-med student (he was considering psychiatry as a career) before transferring to U. C. L. A., where he earned a bachelor’s degree in psychology. But he was “really at sea as to what to do with my life,” he recalled in a 2013 Archive of American Television interview. “I was a leaf in the wind.”

Having played lead roles in high school and college stage productions, he decided to take an acting class. The teacher saw talent and encouraged him to give an acting career a try.

After two years at the Neighborhood Playhouse in New York, Mr. Koenig made his television debut on “Day in Court,” a daytime series. He also had small-screen roles on “Mr. Novak,” “The Alfred Hitchcock Hour” and, luckily for him, “The Lieutenant,” a drama series created by Mr. Roddenberry, who remembered him three years later when he was casting his new space series.

When the “Star Trek” years were over, science fiction called again. In 12 episodes of “Babylon 5” in the 1990s, Mr. Koenig played Alfred Bester, a manipulative, telepathic 23rd-century cop. In 2020, he appeared in “Unbelievable!!!!!,” a “Star Trek” parody starring Snoop Dogg and featuring many other actors from the various series.

An early marriage to the actress Anjanette Comer ended in divorce. In 1965, he married Judy Levitt, also an actress, who appeared in three “Star Trek” films. She died in 2022. Mr. Koenig is survived by their daughter, Danielle Koenig, and a grandson.

Mr. Koenig said that in the early 1970s he “hit rock bottom” financially after the original “Star Trek” series went off the air. In response to his money troubles, he began writing scripts to help pay the bills, and sold several pilots, he recalled in a 1994 interview with a documentary filmmaker. He wrote an episode of “Star Trek: The Animated Series,” and had several other credits in the ’70s and ’80s.

He was modest about the relative importance of his most famous character and generous in his evaluation of the fans, who came to be known as Trekkies. They were not just computer people or college students, he pointed out in the Archive of American Television interview.

“It was people who had a sense of humanity and a sense of justice and a sort of political bent,” Mr. Koenig said. “People who had imagination — and people who loved monsters.”

Ama Sarpomaa and Sopan Deb contributed reporting.

Democrats See a Rare but Fleeting Chance to Shake Up the Senate Map

The New York Times October 26, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Democrats are targeting G. O. P. strongholds that could set them up for new majorities. But if they don’t win those races now, it could be a long time before they have another chance.

By Carl Hulse

Carl Hulse covered his first Senate race in 1986.

Senator Roger Marshall, the first-term Republican incumbent, is under siege in Kansas with the midterms just days off. Ken Paxton, the Republican Senate candidate in Texas and the state’s attorney general, is embroiled in multiple unsavory scandals and struggling.

Polls also show Democratic Senate candidates running strong in Iowa and Alaska, and on the cusp of victory in North Carolina, playing offense in what should be safe Republican terrain. At the same time, independent candidates are within striking distance of Republican Senate candidates in Montana, Nebraska and even South Dakota.

“This is as good a political environment as Democrats could ever wish,” said Amy Walter, the editor of the nonpartisan Cook Political Report, “and as bad as Republicans could ever imagine.”

Yet with the exception of North Carolina, it is far from certain that Democrats can pull off a single upset in any of the red states typically considered out of reach for them. They are competing not only against individual Republicans but also against ideological and structural advantages that have turned those states into reliable G. O. P. strongholds and locked down the Senate map in recent years.

It wasn’t long ago that Nebraska, Montana, Iowa, the Dakotas and Alaska were represented by Democratic senators. But Republicans have solidified their grip on those states, suggesting that if Democrats cannot make inroads in this election, when Republicans are on the ropes, it could be some time before they again have such an opening.

“If you can’t win under these conditions, you ain’t gonna win for a long time,” said Jon Tester, the former Democratic senator from Montana who lost his seat in 2024 after three terms as his state moved away from Democrats. He pointed to anti-Trump fervor, soaring fuel costs and the economic struggles of everyday Americans as reasons Republicans were highly vulnerable on their home turf.

The Senate map is always evolving, with population shifts and social conditions sparking changes in party thinking about where to devote attention and resources. As recently as the 1990s, the South was the epicenter of new Democratic thinking, as President Bill Clinton showed that Democrats could still appeal to rural and lower-income voters, and he had plenty of allies from the region on Capitol Hill.

At the time, states like Louisiana and Arkansas were represented by at least one and often two Democratic senators. Conversely, Republicans could still be elected in places like New York, Illinois and the Pacific Northwest.

But that political environment steadily eroded, and Republicans rose in the South and the Great Plains while elected Democrats mostly disappeared there. Pushed out of spots like North Dakota and vast expanses of Middle America, Democrats concentrated on urban areas, promoting a more progressive brand of politics.

That was a big mistake, critics say.

“The national Democratic Party hasn’t done what it should in places like Montana,” said Seth Bodnar, an Army veteran and former president of the University of Montana, who is running as an independent candidate in that state. “This strategy of trading blue-collar workers in rural areas to win in the cities and suburbs — that’s not a strategy for success in Montana.”

Over the years, changes in the map have had a profound effect on the way the parties treat elections, with some states essentially considered the property of one party or another, limiting the battlefield. The number of seats considered truly competitive has dwindled significantly, a phenomenon that started in the House but has taken hold more recently in the Senate.

That has had a major impact on the way the Senate operates, as senators have increasingly retreated to their partisan corners, unconcerned about a threat from across the aisle. In a growing number of states, they need to worry only about primaries, in which the incentive is to move right in the case of Republicans and left for Democrats, which has yielded a profoundly polarized Senate.

At present, just three states — Maine, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin — have split Senate delegations, illustrating how rigid the one-party hold is on Senate seats. It is the lowest total since the direct election of senators began more than a century ago.

But Democrats spied red-state openings this year amid the backlash to Trump administration policies, including tariffs and the war with Iran, which have contributed to high costs and economic pain in parts of the nation that might not otherwise seriously entertain a Democratic candidate. And they have had strong candidates step up.

The contested Senate map has steadily expanded into red states. In recent days, the super PAC aligned with Senator Chuck Schumer, the New York Democrat and minority leader, put more than $1 million into advertising in Mississippi, a state that has not elected a Democratic senator since 1982. But Democrats believe Scott Colom, a state prosecutor, has a chance against the Republican senator, Cindy Hyde-Smith.

Mr. Schumer, who plays a major role in crafting his party’s Senate strategy, dismissed the idea that a failure to cash in on some of the red states this time would mean they would remain out of reach for a stretch.

“I’ll never say never,” Mr. Schumer said. But he acknowledged that this year presented a “unique opportunity.”

“We have so many opportunities in reddish states,” he said. “Two years ago, they would have said this is the most impossible map. Who would have thought Alaska? Who would have thought Kansas? Who would have thought Iowa?”

Just how far Democrats can reach into red America won’t be known until after Election Day, but party strategists say that any wins could position the party for future gains.

“Every once in a while, the bottom falls out for the party in power, and when that happens, it’s possible to dramatically expand the number of states that you can win,” said Adam Jentleson, a former top Democratic Senate aide. He is also the founder of the Searchlight Institute, which aims to expand the Senate battleground and build an enduring Democratic majority.

Mr. Jentleson noted that most senators elected next month will serve through the entirety of the next president’s first term. And history shows that incumbent senators, with all the advantages of office, tend to get re-elected.

With Democrats also poised to win some red-state governorships, Mr. Jentleson said those governors could work with new Democratic senators to restore the party’s presence in states where it has been written off, providing a foundation to build on in coming elections.

He pointed to Republican-held seats in states like Wisconsin and North Carolina that could then be vulnerable in the next election. He said this year’s election could prove similar to 2006, when Democrats seized House and Senate majorities in Congress and then expanded those gains in 2008.

“What this should be for us is 2006 and 2008, when one good cycle leads to another,” Mr. Jentleson said.

But Democrats first have to win next month in states where they have had little success — and that is no sure thing. It presents a test of their possible appeal in states that seemed all but lost to the party.

“If you can’t win now,” said Mr. Tester, the former Democratic senator, “when can you win?”

Carl Hulse is the chief Washington correspondent for The Times, primarily writing about Congress and national political races and issues. He has nearly four decades of experience reporting in the nation’s capital.

Anthropic Reveals Skyrocketing Growth and Spending Plans in I. P. O. Filing

The New York Times October 26, 2026

Artificial Intelligence

Advertisement

Supported by

Ahead of what could be the largest public listing ever, Anthropic said revenue soared to $16.3 billion in the first half of the year, and it planned to spend $807 billion on A. I. infrastructure.

By Mike IsaacErin GriffithLauren Hirsch and Sri Muppidi

Mike Isaac and Sri Muppidi reported from San Francisco, and Erin Griffith and Lauren Hirsch from New York.

Anthropic, a five-year-old company whose artificial intelligence tools have made it a world leader in the technology, on Monday fully laid out the business behind its big ambitions for the first time.

In a financial prospectus for what could be the largest ever initial public offering, the San Francisco company revealed that sales of its A. I. products like the Claude chatbot to other businesses had grown at an astonishing clip. But it also said that it was losing money and planned to spend at an even faster rate as it invests heavily in A. I. infrastructure to support that growth.

Anthropic’s revenue was $16.3 billion in the first half of the year and its net loss was $80.7 billion, driven largely by a one-time charge. Stunningly, the company has committed up to $807 billion in contracts for data centers, chips and computing power, many of which cannot be canceled, over the next 10 years, according to a tally by The New York Times. Many of the contracts span different lengths of time, and the terms have yet to be finalized for some.

The numbers underscored how much Anthropic is betting that its future business will justify its outlays. Even its public offering, which could raise more than $100 billion, may not provide the company with enough money to fund its intense infrastructure needs, as it warned that it might need to seek additional financing sooner than anticipated.

Dario Amodei, the chief executive of Anthropic, and the company’s six other founders said the power of A. I. has driven the work and the sums.

“We believe that A. I. is one of the most consequential technologies in human history,” they wrote in the prospectus. They added that their company aimed to “realize” the benefits of A. I. “while navigating and preventing the risks that come with a technological revolution this fast and this powerful.”

Anthropic’s listing, which is expected to happen in the next month, is in many ways a test of the business of leading A. I. labs, which make cutting-edge models and sit atop an ecosystem of chip and cloud computing suppliers.

The listing could value Anthropic at $2 trillion, pushing it past Elon Musk’s SpaceX as the world’s biggest I. P. O. The privately held company had already surpassed rival OpenAI’s valuation in May, reaching $900 billion compared with OpenAI’s $730 billion. (OpenAI is considering a new funding that would value it at about $1.5 trillion in advance of its own public offering.)

But some companies have recently pulled back from going public amid uncertainty in the stock market. Oura, a maker of smart rings, recently delayed a listing, as did SB Energy, a subsidiary of the Japanese conglomerate SoftBank that has proposed to build the world’s largest data center project in Ohio. And fears have grown over whether the spending on A. I. will pay off if demand for the technology cools.

Anthropic’s filing showed that revenue soared to $16.3 billion in the first half of the year, 14-fold from a year earlier, largely from businesses using its A. I. software, including Claude.

The company lost more than $80.7 billion in the first half of the year, compared with a loss of $13 billion a year earlier. The net loss was abnormally large because it included a one-time $72.4 billion charge related to convertible notes, a type of debt that will later turn into equity. Anthropic posted a smaller operating loss, which excludes certain costs, of $693 million during that period.

Anthropic’s filing was unusual in that it warned its products could bring about disasters, including loss of control of the technology and authoritarian abuses. “To build A. I. is to harness cognition itself, and anything so powerful can be used for ill as well as good,” Dr. Amodei and the other founders wrote.

One jaw-dropping risk factor: Advanced A. I. systems could “pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity,” the company said.

Anthropic’s technology is regarded as so powerful that it plunged the start-up into disputes with the Department of Defense, rattled governments worldwide with how it could penetrate security systems and brought company leaders into conversation with heads of state and even the head of the Catholic church. Last month, Dr. Amodei called for a slowdown in development of its A. I.

If the company’s public offering is successful, it would likely unleash an avalanche of wealth for Wall Street and Silicon Valley. It would be the second “mega” I. P. O. this year, following SpaceX’s listing in June, which briefly turned Mr. Musk into the world’s first trillionaire. OpenAI is also aiming to list its shares in an offering that could come next year.

(The Times has sued OpenAI and Microsoft, claiming copyright infringement of news content related to A. I. systems. The two companies have denied those claims.)

Anthropic was founded in 2021 when a group of employees left OpenAI over disagreements about how A. I. should be developed. Dr. Amodei, who was OpenAI’s vice president of research, created Anthropic with his sister, Daniela, and others who were focused on developing a superintelligent computer system as quickly and safely as possible.

“I think that most people are underestimating just how radical the upside of A. I. could be, just as I think most people are underestimating how bad the risks could be,” Dr. Amodei wrote in an October 2024 essay titled “Machines of Loving Grace,” inspired by a Richard Brautigan poem on a future in which all-powerful robots commingle with humans in “harmony.”

Interpretations of the poem — and of Dr. Amodei’s writings — range from techno-optimism to a pessimistic view of A. I.’s impact on the world. Dr. Amodei and the other Anthropic founders have sometimes been called “doomers” about A. I.

Venture capital investors initially dismissed Anthropic as a science project. Many early backers were prominent figures in the effective altruism movement, which applies data and analysis to social causes. Dustin Moskovitz, a co-founder of Facebook; Jaan Tallinn, an entrepreneur; and Sam Bankman-Fried, the disgraced founder of the bankrupt cryptocurrency exchange FTX, were among Anthropic’s first investors.

Anthropic toiled largely in obscurity as OpenAI broke through with the 2022 release of its ChatGPT chatbot. Anthropic eventually focused on A. I. coding tools, which were so effective at generating software code that they sent shock waves through Silicon Valley’s engineering ranks. After the start-up released updates to its coding chatbots last fall, its business surged as tech companies worldwide adopted the programs.

Investors including Menlo Ventures, Lightspeed and Iconiq Capital poured billions into the company. Anthropic has raised roughly $130 billion in private funding.

Along the way, Anthropic also became a singular target for criticism. The company has incurred the ire of many in the tech industry for Dr. Amodei’s hard-line stance in support of A. I. regulation and his wariness of open-source software. Other tech leaders including Jensen Huang of Nvidia and Mark Zuckerberg of Meta have criticized Anthropic, accusing Dr. Amodei of trying to centralize A. I. power.

The company warned investors that its backing of A. I. regulation and safety could subject it to “heightened scrutiny, political backlash or disproportionate regulatory action.”

To maintain its competitive edge, Anthropic has struck deals with the cloud computing giants Amazon, Google and Microsoft, as well as the chip suppliers Broadcom and Nvidia, to secure the A. I. infrastructure to advance the technology. The company said it spent nearly $9 billion on computing power and infrastructure in the first half of this year, nearly $2 billion more than it spent all of last year, and comprising half its total operating expenses.

The deals, some with competitors, led the company to warn investors that its “reliance” on partners, “some of which have strategic and investment relationships with us and are our customers, creates complex dynamics that could give rise to conflicts of interest and adversely affect our access to compute.”

The prospectus does not include details about Anthropic’s third quarter performance, which it previewed to investors at a private meeting this month. Analysts will likely watch closely for the company to update its numbers because the market for A. I. tools shifts constantly, with companies often leapfrogging each other in a matter of months.

Brandon Ross, an analyst at LightShed Partners, said investors were focused on “near real-time” results as they tried to project whether Anthropic could meet its spending commitments and grow into its valuation.

Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley are the investment banks leading the public offering.

Anthropic did not say how many shares it would sell in the I. P. O. or at what price. It will trade on the Nasdaq exchange under the symbol ANT.

Mike Isaac is The Times’s Silicon Valley correspondent, based in San Francisco. He covers the world’s most consequential tech companies, and how they shape culture both online and offline.

Erin Griffith covers tech companies, start-ups and the culture of Silicon Valley from San Francisco.

Lauren Hirsch is a Times reporter who covers deals and dealmakers in Wall Street and Washington.

Sri Muppidi is a business and technology reporter for The Times and DealBook, covering artificial intelligence. Contact her securely on Signal: @srimuppidi.13.

She Killed Her 4-Year-Old Daughter. Can She Ever Be Considered Sane?

The New York Times October 26, 2026

Lindsay Clancy Trial

Advertisement

Supported by

Marci Webber was institutionalized after being acquitted by reason of insanity for killing her 4-year-old daughter. For years she has said she is cured and should be freed.

By Shaila Dewan

Sixteen years ago, Marci Webber killed her 4-year-old daughter, Maggie, in the midst of a psychotic episode, then cut her own wrists. When Ms. Webber’s eldest daughter, then 18, found them in the bathroom, Ms. Webber told her, “Shhh, don’t wake the baby.”

She has been institutionalized in Illinois ever since, but for over a decade she has argued that she no longer needs inpatient care. In November, a judge will decide whether she can go free.

The particulars of Ms. Webber’s case are different from those of Lindsay Clancy, whose recent trial on charges of killing her three young children resulted in a hung jury. Ms. Clancy is scheduled to have a hearing to determine next steps in her case next month. But Ms. Webber’s case offers a look at what long-term institutionalization and involuntary treatment can mean for someone found not guilty by reason of insanity.

Ms. Clancy’s trial lasted three weeks, during which the jury saw autopsy photos and children’s pajamas, and even took a trip to the crime scene. Defense lawyers argued that she was insane, and persuaded all but one juror that she should be found not guilty. Now the prosecutor must decide whether to put her on trial again.

Ms. Webber’s trial, on the other hand, took one day and had one witness, a forensic psychologist. She chose not to have a jury. A judge in DuPage County, the suburban county outside Chicago where the killing occurred, found her not guilty by reason of insanity.

The result has been years of debate and hearings over the role of medications and whether she is stable enough to live outside of a mental health facility. As Ms. Webber has tried to win her freedom, the court has heard conflicting testimony on Ms. Webber’s diagnosis, treatment, behavior and what she says are attempts to force her to take psychiatric drugs.

Prosecutors say Ms. Webber fails to fully grasp the harm she caused, in part because she blames medications, not mental illness, for Maggie’s death.

Involuntary commitment for those found not guilty by reason of insanity is supposed to be for treatment, not punishment. In Illinois, patients may be committed for no longer than what their prison sentence would have been if found guilty — in Ms. Webber’s case, 100 years. There is no minimum.

In many states, such patients receive periodic assessments to determine if inpatient treatment is still needed. In Illinois, a patient may petition the court for release.

In phone interviews from the state hospital where she is being held in Illinois, Ms. Webber spoke of how acutely she missed Maggie. “She was everything to me,” she said.

Years of imprisonment or institutionalization, she argued, will not prevent more children from dying at the hands of their parents. “These mothers are trying to protect their child from something in their heads.”

Ms. Webber, an Army veteran, began taking an antidepressant in the mid-1990s when she was embroiled in a custody dispute with the father of her eldest daughter. Over the years, she was prescribed a host of other antidepressants and antipsychotics, along with a beta blocker sometimes used to treat acute anxiety.

Millions of Americans use medication to treat mental health disorders, and they are considered both safe and effective. A regimen involving several drugs is not necessarily a red flag — experts said it can be desirable in complex illnesses.

But Ms. Webber’s case raises questions that also arose in the Clancy trial, about whether a shifting regimen of psychiatric drugs can contribute to violence. Psychiatric drugs can have adverse effects, particularly when treatment is initiated, doses are changed, or medications are discontinued. If unaddressed, experts say, these side effects may increase the risk of suicide or violence.

Ms. Webber said she had experienced akathisia, an involuntary and sometimes torturous restlessness.

“What they did for years was add meds, switch meds and just continue on,” Ms. Webber said. “Nobody thought to say, ‘You know what? I think she’s allergic to this stuff.’”

Dr. Gerard Sanacora, director of the Yale Depression Research Program, said it can be difficult to tease out whether conditions like psychosis are the result of disorders or the drugs being used to treat them.

“These medications are much more likely to help somebody than hurt somebody, but that doesn’t mean that an individual can’t be harmed,” he said.

Ms. Webber was raising three daughters and attending law school in upstate New York when she became obsessively religious, attending Mass daily and traveling 100 miles to a prayer group on weekends, children in tow. When she spotted a praying mantis at a gas station she “rescued” it, believing it was a sign.

Her older daughters had been named after a sitcom character and a president. She named Maggie after Mary Magdalene.

In the Clancy trial, prosecutors sought to portray the defendant as manipulative and controlling, saying she had meticulously planned her children’s death as she had planned their meals and activities.

Ms. Webber said such evidence proved nothing.

“Planning has nothing to do with whether a person is psychotic and insane,” she said. “You will have things that you’re doing that seem totally normal, but on the inside — unless people ask questions — you’re not normal.”

In 2010, Ms. Webber was increasingly worried for Maggie’s safety, believing that she was the target of sexual predators, and moved the girl to her grandmother’s townhouse in Illinois.

Ms. Webber was convinced that Satanists had rented the surrounding properties, and that she was being followed. She kept a knife under her mattress for protection. She felt evil as a physical sensation on her skin.

On a trip to the grocery store, she remembers asking others, “Is there a pill we can take to end our lives if they capture us?”

“You think you can handle it,” she said, “You think, ‘Oh, it’s going to go away or something.’ Until it’s too late.”

Relatives noticed that something was wrong, but Ms. Webber denied it. She now wishes they had asked more questions. She is no longer in touch with her family and asked that they not be contacted, saying that they had been through enough.

In a recent interview on “60 Minutes,” Patrick Clancy, Ms. Clancy’s former husband, offered a glimpse into what friends and relatives face when trying to respond to a deteriorating mental state. “Mental illness has this ability to be tragically deceptive,” he said.

Ms. Webber was having nightmares and not sleeping. Her paranoia coalesced into “a firm, fixed, false belief,” and she heard a voice telling her that Maggie needed to be saved, she said. She wishes she had been involuntarily hospitalized.

Instead, on Nov. 3, 2010, Ms. Webber’s teenage daughter entered the bathroom to find her sister’s body and the words “divine mercy” written in blood on the wall. Ms. Webber had turned on an audio recorder to capture angels arriving to take her and Maggie to heaven.

In 2014, after the judge’s not guilty verdict and several years of inpatient treatment, Ms. Webber refused psychiatric drugs. Her psychosis did not return, a judge found. Still, in 2017, he denied her release, saying both Ms. Webber and the state needed to do more to prepare. She attempted suicide.

In 2019, that judge released Ms. Webber with a treatment plan, after expressing concern that the state was not treating her fairly.

She returned to her apartment, but prosecutors appealed the judge’s decision and won. After less than two weeks, she returned to the mental institution.

Ms. Webber says that her institutionalization has gone on too long and is harming her physical and mental health.

In one conversation with Ms. Webber, prolonged screaming could be heard in the background. It was a fellow patient who, Ms. Webber said, was in a wheelchair and calling for help.

“God, I can’t stand living like this. Do you hear this?” she asked. “It is the most untherapeutic place you could ever be in.”

Prosecutors have argued that Ms. Webber remains dangerous, citing the suicide attempt, “aggressive, unruly and hostile behavior” and rule infractions. They say that her symptoms improve when she takes medication and worsen when she stops.

Under Illinois law, the burden is now on Ms. Webber to convince a judge that she is not likely to harm herself or others, or would not benefit from continued inpatient care. Her next hearing is in November.

Because of an editing error, an earlier version of this story misstated the court’s decision in Marci Webber’s case. She was acquitted, not convicted.

We acknowledge mistakes in our reporting with corrections. If you spot an error, please let us know at corrections@nytimes. com. Learn more.

Shaila Dewan is a Times reporter covering criminal justice — policing, courts and prisons — across the country.
