Connections Coach

She made her name as a pioneer at Google, then as chief executive at Yahoo. Now Mayer is entering the crowded marketplace for A. I. assistants — and hoping to draw in more women with a product that tackles the mental load.

Marissa Mayer has reinvented herself as a start-up founder, with a team of 10 engineers — a fraction of the armies of programmers she once commanded at Yahoo and Google. Credit... Kelsey McClellan for The New York Times

Supported by

By Alexandra Alter

Reporting from Palo Alto

Late last year, Marissa Mayer was struggling with what felt like an impossible task.

Her daughter Marielle was turning 10, and Marielle’s teacher wanted three bullet points summarizing what made her special. Mayer — the former chief executive of Yahoo and a pioneer at Google, where she was the first female engineer — likes cracking a hard problem. But she felt overwhelmed by the range and complexity of potential answers.

So Mayer asked her personal A. I. assistant, Dazzle. Within a few seconds, Dazzle delivered an answer.

“It came back and was like, your daughter is empathetic, creative and an animal lover,” Mayer said. She thought it was perfect.

Dazzle is a new consumer tech product from Mayer’s start-up, and her first push into the competitive marketplace for A. I. personal assistants. With Dazzle — which analyzes images in users’ camera rolls to answer questions, perform tasks and make suggestions — Mayer is aiming to build an A. I. tool that can handle everyday hassles, like buying a pair of pants you took a photo of, or finding a birthday present for your picky spouse.

“A lot of what excites me is taking something that used to take you hours or minutes, and now getting it done in seconds,” Mayer told me at her company’s office in Palo Alto last month.

Dazzle may seem smaller in scope than the monumental challenges Mayer tackled earlier in her career — leading search at Google, or working to resurrect Yahoo when the company was flailing. And other people are using artificial intelligence to cure diseases and solve impenetrable problems in physics and math. Yet to Mayer, harnessing A. I. to tackle mundane tasks feels big.

She thinks normal people who are not tech obsessives — and busy women in particular — will be drawn to an A. I. assistant that’s trained on their visual aesthetic.

“Women, this is my own bias, tend to take more photos and are more visual, and so being able to work with A. I. in a visual medium is fun,” Mayer said. “It essentially understands your personality, your likes, your dislikes, because it knows what you think looks good.”

And maybe what overextended professional women need is an A. I. wife, an emotional labor bot that can plan a birthday party and knows when it’s Crazy Socks Day or Crazy Hat Day at the kids’ school, because it has photos of the fliers that came home crumpled in a backpack.

Mayer is rolling out her A. I. product at a moment when high-profile women in Silicon Valley are worried A. I. has a gender problem. Even Anthropic’s own Daniela Amodei, the leading lab’s president and co-founder, has raised alarms about A. I. becoming “a tool that’s just for the guys.” Women don’t use it as much as men do. The models themselves have been forged by a male-dominated culture and, some studies have found, have ambient sexism baked in. And there are very few women leading frontier A. I. companies, which are shaping not only the future of tech, but the future of basically everything.

“I’m very disappointed in what’s happening in tech and across the board,” said Sheryl Sandberg, the former chief operating officer of Meta, whose organization, Lean In, has been tracking the gender gap in A. I. “There is deep cultural stagnation for growth of women in leadership roles. It’s a very scary moment for women.”

All of that could be fertile ground for launching an A. I. assistant that promises to shoulder some of the domestic load, a product that might bring more women into the world of constant A. I. users.

Building a life-hacking A. I. assistant is in some ways a fitting move for Mayer, 51 — who was once a widely recognized avatar for ambitious women trying to have it all.

In her nearly three decades as an engineer and tech titan, Mayer has shaped some of industry’s biggest innovations. At Google, she led search for a decade and oversaw Google maps, news and Gmail — products that changed the way billions of people use technology.

She has also faced intense scrutiny as one of the most visible women in tech. As the chief executive at Yahoo, she drew withering criticism for failing to revive the struggling company, and was often judged in sharply contradictory ways, as frivolous and attention-seeking when she threw lavish parties, or as too hard-driven when she worked during her abbreviated maternity leave.

Now Mayer has reinvented herself as a start-up founder, with a team of 10 engineers — a fraction of the armies of programmers she once commanded. And she is doing so during another technological revolution, as women in tech are once again feeling pushed to the sidelines.

Mayer said she is more excited than scared by the promises and perils of A. I., firm in her belief that artificial intelligence will help humanity and not destroy it, and in her conviction that eventually, women will rise in the ranks.

“I think gender balance will come in time, because this is a field that’s moving so quickly,” she said. “I’m generally an optimist.”

Dazzle’s headquarters sit in a bland, brown shingled commercial office building in downtown Palo Alto. But through the glass doors, it’s all rainbow hues and sparkles.

Small and cheerfully decorated, with whimsical touches like glittery rainbow sequin pillows, a foosball table and a giant teddy bear, the office looks like the set of a children’s television show, except for a poster with Dazzle’s mission statement: “To close the gap between what people want and what people can do with A. I.”

It was a sunny day in late September, the week before Dazzle’s launch. At an all-hands meeting, Mayer’s two chief technology officers updated her on design tweaks and Dazzle’s ability to search the web and make purchases.

“I know it’s a busy time,” Mayer said, glancing around the conference table. “But is there anyone who’s like, Wait, I need more on my plate?” she asked, drawing silence.

Mayer has a startling staccato laugh. When she’s excited about something, which she often is, she speaks in a frenetic rush, as if her words are racing to keep up with her thoughts. As we sat in her office, which is festooned with family photos, artwork by her three children, and knickknacks and souvenirs she’s collected, Mayer’s human assistant brought her a mug of tea, anticipating that she would need it during a long day of meetings.

“She never gives me tea, but obviously, I’ll take advantage of it today,” she said.

Mayer was eager to show me what Dazzle, which she called “one of my babies,” could do.

“The play dates are better, the travel is better,” she said of her be-Dazzled life.

She’s used it to find a family activity during a vacation in Venice (Dazzle proposed a Venetian mask-making workshop that the whole family loved); to plan a play date for one of her twin daughters (Dazzle knows Marielle is into magic, and suggested visiting a magic shop in San Francisco); and to choose a theme for her son Macallister’s 14th birthday party (Dazzle recommended a glow-in-the-dark pool party, and found glowing pool toys and corn hole).

“He was like, ‘Mom, I don’t want to hit the theme that hard,’” she said. “I just can’t help myself.”

Mayer has also turned to Dazzle for advice on what to wear, and asked it for Halloween costume ideas. “Halloween is very big in our house, and I’m terrible at Halloween, I never know what to be,” she said.

She held out her phone to show me the image Dazzle sent her of a woman in a gown shaped like a frosted layer cake, inspired by the famous cake paintings by the artist Wayne Thiebaud. (Dazzle knows she loves baking and art; she’s going to wear the cake dress to take her kids trick or treating, she said.)

It’s a tricky moment to launch an A. I. assistant, and not just because Mayer is competing with giants like Meta and OpenAI. Each week brings disturbing revelations about A. I. agents escaping human control; many people, one imagines, might not want A. I. loose in their camera rolls.

Even setting aside doomsday predictions about the A. I. apocalypse, there’s still widespread anxiety that A. I. is siphoning away what makes us human, shaping not just how we work, but how we celebrate life’s milestones and spend our leisure time.

To Mayer, outsourcing some of the mental load to the machines isn’t a bad thing. (At one point, she mused enthusiastically about the potential efficiency gains of having her A. I. assistant talk directly to her husband’s A. I. assistant).

Emotional labor, after all, is still labor.

“A lot of these things, like figuring out what you want to be for Halloween, figuring out the theme for your child’s birthday party, they should be fun, but in many cases, they become such a chore and so time consuming,” she said.

When I asked Mayer if it’s somewhat depressing to imagine a frictionless future when birthday celebrations, holiday gifts and family vacations are planned by A. I., she seemed caught off guard.

“I haven’t really thought that through,” she said.

Long before the A. I. boom, Mayer was fascinated by the promise of artificial intelligence, which she studied as a computer science major at Stanford.

At the time, there were few women in her field, and Silicon Valley had a “bro culture,” she said. Still, as an engineer who describes herself as “data driven maybe to a fault,” Mayer thrived. In 1999, she became the 20th hire at Google, where she eventually oversaw a team of thousands of engineers.

“I don’t remember her as someone who was constantly evangelizing for women at Google, but behind the scenes she was very conscious of hiring women and helping the women that worked for her,” said Jonathan Rosenberg, an adviser at Alphabet who worked with Mayer at Google.

When Mayer was tapped to lead Yahoo in 2012, her appointment was hailed as a breakthrough for women in tech, and for women in general. Then she announced that she and her husband, the venture capitalist Zachary Bogue, were expecting their first child. Once again, Mayer was an unwitting pioneer — as the first pregnant chief executive of a Fortune 500 company.

The media frenzy escalated when Mayer returned to the office two weeks after Macallister was born. Her choice was endlessly dissected in the media, stirring up a ferocious debate about whether a new mom could successfully lead a floundering company, and whether a hard-charging chief executive could be a good mother.

A swarm of bloggers, columnists and even the a German government official condemned her choice. Outlets ran articles with headlines like “Is Marissa Mayer a Role Model or a Feminist Failure?”

Mayer mostly tried to tune out the backlash.

She did read one snarky listicle.

“The article headline was something like, five things that Marissa could do on the maternity leave she so stubbornly won’t take,” she said. “I was like, right, the company’s in total turmoil, I’m telling everyone it’s all hands on deck — but I’m going to go peace out for three to six months and watch soap operas and scrapbook at home. So that one was a good laugh.”

In 2016, after Verizon agreed to buy a much diminished Yahoo, Mayer took a rare shot at her critics, noting how “gender-charged reporting” undermined women leaders, largely focusing on their personal lives and appearance.

A decade later, it’s a source of bitter disappointment to many women in tech that the ascension of Mayer, Sandberg and a few other women to C-suite roles didn’t lead to sweeping change. Now, some worry the push to recruit and promote women has not only stalled, it’s been largely abandoned.

Bro culture is back: Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg lamented to the podcaster Joe Rogan last year that corporate culture has become “neutered” and needs more “masculine energy.”

“Even women themselves have decided that they’re not going to bring this up because the backlash is so strong,” said Timnit Gebru, a computer scientist who has spoken out against gender bias in the tech world.

Given Mayer’s history, it can be jarring when she says she doesn’t see gender inequality in tech as a pressing issue. She acknowledges that women are underrepresented “There could always be more and there should be more, I’ll leave it at that,” she told me. But she also maintains that being a woman isn’t a barrier to succeeding in Silicon Valley. It’s a position that seems to require some cognitive dissonance.

“To me, gender fades into the background. I talk about passion as a gender neutralizing force,” she said. “If you’re excited about something, gender doesn’t matter.”

When I asked Mayer if she worries about the apparent gender bias that’s built into A. I. models, and whether it can be fixed with so few women leading frontier A. I. companies, she seemed conflicted.

At first, she name-checked women who have become A. I. titans, like Fei-Fei Li, who recently struck an $8.2 billion deal to sell her A. I. lab to a chipmaker. Then her optimism seemed to waver.

“A lot of interest, capital, technology, is all getting concentrated in a really small number of companies, so the management of those companies starts to matter disproportionately” she said. “Selfishly as a woman, you always want to see more people like you at the table, making those decisions.”

But just as suddenly, her idealism returned.

“At the same time,” she quickly added, “I feel like it will happen.”

Mayer has an estimated fortune of $1.4 billion. After leaving Yahoo in 2017, she could have turned to a glamorous life of parties and philanthropy — or done any of the things on that hypothetical maternity leave listicle.

Instead, a year later, she started a tech incubator focused on artificial intelligence.

From the beginning, Mayer wanted to build an A. I. product that would catch on outside of Silicon Valley. But the start-up’s early efforts, like Sunshine Contacts, an address book manager, and Shine, a photo sharing app, failed to take off, and were scrapped.

The idea for Dazzle came from the defunct photo app, when Mayer realized how much information is buried in images. Dazzle functions like other A. I. agents, but it trains on images to build a detailed dossier of the user. With that information, it can answer questions and make proactive suggestions including by creating a to-do list called “Get it Done,” and an “Ideas” list of possible fun activities.

Mayer didn’t set out to design an A. I. assistant specifically for busy women and working moms, and she stressed that Dazzle “works as well for the guys” as it does for women. Still, she thinks Dazzle could help overburdened women who’ve been reluctant to use the technology, perhaps, in Mayer’s view, in part because of the technical expertise it requires.

“So much of what I see with these assistants, they’re quite technical,” she said. “There’s definitely a cohort of people, probably more women than men, that are too busy for that, and it’s also extremely jargon loaded and intimidating. So we built Dazzle to be more approachable.”

After lunch with her employees at a restaurant near the office — Mayer had a kale salad and picked up the tab — Mayer and Dazzle’s tech and design team gathered in the conference room. A young mother who described herself as someone who took lots of photos and rarely used A. I. was there to test the app.

The session revealed some potential flaws. Dazzle asked the woman if she wanted help finding a replacement for a screen; in fact, she’d taken the photo because there was a bee. Dazzle suggested the woman might like to go golfing. The woman is not a golfer.

Mayer noted that her own Dazzle had recently suggested she go golfing.

“I don’t know what’s happening with golf,” Mayer told her team after the meeting. “We should figure out why it suddenly thinks everyone’s a golfer.”

Other early feedback has been promising. Mayer was encouraged to see power users spending hours a day with Dazzle; some reported they were “interacting more with Dazzle than their spouse,” she said.

In the late afternoon, Mayer swapped her high heels for sneakers and we took a brisk walk around Palo Alto, past busy restaurants and multimillion dollar homes. She was planning to head home to have dinner with her kids, and then return to the office.

All the while, her Dazzle assistant had been at work in the background, occasionally texting her with ideas. It had found an indie folk rock concert and an immersive theater experience it thought Mayer would enjoy, and helped find a present — a pair of retro Nike sneakers — for her son’s friend’s birthday.

She wasn’t sold on the concert. “I’m not sure I’m cool enough,” she said. But the shoes were perfect.

Last month, I spent the day in Palo Alto with Marissa Mayer, one of the most prominent women in Silicon Valley, as she prepared for the launch of her startup’s A. I. personal assistant, Dazzle. I was curious to hear what she thought about the gender gap in A. I. use, the persistence of gender inequality in the tech industry and how she thinks about her own career as a female tech titan who has often been judged for her ambition. She spoke about all of that, in frank and sometimes surprising ways. But it also became a story about what we might lose when we hand over more and more of our personal lives to A. I.

Alexandra Alter is a features writer for the Styles section of The Times.

Why Some People Are Paying to Make Friends

The New York Times October 26, 2026

Apps that match personalities — for a price — have surged in popularity amid a loneliness epidemic.

Apps that match personalities — for a price — have surged in popularity amid a loneliness epidemic.

Strangers matched by the social app 222 spend a day together in New York’s Hudson Valley. Credit... Katie Orlinsky for The New York Times

Supported by

By Aruni Soni

Aruni Soni met groups of strangers for dinner through friendship-matching apps in Washington.

Last year, Alexandra Pitzer paid $290 to meet a group of strangers.

Ms. Pitzer, 33, had just relocated from Nashville to Honolulu for her husband’s Army job when an Instagram ad for a friendship matching app caught her attention. The app, Real Roots, organizes get-togethers for groups of women after they fill out a personality survey. If the women get along, they can pay Real Roots to arrange meet-ups with the same group for the next several weeks.

Ms. Pitzer clicked in, signed up and soon found herself at a brewery with eight other women. They quickly bonded, and she continued meeting some of them after the package ended, going camping and to the beach.

“I can see most of them being lifelong friends,” Ms. Pitzer said. “We have a genuine connection.”

Fueled by a loneliness epidemic and increasingly online lifestyles, more people are paying start-ups to make new friends offline. And friend-matching companies such as Real Roots, 222 and Timeleft are exploding in popularity as a result, each one generating millions of dollars in revenue annually.

The start-ups are meant to remove the strain caused by online dating and other meet-up apps — no profiles to swipe through, no schedules to align, no locations to discuss.

When they sign up, the apps’ tens of thousands of users, typically in their 20s to their 50s, fill out questions related to their background, interests and values. The companies consider unusual criteria like sense of humor, how you like to spend time with friends and if you like meeting people on the other side of the political spectrum.

Once users pick an event off the apps’ calendars, the companies’ algorithms kick into motion. Users are matched with a small group from all the people who signed up — based on characteristics like age and other answers — and told to meet at a predetermined location.

Sometimes it’s a designated table at a restaurant. Other times it’s a bus to a hike, a dumpling-making class or shuffleboard. Once they have paid, all they have to do is show up.

“I think our generation craves the in-real-life environment of meeting each other in a more intimate setting, without digital preconceptions,” said Arman Roshannai, one of 222’s co-founders.

The concept of connecting strangers in person has proved successful, and more start-ups have entered the market. In September, Tinder, the dating app, started a “Group Hangout” feature to help friends plan “in-real-life activities together.”

The apps are taking off at a time when about 67 percent of adults have reported social-emotional loneliness, in part because they did not feel part of a meaningful group, according to a 2024 study by the Making Care Common Project at Harvard University. About 45 percent of lonely adults said they “don’t really know how to develop close friendships.”

“I think it’s a fragile time in the world, and a lot of young people are also feeling vulnerable in a variety of ways,” said Richard Weissbourd, a psychologist and senior lecturer at Harvard and co-author of the report.

In August, 25-year-old Sylvia Le paid around $170 to attend a mountain day-trip organized by 222. Ms. Le, who works in marketing, moved to New York in April after growing up on the West Coast.

The day of the event, she went to a meeting point at Washington Square Park, after which she rode on a bus with her assigned group for an hour and a half. They hiked and had lunch before heading back into the city.

“It can kind of feel kind of awkward for me, sometimes, to socialize when that’s the whole point of the dinner, or something like that,” she said. “So having the activity just makes it more natural.”

That type of human connection was the reason Mr. Roshannai, Keyan Kazemian and Danial Hashemi came up with 222 as part of a research project in college to “crack the code on human compatibility.”

A year after the country had shut down during the pandemic, the students received a $1,000 grant from University of California, Irvine, to study whether personality survey data could help predict social compatibility. They got their friends to fill out surveys, then expanded the effort by recruiting other students.

After first connecting groups over video calls, the 222 founders started hosting dinners in their backyard. The project became a full-time job in 2023.

Since then, 222, which employs 27 people, has expanded into 21 cities and hosts at least one experience a day. The app asks potential matches questions like “What do you think about astrology?” and “How attractive do you consider yourself?” It charges $22 a month to match people and curate the event, on top of costs that may be associated with experience, like the fees for a yoga class or the meal paid for a dinner.

The company tripled revenue last year and is on track to quadruple revenue this year to the high seven figures, according to the co-founders.

Real Roots and Timeleft have experienced similar demand. Real Roots got its start when a co-founder, Dorothy Li, was looking to make friends after moving to San Francisco and hosted group hangouts in her apartment with women she met online. She decided to build the experience into an app, which was introduced in 2024. Real Roots, which arranges activities for groups of women from bowling to scavenger hunts, is in 120 cities.

Timeleft started a similar app to coordinate dinners with strangers in 2023, after several prior iterations failed, the start-up’s founder, Max Barbier, said. The app is now available in more than 200 cities.

The apps are not always a hit. Some users complain on social media that they did not click with their group or that the experiences can feel awkward and forced.

Alex Cheney, 34, attended several friendship-matching events in cities including Los Angeles — organized by apps like Timeleft, Groupvibe and Kin — over the last two years. But he did not form any meaningful friendships, he said.

“In terms of building a deep friendship, it’s almost something that you have to explore and co-create and build in real time,” said Mr. Cheney, who had also tried building a matching algorithm for coffee meet-ups. “I don’t necessarily know if it’s something that you can build into a matching algorithm because you might have a lot of compatibility on paper with someone.”

For others, it has proved more successful.

Lauren Valenti, an executive assistant in finance, tried a Real Roots meet-up in San Francisco in February. Ms. Valenti, 38, was single at the time and lived alone, while many of her friends had families. She realized she was stuck in a trap of dating for social connection.

At her first meet-up at a wine bar, she connected with two other women who were similarly the single friends in their friend groups. They felt so comfortable, they even talked about personal topics like freezing their eggs.

“It felt so good to finally see someone equal to myself and share that connection,” she said. She paid roughly $290 for the package and committed to a six-week-long series of meet-ups.

Today, she has a group chat with her friends from her first meet-up and sees them regularly. They also reach out to one another for advice.

“There’s one girl that I’m about to message and be like, ‘Hey, girl, I have a ton of clothes I’m trying to get rid of in my closet — they’re all yours if they want them,” Ms. Valenti said.

As someone who moved a lot in her 20s, I've thought a lot about how my generation builds community. To me, these apps are a clear sign of cultural push: People are tired of screen time and are actively hunting for "third spaces."

Aruni Soni is a business reporter and a member of the 2026-27 Times Fellowship, a program for journalists early in their careers.

DraftKings Faces Growing Pressure Over How It Targets Customers

The New York Times October 26, 2026

Artificial Intelligence

Advertisement

Supported by

In Congress and in several states, officials have been questioning online gambling companies about their use of artificial intelligence.

By Alex Klavens

DraftKings and other online gambling companies are facing mounting scrutiny as federal lawmakers and officials in several states have begun questioning them in recent weeks about their use of artificial intelligence and behavioral data to target repeat customers based on their losses.

In New York, consumer protection lawyers from the attorney general’s office have contacted former DraftKings employees to discuss the company’s data practices, according to three former employees who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss a confidential inquiry or out of fear of retaliation, and messages reviewed by The New York Times. At the same time, the state’s gaming commission has proposed sharp limits on how operators can deploy A. I.

In Louisiana, gambling regulators voted to delay a routine license renewal for DraftKings, partly to allow themselves time to investigate how the company uses A. I. and customer data.

And in Congress, three lawmakers sent letters last week to online gambling companies, including DraftKings, requesting details about their “V. I. P.” programs and their use of A. I.

The actions follow reporting from The Times in September that found DraftKings had deployed machine learning, a form of artificial intelligence that seeks patterns in data, to analyze customer records and identify those most likely to continue gambling and losing when sent promotions. Former employees who built those systems told The Times that they worried the technology would harm gamblers struggling with addiction. Regulators in Massachusetts and Michigan announced shortly afterward that they were looking into the issue.

What you should know about anonymous sources. The Times makes a careful decision any time it shields the identity of a source. The information the source supplies must be newsworthy, credible and give readers genuine insight.

DraftKings “does not use artificial intelligence to target customers based on losses and does not market to customers based on indicators of potential problem gaming,” a spokesperson said in a statement, adding that the company “values an open and ongoing dialogue with regulators” and that “regular conversations and check-ins with regulators are normal course of business.”

Senator Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut and two other Democrats, Representatives Paul Tonko of New York and Valerie Foushee of North Carolina, published a letter to DraftKings late last week, demanding a response by Nov. 5.

They cited The Times’s findings as well as recent reporting by ProPublica, which found that DraftKings granted V. I. P. status to a reporter deliberately mimicking signs of problem gambling, and other articles about online gambling by the Philadelphia Inquirer and The Guardian. They have also sent letters to FanDuel, BetMGM, Caesars, Fanatics, Kalshi and Polymarket.

“Sportsbooks are supercharging addiction, using A. I. to target users and keep them hooked on gambling,” Mr. Blumenthal told The Times in a statement.

Lawyers from the New York attorney general’s office have been asking former DraftKings employees about issues raised by The Times’s story, the three former employees said. The lawyers work for the Bureau of Consumer Frauds and Protection, as well as the Bureau of Internet and Technology, which has recently led high-profile lawsuits against social media giants, including Meta and TikTok, over addictive algorithms.

The extent of their inquiry remains unclear. The attorney general’s office declined to comment on the matter.

Separately, the New York State Gaming Commission voted unanimously this month to propose regulations that would effectively bar gambling companies from using automated systems to target customers with personalized promotions, or from suggesting wagers based on their betting history or losses.

The proposed rule will undergo a 60-day public comment period, possible revisions and a final vote before taking effect. It expands on a brief initial version that regulators released for feedback in March, which drew pushback from DraftKings and other major sports betting companies. In written comments in May, DraftKings argued that the proposal could result in “broad restrictions on legitimate business uses of A. I.” and that the technology had the potential to “improve the customer experience.”

Brian O’Dwyer, the commission’s chairman, said in a statement that while legalized sports betting has brought New York billions in tax revenue since the state legalized the practice in 2022, it can still pose a danger.

“I don’t believe anyone gave real long-term consideration of how quickly technology could be developed and used to extract as much money as possible from unsuspecting individuals,” he said.

In Louisiana, the state’s gaming control board voted this month to hold up a standard five-year license renewal for DraftKings and place the company on a four-month conditional extension instead.

The board ordered DraftKings to answer formal questions from its investigators about its use of A. I., and to submit overdue paperwork. DraftKings’ spokesperson said the board was allowing the company “additional time” to complete its application, which is “common in such administrative matters.”

The order happened during an Oct. 15 hearing in Baton Rouge in which the board grilled two DraftKings executives. Christopher Hebert, the board’s chairman, said that The Times’s report raised “serious questions.”

Paul Liberman, a DraftKings co-founder and president, acknowledged that DraftKings had the ability to track winners and losers, but denied that the company was singling out losing bettors.

“Most customers that play on the platform are not going to be winners,” Mr. Liberman told the board. He added that he preferred the phrase “spending money” — rather than losing money — because customers were paying for entertainment.

Bianca Pallaro, Jenny Vrentas and Walt Bogdanich contributed reporting.

Alex Klavens is a data journalist at The Times, building computational tools that power data-driven reporting.

Ken Paxton’s State-Funded Jet-Setting Draws Campaign Scrutiny

The New York Times October 26, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Mr. Paxton, the Republican candidate for Senate in Texas, has taken about 350 trips outside of the state since he was sworn in as attorney general.

By Beth Reinhard and Lauren McGaughy

Where in the world is Ken Paxton?

In 2021, Mr. Paxton, the Republican attorney general of Texas, and his wife left town for Utah during a deadly winter storm that left millions in his home state without power. When lawyers tried to depose him in a securities-fraud case in 2023, he was roving around Europe. And this past summer, in the middle of his hotly contested U. S. Senate campaign, a British tabloid spotted Mr. Paxton in Iceland and London.

Since his 2015 swearing-in as the state’s top lawyer, Mr. Paxton has taken about 350 trips outside of Texas with a taxpayer-funded security detail, including 25 to foreign countries such as South Africa, India and Aruba, according to a New York Times analysis of data from the Texas Department of Public Safety. Texas law does not limit Mr. Paxton’s use of state-sponsored protection to official business.

Mr. Paxton also has benefited from the largess of wealthy friends, who donated $730,000 toward his legal bills in the securities-fraud case and have treated him to hunting and fishing trips, airplane flights and lodging, and tickets to various events, including the Grammy Awards, records show.

Mr. Paxton’s Democratic rival, James Talarico, has sought to turn the attorney general’s lifestyle into a liability, repeatedly accusing him of exploiting the perks of his office to enrich himself. Mr. Talarico, a state representative, has dinged Mr. Paxton on his apparent affinity for luxuries big and small — from his real estate portfolio that includes at least 15 properties worth about $9 million to the $1,000 pen he once swiped from a courthouse security tray. Polls indicate a tight race in a conservative state that hasn’t elected a Democrat in more than three decades, suggesting that Mr. Talarico’s attacks may be resonating with some voters.

“He became a multimillionaire on a government salary,” Mr. Talarico said in a widely viewed social media post. “He takes lavish vacations in Iceland while Texans can’t afford the basics. Ken Paxton doesn’t serve us — he serves himself.”

Mr. Paxton’s campaign and office did not respond to that criticism or to questions about his travel, security or personal finances.

He has long denied any wrongdoing. Several of his trips were to conferences with other attorneys general. Mr. Paxton also has traveled frequently to Washington during a career in which he brought dozens of lawsuits against the Biden and Obama administrations.

Mr. Paxton’s allies say criticism of his travel unfairly distracts from his record battling for conservative causes.

“What does that have to do with his ability to take on the Obama administration and win cases?” said Bob Hall, a Republican state senator. “Ken Paxton has gotten the job done, and I think that’s what is important.”

Mr. Talarico has not reported accepting any gifts while in office. In a form filed with the U. S. Senate in August, he said he earned about $51,500 as a state lawmaker and about $33,000 from a consulting firm from January 2025 to May 2026. He also reported several mutual funds and a book deal for an unspecified amount. In a separate form filed in Texas, Mr. Talarico listed one piece of property.

Security costs for Mr. Paxton’s travel since 2015 have exceeded $3.1 million, according to state records, which do not specify whether a trip is related to his official duties. That tally does not include other travel-related expenses charged to taxpayers. He has visited nearly 225 cities, making multiple trips to destinations like Park City, Utah, and New Orleans. Security costs peaked in 2024 at more than $483,000.

Gov. Greg Abbott, a Republican, has also traveled across the country and abroad, with security costs topping $5.4 million since 2015, records show.

“Business or pleasure — security detail goes,” said Arnold Alejandro, a former member of the state security detail who protected Mr. Paxton and other Texas officials. “I don’t care if it’s the Bahamas on vacation in a bikini or Washington, D. C.”

A recent ProPublica investigation found records indicating a work-related purpose for only one in six of the locations logged by Mr. Paxton’s security team. Mr. Alejandro added that many politicians, including Mr. Paxton, mixed business and personal activities while away from the office.

“You schedule one meeting with a politician or state representative and then you go play — you have dinners, you have sightseeing, but as long as you call it state business, it’s business,” he said.

Chris Toth, who served as a top official of the National Association of Attorneys General for 18 years, called Mr. Paxton’s travel “incredibly excessive.”

“It’s beyond the pale of anything that’s ever been brought to my attention,” said Mr. Toth, an outspoken critic of Mr. Paxton. “When you are running an office the size of the Texas attorney general’s office, it’s very demanding, and there is a cost to being out of the office.”

Security for a 2017 trip by Mr. Paxton to Israel, which was organized by the national attorneys general group, cost nearly $75,000 and was one of his most expensive trips. Mr. Toth said Mr. Paxton insisted on his own security detail even though the Israeli government provided protection for the entire delegation, which included six other attorneys general. Mr. Paxton also traveled in a separate vehicle from the rest of the group, Mr. Toth said.

Records show the attorney general’s security team also accompanied him to Louisville, Ky., in May 2024, when Mr. Paxton was photographed at the Kentucky Derby with a group that included Tracy Duhon, an aspiring Christian influencer he is currently dating. Security for that trip cost $13,235. One month later, Mr. Paxton and his wife, Angela, separated, according to her divorce petition the following year, which accused him of adultery.

In response to questions from The Times about security costs for Mr. Paxton’s trips to Louisville, Israel and other destinations, the Department of Public Safety called the expenses “appropriate” and in line with the agency’s “strict standards.”

It’s unclear how often Mr. Paxton has traveled without Texas law enforcement, but a few foreign trips that were not listed in state logs drew media attention.

In 2019, he traveled to China with other attorneys general and met with government officials there, despite warnings from staffers about surveillance by the communist government, according to Fox News. In 2023, The Associated Press reported that Mr. Paxton went to Qatar for the World Cup.

Another foreign trip not reported in state security logs: Mr. Paxton’s excursion in 2024 to Dubai, where he celebrated New Year’s Eve with two fugitives wanted on federal fraud charges, according to a lawsuit and video from the party. Ms. Duhon also appears in the video and in photos with Mr. Paxton in Europe this past summer; she has declined interview requests. Mr. Paxton’s campaign did not respond to questions about who paid for the Dubai trip.

In a rare instance in which Mr. Paxton faced questions about his travel in a public forum, state senators grilled him in February 2021 about his appearance at the pro-Trump rally that preceded the Jan. 6 riot at the U. S. Capitol. Mr. Paxton declined to say who paid for his trip to Washington. “I didn’t spend money personally,” said Mr. Paxton, who had tried to help President Trump overturn the 2020 election.

Mr. Paxton’s security detail spent about $7,000 to go to Washington in January 2021, though it’s not certain that trip included the rally since the logs do not specify exact dates.

Robert Nichols, one of two Republican state senators who voted to convict Mr. Paxton at his 2023 impeachment trial, said elected officials should expect rigorous scrutiny of their travel.

“Most people would ask who is paying for these trips,” he said. “Why is he gone all the time? It’s not like he’s selling economic development.”

Shortly after he took office as attorney general in 2015, Mr. Paxton was indicted on securities-fraud charges. Because the allegations were not connected to his job, he could not use tax dollars or campaign donations to pay for his lawyers. Instead, he accepted hundreds of thousands of dollars from about 50 people, including campaign donors, for a legal defense fund. He relied on an exemption in state law that allows government officials to take gifts from people with whom they have an existing relationship, separate from their public office.

In 2017, a $100,000 donation to the fund from an executive under investigation for health care fraud led to bribery allegations against Mr. Paxton. The prosecutor handling the case, Erleigh Wiley, ended the inquiry after Mr. Paxton’s attorneys argued that he had an existing relationship with the donor.

“If you’re going to take down a big fish, you better make sure you can go all the way,” Ms. Wiley said.

Mr. Paxton later cut a deal in which the securities-fraud charges were dropped and he did not admit guilt.

His impeachment trial, in which he was acquitted, centered on allegations that Mr. Paxton had misused the power of his office to help a donor in legal trouble who had paid for expensive renovations to Mr. Paxton’s home. In the lead-up to the trial, one of Mr. Paxton’s top aides said the attorney general had asked him to review the donor’s case — during a call from a Mexican resort town.

“He always cared about what trip he was going on, who was taking him to dinner,” the aide, Blake Brickman, told investigators for the Texas House. “He likes the perks of the office.”

Other high-level staffers also described what they said was Mr. Paxton’s penchant for freeloading during the investigation that led to his impeachment. David Maxwell, Mr. Paxton’s director of law enforcement, accused the attorney general of charging a $600 sport coat in a hotel gift shop to a conference organizer. “He always had his hand out,” Mr. Maxwell said.

As criticism of his lifestyle has mounted during the Senate campaign, Mr. Paxton has tried to remind voters of his humble upbringing as the son of an Air Force pilot.

“Growing up, we lived in a white trailer with no air conditioning outside of an Air Force base,” Mr. Paxton said at the Republican Party’s convention in Dallas last month. “We didn’t have much but I learned more about service to my country in that trailer than I did in any classroom.”

Now, his real estate holdings — the target of attacks by Mr. Talarico — include four condominiums at a luxury resort in Utah, three homes in Florida and a plot of land in Hawaii.

And photos on social media offer a glimpse of his cross-country travel, including a black-tie charity event in Palm Beach, Fla., and a luxury golf resort in South Carolina.

During Mr. Trump’s inauguration in January 2025, a men’s clothing store near Dallas, Lombardo Custom Apparel, posted a photo of Mr. Paxton in a tuxedo.

“We started doing his clothes a couple years ago as he started to build a pretty nice wardrobe,” said the owner, Jay Lombardo. “He’s trying to look the part as he runs for office.”

Beth Reinhard is an investigative reporter for The Times covering politics.

Lauren McGaughy is the Texas politics correspondent for The New York Times, writing about the ways that policymakers in the second largest state are changing lives for their citizens and influencing American politics.

Meet Anthropic’s Seven Founders as It Prepares to Go Public

The New York Times October 26, 2026

Artificial Intelligence

Advertisement

Supported by

Former OpenAI employees started the company in 2021 after disagreements over how to safely build artificial intelligence. An I. P. O. could make them billionaires.

By Emmy Martin

Reporting from San Francisco

Anthropic, the artificial intelligence company behind the Claude chatbot, is preparing to go public in a debut that could value it at $2 trillion and become the largest-ever initial public offering. That would turn the San Francisco start-up’s seven founders, who left OpenAI to create Anthropic in 2021 after disagreements with OpenAI executives over how A. I. should be built, into the latest tech billionaires.

Here’s a who’s who of Anthropic’s founders:

Dr. Amodei, 43, is the chief executive of Anthropic. In the past year, he clashed with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth over the use of A. I. in autonomous lethal weapons and for mass domestic surveillance, and has been at odds with other tech leaders over whether A. I. should be openly shared or tightly controlled.

In a 3,800-word essay in September, Dr. Amodei called for a global slowdown of A. I. development. Weeks later, he had a private dinner with President Trump and attended a luncheon the president hosted with other A. I. leaders.

Dr. Amodei grew up in San Francisco’s Mission District with his younger sister, Daniela, who is also an Anthropic founder. Their father, who died when Dr. Amodei was in his early 20s, was a leather craftsman, and their mother managed renovation projects for libraries in San Francisco and Berkeley, Calif. The siblings attended Lowell High School in San Francisco.

Dr. Amodei studied physics at the California Institute of Technology and transferred to Stanford to finish his undergraduate degree. He attended Princeton for a doctorate in biophysics and computational neuroscience as a Hertz fellow and later returned to the Bay Area as a postdoctoral researcher focused on “trying to improve diagnostics and curing cancer” at Stanford’s School of Medicine, he told The New York Times’s Ross Douthat in February.

In 2014, Dr. Amodei joined the Chinese internet company Baidu as a researcher, before moving to Google and then OpenAI in 2016. At OpenAI, he had roles including vice president of research, leading the development of large language models like GPT-2 and GPT-3.

Ms. Amodei, 39, is the president of Anthropic. She manages business operations and the company’s executive leadership.

“Dario and I have been fighting and getting over it for almost 40 years because he’s my brother and I used to steal his toys,” she said at the Stanford Graduate School of Business in May. “So we know how to work through conflict together.”

Ms. Amodei attended the University of California, Santa Cruz, for a degree in English literature. She worked in global development in Maryland and Uganda, then on Matt Cartwright’s successful Democratic campaign for a U. S. House seat in Pennsylvania in 2012 and in communications for his office in Washington.

In 2013, Ms. Amodei returned to San Francisco for a recruiting job at the payments company Stripe, then rose to the head of risk operations. She joined OpenAI in 2018 as an engineering manager, later becoming vice president of people and then, in 2020, vice president of safety and policy. Her husband, Holden Karnofsky, was one of the founders of the effective altruist movement, in which philanthropists seek to maximize the positive impact of their giving. As adults, the Amodei siblings once lived together in a San Francisco group house.

Dr. Kaplan, 42, is Anthropic’s chief science officer. He helped develop the company’s method of training models to align with a set of written policies and principles, called “constitutional” A. I.

Dr. Kaplan went to the Illinois Mathematics and Science Academy outside Chicago. At a start-up event last year, he said he had become curious about physics because his mother was a science fiction author. He studied physics and math at Stanford and earned a Ph. D. in physics from Harvard. Dr. Kaplan met Dr. Amodei in the mid-2000s while car-pooling to an event for the Hertz fellowship, which both received in graduate school.

“We mostly spent the car ride talking about philanthropy,” Dr. Kaplan said at a Hertz Foundation event last year.

He did postdoctoral research at the SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory before working as an associate professor at Johns Hopkins University. He joined OpenAI as research consultant in 2019.

Dr. McCandlish, 36, is the chief architect of Anthropic. Among other things, he focuses on large-scale model training. Before taking that position in October, he was chief technology officer.

Dr. McCandlish studied math and physics at Brandeis, earning a master’s degree in physics. His Ph. D. at Stanford focused on theoretical and mathematical physics. He later worked as a postdoctoral fellow at Boston University. In 2018, he joined OpenAI as a safety fellow and was a member of the technical staff building GPT-3 and Codex, a coding and productivity tool.

“None of us wanted to found a company — we just felt like it was our duty,” he said in a round-table discussion with the other founders posted on Anthropic’s YouTube channel in 2024.

Mr. Brown, 39, is Anthropic’s chief compute officer. He oversees the computing infrastructure used to train the company’s A. I. models. A public advocate for data center expansion, he recently helped lead negotiations with the federal government after the administration told the company to suspend foreign nationals’ access to its most advanced A. I. models, Fable 5 and Mythos 5. He, along with Dr. Amodei, attended a luncheon to discuss A. I. safety with Mr. Trump and other A. I. leaders at the White House in September.

Mr. Brown grew up in San Francisco and earned his bachelor’s and master’s degrees in engineering at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, studying computer science and cognitive sciences. He worked at and founded a few start-ups and joined OpenAI in 2016 as one of the first 20 employees. He then left for Google but returned to OpenAI in 2018 as research engineering lead.

Mr. Brown previously lived in a group house in San Francisco called Archive, along with Amanda Askell, Anthropic’s resident philosopher, and Benjamin Mann, who co-leads the company’s Labs team, which tests experimental products.

Mr. Clark, 38, was head of policy at Anthropic but moved into a new role in March as the head of public benefit. In this role, he started the Anthropic Institute, an internal think tank focused on A. I.’s societal, economic and security impacts.

He grew up in Brighton, England, and attended Varndean School, Varndean College and then the University of East Anglia, where he studied English literature and wrote for the student newspaper. Mr. Clark then worked as a technology journalist, writing for The Register and Bloomberg. While a journalist, he met Dr. Amodei in 2015 at a conference, he said in the discussion posted on Anthropic’s YouTube channel.

Mr. Clark joined OpenAI in 2016 to run strategy and communications and then became the policy director. He writes a weekly newsletter about A. I. called Import AI.

Mr. Olah, 34, is Anthropic’s interpretability research lead. He works on reverse-engineering artificial neural networks into human-understandable algorithms, according to his personal website. In May, he joined Pope Leo XIV at the Vatican for his encyclical, which called for protections against the rise of A. I. At the presentation, Mr. Olah made a seven-minute speech urging the world to scrutinize A. I. development and “tell the labs when we are failing.”

Mr. Olah grew up in Toronto and went to the private Abelard School. He was selected as a Thiel Foundation fellow at 19 and received $100,000 to launch independent machine learning and neural network research.

He worked on a 3-D-printing start-up and interned at Google before joining the company full time in 2015. At Google, he sat next to Dr. Amodei and also worked with Mr. Brown. In 2016, Mr. Olah co-founded Distill, a peer-reviewed journal about machine learning.

In 2018, he joined OpenAI, where he led interpretability research to understand and explain the inner workings and decision-making processes of A. I. systems.

Emmy Martin is a reporter covering the technology industry from San Francisco and a member of the 2026-27 Times Fellowship class.

Connections: Sports Edition

Connections: Soccer Edition

Connections Coach

OpinionLydia Polgreen

Protests in New Delhi on Oct. 10 and 15. Credit...

Supported by

By Lydia Polgreen

Visuals by Abhishek Khedekar

Lydia Polgreen is an Opinion columnist. She reported from New Delhi.

Narendra Modi, the barrel-chested strongman leader of India for the past dozen years, has finally met his match — and it looks a lot like Mohini Majumdar. Just 20 years old, slender and voluble, Majumdar is an English student at Delhi University: an unlikely antagonist for an omnipotent autocrat.

Yet early on Oct. 10, she shared an early morning taxi to the center of Delhi with a gaggle of classmates. Dressed casually in flowing cotton and sensible shoes, Majumdar and her friends could just as easily have been on their way to a stroll in one of this city’s splendid gardens. But their plan, she told me, was to march across the street to a place called Jantar Mantar, a historic monument at the center of Delhi that has for decades served as a designated ground for protest.

They had been there before, over the summer, joining thousands of other young people in raucous, meme-driven protests after a leaked paper led to the cancellation of a college entrance exam. Eventually, under the banner of the upstart Cockroach Janata Party, they forced the resignation of India’s education minister. It was the first time Modi’s government had dismissed a top official under pressure from public protests.

Now, they were back for an even bigger fish: Modi’s handpicked chief election commissioner, who had overseen the deletion of more than 130 million people from the country’s voter rolls in a murky process that threatened to undermine faith in the voting process in the world’s largest democracy. “These kinds of protests really prove that you should be political, and everything is political in our life,” Majumdar told me as she waited for the march to begin.

She never did get to march that day. A few minutes after I spoke with her and her friends, a column of police officers decked out in camouflage descended on the students, manhandling them into a waiting bus. The officers drove them 40 minutes north of the city center and held them in a police station until after dark, eventually letting the women go; only when they refused to leave did the officers also release the men.

So great was the threat these students presented to Modi’s rule that his government reportedly deployed over 50,000 security personnel to the streets, shut down dozens of metro stations, blocked long-distance trains from arriving in Delhi and threw up yellow steel barricades across the capital, leaving its usually teeming streets eerily deserted. Majumdar was one of thousands of people detained that day by the authorities in an all-out attempt to quash the protest.

Despite these efforts, Modi appears more vulnerable than at any time since he was first elected prime minister. Young people like Majumdar, educated, middle-class and Hindu — the children of a generation that rocketed him to power — are in open revolt, incensed by the government’s derogation of education and democracy. Willing to risk detention and the baton blows of the feared lathi, they are setting out to make Modi, who has carefully managed his image as a civilizational figure who will lift India into glory, an object of fun. Majumdar, undeterred by her detention, joined another protest the very next day.

“The moment you oppressed me, the fear was gone,” she told me.

For Modi, it is a stunning turnabout. For over a decade, his rule seemed durable and unshakable. His rise to power, initially inconceivable and then inevitable, was a foretaste of the world to come. Before Brexit blew apart Britain, before Donald Trump ascended to the American presidency, before an influx of Syrian refugees turned European politics rightward, Modi led the world’s largest democracy toward a vision of nationalist, right-wing populism, promising a civilizational restoration.

Today, India is once again in the vanguard — this time leading, perhaps, in the opposite direction. As Modi has consolidated his power over this vast nation and its sprawling state apparatus, many Indians have grown weary of the bargain he has offered: growth and national prosperity in return for a hardening authoritarianism. Beset as Modi is by crises within and without, his iron grip on power is clanging against the steel of India’s messy democracy. As governments struggle and discontent flourishes worldwide, the country offers a lesson for us all.

When I moved to India as a correspondent for The New York Times in 2009, I discovered a place brimming with optimism and ripe with possibility. Fresh off an election victory, the Congress Party formed a sturdy coalition government led by Manmohan Singh, a soft-spoken, teetotal technocrat with a Ph. D. in economics. Unfettered by its most irksome left-wing coalition partners, his government would be free to make deep reforms and get India’s economy soaring.

It didn’t work out that way. Indians saw their dreams of prosperity founder in the wake of the global financial crisis, while their government was snarled in scandals of grubby self-dealing. An anti-corruption protest movement sprang up, expressive of deep discontent that Modi’s right-wing Hindu nationalist party rode to power. Modi pointed to the prosperous state he governed, Gujarat, and promised to do the same for the rest of India.

Abstemious and devout, Modi offered himself up as a servant leader with no personal interests to pursue beyond the uplift of the nation. For many Hindus, his assertion of Hindu pride and even supremacy proved enticing. That he allegedly stood by idly as hundreds of Muslims died in religious riots in the state he governed in 2002 — his role in this tragedy led the United States to deny him entry for nine years — was mostly ignored by the public.

One of the voters who rolled the dice on Modi was a man named Surender Kumar. I met him outside a popular market in Delhi, where he was waiting for passengers in his motorized rickshaw. Back in 2014, he was angry about corruption and thought it was time for a change. He cast his ballot, with some hesitation, for Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party. But a dozen years on, he is disappointed. “The government came with certain kinds of promises during the elections, and none of them we see right now,” he told me. “Just to protect kingmakers in the government, they are letting kids be beaten.”

Though Kumar’s parents had been penniless manual laborers, he managed to leave their world of physical toil behind. Driving his rickshaw could net him between $200 and $300 a month, before expenses, a decent working-class living. But his son and daughter, growing into adulthood during Modi’s tenure, haven’t been able to make a similar leap.

Kumar could not afford private school or tutoring classes for them, so neither made it to college. His daughter studied cosmetology and opened a small beauty salon, but has struggled to make a go of it. His son works at McDonald’s, earning what his father describes as pocket change. Inflation eats away at his own earnings: The price of the natural gas that fuels his rickshaw has more than doubled, he told me. “You can’t name a thing which has retained its price,” he said. “Rice, cooking oil, mustard oil, cooking cylinders.”

Further up the economic ladder, among the middle-class Hindu families that make up many of Modi’s most fervent supporters, the struggle to provide economic advancement for the next generation is both all-consuming and increasingly uncertain.

In a sprawling, tree-filled apartment complex at the northern edge of Delhi, Shivani Sharma, a teacher, described a life that revolved around a singular goal: getting her 17-year-old daughter, Sanskriti, into a good public university and launched into a well-paying career. This has involved expensive private schools and costly tutoring sessions to sharpen her math and science skills in preparation for the relentless battery of highly competitive government-administered entrance exams.

“You have to have a very good score,” Sharma said. “Only then you can get entry into the Delhi University,” the prestigious school where she had gotten her bachelor’s degree in the 1990s.

For middle-class families, admission to a good public university is akin to a lottery ticket — the tuition is low and the credential confers real prestige. If Sanskriti does not make the cut, the family may have to come up with upward of $15,000 per year to pay for a private college. As it is, they struggle to keep up with her current educational expenses. In addition to running a school with her husband, Sharma earns extra money by tutoring children in the neighborhood. Her husband has a part-time job in a clothing showroom.

“We live simply,” she told me. “We don’t take international tours. We don’t wear expensive clothes. We don’t spend money here and there. We try to save money for our daughter’s education.” Sharma grew up in a big family, with five sisters and a brother. Yet none of her siblings has more than two children, she said. “We didn’t opt for the second child because I knew it’s very expensive and it’s very difficult to raise both the children and give them a good lifestyle and good education,” she told me.

Given the stakes, the leaked exam paper — expressive of deep corruption in the education system — rattled Sharma. “Some children committed suicide,” she said. “Only insiders can leak the paper. Who else can leak the paper? It’s a lot of corruption.”

Even a bachelor’s degree from a prestigious college is no guarantee in a country where graduate unemployment is at nearly 40 percent for those ages 15 to 29 and starting salaries are abysmally low. Food delivery drivers often earn more than entry-level tech workers with engineering degrees. To improve Sanskriti’s chances in life, Sharma said they are considering sending her abroad for a master’s degree. That would probably cost $100,000, an unfathomable sum that would require them to go into debt.

Young people across the country increasingly see this as a fool’s bargain, a debt-filled dead end. And they are not afraid to say so, loudly and publicly. Aditi (she goes by one name), the 29-year-old president of the students’ union at Jawaharlal Nehru University, is emblematic. Her parents are stalwart supporters of the B. J. P. But like many members of Gen Z, she rejects the empty promises of Hindu nationalism. “People have gotten bored with Modi’s narrative,” she told me. “Young people have tasted blood.”

Modi’s government has faced down discontent before. In 2019, a new citizenship law that targeted Muslims was rightly seen as an affront to India’s foundational ideal of secularism, enshrined in its constitution. But Modi was mostly able to wave that away as minority special pleading. Protests the next year by farmers, heavily drawn from India’s Sikh minority, could be dismissed as separatist agitation, even as the government mostly ceded to the farmers’ demands.

But this time, the protests have been driven in part by the concerns of the aspirational Hindu families that are the bedrock of Modi’s coalition. For many of these Indians, it may have been possible to ignore the ugly aspects of Modi’s rule, indeed to retreat from politics altogether and focus on building futures for themselves and their children. But many are realizing that all their hard work can be scuppered by a purloined exam answer sheet; by the devaluation of college degrees, which command little premium in an oversupplied labor market; and by a compromised election commission that could silence their most fundamental individual choice in a country of over 1.4 billion people.

Modi’s centralization — the very thing that seemed destined to consolidate his power — has become a booby trap. He captured and muzzled the mainstream press, especially television news, only for an enormous ecosystem of independent and influential journalists to rise up on YouTube and Instagram. He centralized the process of college examinations, leaving him no one else to blame when evidence of systemic leaking of exam papers emerged. His control over the election commission has left him with few options when faced with difficult questions over deleted voters.

Modi has also discovered that despite his efforts to project global leadership, his power quickly fades at the water’s edge. After promising to elevate India to great-power status, he has found himself stuck, subject to the mundane gravity of global events over which he has little control. He has suffered a series of embarrassments on the world stage, especially at the hands of the Trump administration.

What’s more, the pressure valve of migration is tightening. On the upper end of society, the dream of sending a child abroad, especially to the United States, is dying. On the lower end, uncertainty in the Persian Gulf is making migrant labor there a shakier proposition too. For a country that is the world’s largest receiver of remittances, amounting to roughly 4 percent of gross domestic product, that’s a big problem. That’s before you consider rising prices for fuel and tariffs on exports.

There will be no sudden fall for Modi. Though leaders in neighboring South Asian countries like Nepal, Bangladesh and Sri Lanka have been swept aside by youth uprisings, there is little chance of that happening here. India may seem like a chaotic and cacophonous place, and in many ways it is. Yet India’s government has always changed through the orderly process of elections, and Modi will not face the national electorate again until 2029.

But something profound has shifted. Modi’s aura of omnipotence and serene competence has been shattered. The protests have transformed his main challenger, Rahul Gandhi of the Congress Party, as well. They have given him the chance to shed his image as the pampered and ineffectual scion of a storied political dynasty. The political landscape, settled for so long, is suddenly altered.

India’s democracy has always been improbable. It is a society of boggling diversity and deep divides of religion, ethnicity and caste. Inequality, always pervasive, has deepened as the country has grown richer in ragged, uneven ways. And yet its constitutional democracy has endured, with the brief exception of Indira Gandhi’s emergency rule, since its independence from Britain nearly eight decades ago.

It is telling that this unexpected challenge to Modi’s power was catalyzed by affronts to two fundamental features of Indian democracy. As the political scientist Pratap Bhanu Mehta explained to me, taking exams and voting in elections are perhaps the two most important pillars of individual agency in India. Each contains the possibility of self-actualization, something that can seem nearly impossible in a country that is simultaneously so multitudinous and so hierarchical.

Exams hold the promise that anyone from anywhere, with enough hard work, can improve his or her station in life. Even more fundamental, if diffuse, is the individual franchise, which carries the notion that each citizen has an equal role in choosing who governs India. These two pillars, Mehta told me, are “the self-conscious revolt against caste, kinship, religion.” This is perhaps why copies of the Indian Constitution have figured so prominently in the protests, along with images of its main architect, Bhimrao Ramji Ambedkar.

It is easy to harbor romantic notions about Indian democracy. It is a project never before attempted in human history — for so many people with so much diversity to live together by common assent, under a written constitution that guarantees rights for all. For the past 12 years, India has engaged in a different experiment, one all too willing to brush aside the unfulfilled aspirations of the Constitution in the name of material progress and Hindu pride.

But a new generation of Indians has risen up, insisting that the price of that trade is far too high. Armed only with witty slogans and astonishing bravery, these young people have revived their country’s glorious tradition of nonviolent dissent. As peers from Paris to Tirana, Milan to Madrid, take to the streets demanding radical change, they would do well to look to Delhi as a guide.

A progressive student party created out of a protest movement has just won the parliamentary elections in staunchly conservative, authoritarian and pro-Russian Serbia. After Hungary the second authoritarian regimen that gets toppled by public discontent in Europe. Whereas in France and Germany the electorate is leaning to the right to air their discontent, those who have experienced strongman populism want to get back to liberal democracy. Hopefully the same will happen in the US during the November elections.

Having taught young adults in Odisha, India, I can attest to the profound commitment they have to the ideals of the Indian state. Unlike the people profiled in this story, most of my students dismissed performative street demonstrations as insufficient to dislodge corruption, communalism, and pollution - three of the banes of India's quality of life. Rather, many put their faith in boring from within without a lot of flash - becoming teachers, police officers, civil engineers, civil servants, entrepreneurs - and returning to their villages to do so. I encourage you to cover their stories in a future article, as that may be where substantive change will occur.

Modi's platitudes and promisies of restoring old glory does not make up for the genuine aspirations of the younger generation that he has been unable to fulfil. The next gen is unwilling to take his empty words as gospel anymore. His cult of personality is fading and past its shelf life.

Flurry of Diplomacy in Iran as Regional Countries Try to Stave Off War

The New York Times October 26, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan made a rare joint visit to Tehran amid reports that the U. S. and Israel were drawing up plans to renew their attacks on Iran.

By Erika SolomonVivian Nereim and Adam Rasgon

Senior representatives from Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan met with Iranian officials in the capital, Tehran, on Monday, amid widespread concern that the United States and Israel could soon launch fresh attacks on Iran.

Ali Bagheri Kani, the deputy secretary of Iran’s powerful Supreme National Security Council, said the meetings were aimed at promoting regional security, according to an Iranian state news channel, Press TV.

The visit is the latest in a flurry of diplomatic efforts by regional mediators to stave off further turmoil in the Middle East. American and Israeli officials are said to be drawing up plans to potentially attack Iran after the U. S. midterm elections next week, according to U. S. officials and others briefed on the deliberations.

Saudi Arabia’s conflict with the Iranian-backed Houthi militia in Yemen has also escalated rapidly in recent weeks as the two sides have exchanged deadly attacks, including on airports and oil sites around the kingdom.

Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan formed a new collective defense agreement, known as the Mecca Pact, this year. Monday’s talks are their first joint high-level meeting with Iran since the Saudi-Houthi conflict flared up.

The Saudi defense minister, Prince Khalid bin Salman, is representing the kingdom in the talks, according to a statement from Saudi Arabia’s foreign ministry. The prince is joined in Tehran by Pakistan’s army chief, Field Marshal Asim Munir, Iranian state media said, as well as Ibrahim Kalin, head of the Turkish national intelligence agency.

On Monday afternoon, Iran’s state broadcaster reported that the officials were meeting with Iran’s president, Masoud Pezeshkian, and the head of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, Mohsen Rezaei.

A day earlier, Qatari mediators visited Tehran to try to hammer out an agreement between the United States and Iran and stave off renewed regional war, according to Iran’s foreign ministry spokesman, Esmaeil Baghaei. Last week, Mr. Munir of Pakistan also made a visit to Tehran to help in diplomatic efforts.

A Gulf official, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss the negotiations, said the talks on Monday were supporting the efforts of Qatari and Pakistani mediators and were intended, in part, to urge Iran to show enough flexibility to reach a diplomatic solution with the United States.

Qatari mediators have been working on an agreement between the United States and Iran in which the two sides would make a series of concessions over a five-day period, two diplomats briefed on the talks said.

They said that, as part of the concessions, Iran would reopen the Strait of Hormuz, a vital waterway for energy shipping in the Persian Gulf, for commercial shipping, while the United States would lift a naval blockade on Iran’s ports that has deepened the country’s economic crisis.

The main stumbling block to that agreement has been determining when each side would make its concessions, the diplomats said. They added that the mediators have been pushing for Iran to offer a concession on its nuclear program in the initial phase of the agreement.

Iran has repeatedly ruled out giving up part of its enriched uranium stockpile, and last week, Mr. Rezaei vowed that “not a single particle of enriched nuclear material” would leave Iran.

Iranian officials last week signaled pessimism that an agreement could be reached and warned that if Iran were attacked again, its forces would expand their targets to data centers and underwater internet cables in the region.

The visit by senior Saudi officials to Tehran is a significant outreach at a time of profound tensions between the two countries, as Saudi Arabia contends with near-daily attacks by the Iranian-backed Houthis.

Sending Prince Khalid — the brother and trusted envoy of the kingdom’s crown prince — would appear to suggest that the Saudi leadership is intent on avoiding another round of war between the U. S., Israel and Iran, which could bring a fresh barrage of Iranian attacks on Saudi Arabia while it is also battling the Houthis.

For Iran, the visit by Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan on Monday is symbolically significant, as Iranian officials are eager to sideline the United States from regional security and diplomatic arrangements.

The Mecca Pact was signed in August as countries in the Middle East have sought new ways to ensure their security amid uncertainty about the reliability of American protection. That has become particularly important to leaders in the Gulf Arab countries, which faced a barrage of Iranian missiles and drones after the U. S. and Israeli attack began in February.

“From our perspective, the very fact that regional countries are seeking to establish, or at least contemplate, regional security mechanisms based on their own interests and considerations is a welcome development,” Mr. Baghaei, the Iranian foreign ministry spokesman, said at a news conference in Tehran on Monday.

Aaron Boxerman and Sanam Mahoozi contributed reporting.

Erika Solomon is The Times’s bureau chief for Iran and Iraq.

Vivian Nereim is the lead reporter for The Times covering the countries of the Arabian Peninsula. She is based in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia.

Adam Rasgon is a reporter for The Times in Jerusalem, covering Israeli and Palestinian affairs.
